title: Crapo Leads Bipartisan Legislation to Strengthen Idaho Water Infrastructure and Wildfire Resilience
text:
Washington, D.C.—U.S. Senator Mike Crapo (R-Idaho) joined a bipartisan group of lawmakers in introducing two bills to strengthen water infrastructure, improve wildfire preparedness and expand access to critical resources for Idaho communities.

The legislation includes the FIRE SMART Act, which would provide states additional flexibility to support drinking water infrastructure projects that also improve wildfire suppression capabilities in high-risk rural communities, and the Clean Water Allotment Modernization Act of 2026, which would update the formula used to distribute Clean Water State Revolving Fund (CWSRF) funding to states for the first time since the program was created.

"Idaho's communities rely on strong and reliable water infrastructure, whether it is delivering safe drinking water, maintaining clean waterways or improving preparedness for increasingly severe wildfire seasons," said Crapo. "These bills would help to modernize outdated federal policies and provide states greater flexibility to address local infrastructure needs.”

“Idaho’s small and rural communities often face significant infrastructure challenges with limited resources. These bills would provide qualifying communities with greater flexibility and better align clean water funding through the State Revolving Fund to address Idaho’s infrastructure needs. DEQ appreciates Senator Crapo’s effort to advance practical solutions that support Idaho communities.” – Jess Byrne, Director, Idaho Department of Environmental Quality

FIRE SMART Act of 2026

The Firefighting Infrastructure for Rural and Exurban Smaller Municipalities Augmenting Residential Fuels Treatments (FIRE SMART) Act would direct the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to amend Drinking Water State Revolving Fund (DWSRF) rules that currently exclude projects needed primarily for fire protection. The legislation would create a narrowly tailored exception for certain drinking water infrastructure projects that provide both drinking water and wildfire suppression benefits in rural communities at high risk of wildfire.

Eligible projects could include improvements to water storage, distribution capacity and water pressure that support everyday drinking water needs while also enhancing local firefighting capabilities. The bill does not authorize new federal spending or alter existing funding allocations.

Crapo is joined on the FIRE SMART Act by Senators Alex Padilla (D-California), John Curtis (R-Utah), Tim Sheehy (R-Montana), Mark Kelly (D-Arizona), John Boozman (R-Arkansas), Adam Schiff (D-California) and Jeff Merkley (D-Oregon).

Clean Water Allotment Modernization Act of 2026

The Clean Water Allotment Modernization Act of 2026 would replace the current CWSRF allotment formula, which has remained unchanged since 1987, with a transparent, needs-based formula developed through recommendations from a Government Accountability Office (GAO) expert panel.

Under the updated formula, CWSRF capitalization grants would be distributed based on a combination of state clean water infrastructure needs, population and economic factors. EPA estimates more than $630 billion in clean water investments will be needed nationwide over the next 20 years.

According to GAO analysis using 2022 data, Idaho would receive approximately 50.5 percent more annual clean water funding under the modernized formula. The legislation also includes transition protections for states, preserves existing funding allocated for tribes and territories, protects Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act allocations and supports improved data collection to better identify infrastructure needs in small and rural communities.

Crapo joined Senators Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) and Rick Scott (R-Florida) in introducing the bill.

Read the full text of the FIRE SMART Acthere.

title: Crapo Statement at Hearing on President’s Trade Policy Agenda
text:
Washington, D.C.—U.S. Senate Finance Committee Chairman Mike Crapo (R-Idaho) delivered the following remarks at hearing on the President’s 2026 trade policy agenda.

As prepared for delivery:

“Welcome, Ambassador Greer.

“Thank you for appearing before the Finance Committee to discuss the President’s 2026 Annual Trade Agenda.

“We appreciate you and your team working with us to reschedule this hearing.

“Trade policy remains a cornerstone of our nation’s economic strength, our global leadership and our ability to create opportunities for American farmers, ranchers, businesses and workers.

“The trade landscape has evolved significantly since you last testified before the Committee on the President’s trade agenda.

“Today’s hearing is an opportunity to take stock of where we are and where we need to go.

“Together, the Administration and Congress can build a durable policy and enforcement regime around a fair application of longstanding American trade goals.

“First, U.S. trade policy must reflect our strategic priorities.

“The Administration has maintained a firm stance in addressing non-market policies and practices that distort competition and disadvantage American workers and companies.

“The Administration also continues to emphasize rebuilding domestic manufacturing capacity and securing critical supply chains.

“Second, U.S. trade policy must reflect economic realities.

“Market access matters. It remains a fundamental driver of American economic growth. American producers and service providers depend on the ability to compete fairly in global markets.

“Unfair and discriminatory barriers to U.S. exports must be removed—whether through tariff reductions, the elimination of non-tariff barriers or the establishment of clear and transparent rules—creating opportunities for businesses of all sizes and supporting high-quality jobs here at home.

“To understand why, we need look no further than to the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA.

“USMCA supports 13 million American jobs; represents a 55 percent increase in investments in the U.S. from Canada and Mexico compared to pre-USMCA levels; and has led to $60 billion in exports in agricultural goods—nearly one-third of all U.S. agricultural exports.

“Third, market access must be paired with strong enforcement for USMCA and other trade agreements to remain effectual.

“Robust enforcement ensures a level playing field and sends a clear signal that the United States stands behind its farmers, workers and businesses.

“Fair market access and its enforcement are constantly tested by unfair trade practices used against our farmers and ranchers.

“Idaho producers often tell me about how these practices create significant economic hardships for our agriculture community, including among our dairy, onion, potato, sheep and sugarbeet industries.

“Meanwhile, a growing array of discriminatory measures in the form of digital services taxes, online content requirements and data localization target U.S. digital firms and restrict U.S. competition.

“These pose an existential threat to American innovation.

“Similarly, concerns with foreign pharmaceutical price controls are top of mind as the U.S. begins to negotiate pharmaceutical deals.

“Finally, business certainty in the trade environment is crucial for American industry to take full advantage of market-opening opportunities so they can grow and compete effectively.

“In all these matters, close collaboration and consultation between Congress and the Administration is essential to advance the policies needed to promote durable growth and fairness.

“A combined effort between Congress and the Administration is the most effective means by which to identify new opportunities for market access, strengthen enforcement tools and meet emerging challenges in the global trading system.

“The challenges and opportunities in global trade are complex, but they present a chance to strengthen our economy and reaffirm our leadership on the world stage.

“Ambassador, I look forward to continuing to work closely with you to advance a trade policy that delivers fair and open markets for the American people.

“Thank you again for joining us today, and I welcome today’s discussion.”

title: Curtis Bill to Support Next Generation of American Aviation Advances Out of Committee
text:
WASHINGTON—U.S. Senator John Curtis (R-UT) today applauded the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee passage of the bipartisan Aviation Innovation and Global Competitiveness Act, legislation that would improve the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) type certification process for American Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) aircraft companies to help them succeed and cement the United States’ role as a global leader in aviation. The bill, cosponsored by Curtis, was introduced by Senators Peter Welch (D-VT) and Ted Budd (R-NC).

“The Committee passage today brings us one step closer to modernizing the FAA certification process for the next generation of aviation,” said Senator Curtis. “This bipartisan bill will provide greater clarity and accountability, helping American Advanced Air Mobility companies innovate, compete, and lead the world in the future of flight. I’m pleased to see it advance and look forward to its passage by the full Senate.”

“Building on generations of leadership in aviation, American companies are spearheading electric aircraft innovation. That includes companies like Vermont’s Beta Technologies, which completed its historic, first-ever electric flight last year in South Burlington. Ensuring the FAA certification process is safe, efficient, and more transparent for emerging AAM companies like Beta is critical to promoting aviation innovation,” said Senator Welch. “I’m thankful for the support of my colleagues on the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, including my bipartisan co-lead Senator Budd, in helping this bill fly through to the Senate Floor to support American ingenuity, good-paying jobs in Vermont, and our global leadership in aviation.”

“By ensuring that the FAA prioritizes the certification of novel aircraft like eVTOLs, we can quickly incorporate innovative technology into the National Airspace System. I am glad that our common-sense efforts to usher in the next generation of advanced air mobility aircraft will soon be considered by the full Senate,” said Senator Budd.

Background:

AAM technology is a novel collection of technologies that will allow new, innovative aircraft to integrate into our airspace system. Emerging U.S.-based AAM companies are also paving the way for new and innovative electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft. Supporting the United States’ continued leadership in AAM technology development will boost economic growth in American communities across the country.

Since the introduction of the Aviation Innovation and Global Competitiveness Act, the Congressional Research Service (CRS) and the Government Accountability Office (GAO) have both released reports on the AAM certification process and actions that can be taken by Congress to promote aviation innovation.

Specifically, the Aviation Innovation and Global Competitiveness Act:

Establishes non-binding, standard expected timelines for the FAA’s type certification process for AAM aircraft for the Agency to respond to petitions for exemptions of aircraft type, and to develop means of compliance for aircraft outside of the existing types of AAM aircraft.

Sets transparent and reliable non-binding, standard expected ranges of time for the issue paper process, so that type certification applicants know how long reviews will take, reducing uncertainty and delays.

Provides the FAA with the sole discretion to exclude safety-critical matters from established timelines to ensure airspace safety is paramount.

Directs the FAA to define when an issue paper is required in the certification process, while providing flexibility for the Agency on complex safety issues.

Directs the FAA to account for performance-based rules in the certification process.

Directs the FAA to brief the relevant congressional committees on the status of implementing the certification regulations and managing workload.

Clarifies when the FAA can delegate routine compliance findings to qualified personnel, allowing Agency experts to focus on complex, safety-critical issues.

Updates delegation guidance for type certification to cover new and novel technologies related to AAM, including eVTOL aircraft.

The Aviation Innovation and Global Competitiveness Act is endorsed by the Aerospace Industries Association (AIA); Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association (AOPA); Airports Council International – North America (ACI-NA); American Association of Airport Executives (AAAE); American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AIAA); Archer Aviation; Association for Uncrewed Vehicle Systems International (AUVSI); Beta Technologies; Boeing; Eve Air Mobility; General Aviation Manufacturers Association (GAMA); Joby Aviation; National Air Transportation Association (NATA); National Business Aviation Association (NBAA); Professional Aviation Safety Specialists, AFL-CIO (PASS); Vertical Aviation International (VAI); and Wisk Aero.

title: Curtis Leads Bipartisan Wildfire Emissions Prevention Act
text:
Bipartisan legislation removes regulatory burden on proactive forest management efforts to mitigate wildfires

WASHINGTON—U.S. Senator John Curtis (R-UT), member of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee, led his EPW colleagues—including Committee Chair Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV) and Senators Jeff Merkley (D-OR), John Boozman (R-AR), Alex Padilla (D-CA), and Mark Kelly (D-AZ)—in introducing the Wildfire Emissions Prevention Act (WEPA). The bipartisan legislation would streamline states’ use of prescribed fires to prevent wildfire emissions, protect ecosystems and wildlife habitats, and make American forests and communities safer, healthier, and cleaner. It also promotes the efficient use of state air quality resources and provides certainty that states will not be penalized for taking action to prevent wildfires.

“If we’re serious about reducing the size and severity of wildfires, we need to stop punishing local authorities for doing the right thing to improve forest health and remove hazardous fuels,” said Senator Curtis. “By removing unnecessary regulatory burdens on prescribed burns, our legislation helps ensure states and localities can take proactive measures to help keep our forests and communities safe from the threat of wildfires.”

“I am very proud to cosponsor this legislation, which will help reduce the impact of wildfires on our land, our air, and our people,” said Chair Capito. “Wildfires have ravaged many parts of our country over the past several years, and change is necessary to ensure that states can successfully prevent the most dangerous and damaging fires. States should have the right to use known prevention practices, including prescribed fires, to mitigate potential catastrophes and care for their land. This bill gives states another tool in their toolbox, and will reduce barriers to successfully managing wildfires and protecting communities nationwide.”

“When the 2020 Labor Day fires swept across Oregon, I drove over 600 miles and never once escaped the thick, dark smoke that blanketed our state. As Oregonians face yet another record-breaking fire season this year, we need to tackle this crisis at every stage,” said Senator Merkley. “Our bipartisan bill supports more prescribed fire on the landscape—an essential forest management activity—while giving our communities the resources to plan and prepare for smoke events. Climate chaos is fueling more severe wildfires, and I’ll keep fighting to ensure Oregon and communities nationwide have the tools they need to protect public health and save lives.”

“In light of the devastating wildfires we now see far too often, Congress should do everything it can to encourage better forest management practices. Prescribed burns are an important way to prevent large-scale fires that threaten homes and property while damaging natural resources,” said Senator Boozman. “I am proud to join colleagues on both sides of the aisle on this legislation to ensure controlled burns do not generate an adverse Clean Air Act impact or penalize states taking proactive mitigation steps.”

“We know prescribed burns help prevent catastrophic wildfires and save lives,” said Senator Padilla. “This bipartisan bill cuts red tape so California and the whole country can make greater use of this proven, cost-effective tool to protect communities before the next major wildfire. It’s a commonsense step that prioritizes prevention instead of waiting to respond after disaster strikes.”

“Arizona knows the damage catastrophic wildfires can do to our communities and forests. Prescribed burns are one of the best ways to reduce that risk before a fire gets out of control, and states shouldn’t be penalized for taking action,” said Senator Kelly. “This bipartisan effort will help prevent larger, more destructive wildfires, keep our forests healthier, and better protect families from the smoke and pollution they leave behind.”

Background:

Utah fire seasons typically begin in July and end in October. Not even through the first month of the 2026 fire season, Utah has already experienced 594 total wildfires with 379,929 acres burned in 2026—more than the past three years combined.

While topography and natural weather conditions like a historic drought and an increasingly arid, hot climate contribute to an increase in the number of fires and their intensity, land managers can effectively influence fire behavior through proactive measures like prescribed burns. This reduces the number of hazardous fuels, the dry vegetation that catches fire easily—helping protect forests, properties, and communities along the wildland-urban interface.

Implementing these measures has become increasingly burdensome, with environmental reviews for even the smallest projects taking up to four years. Moreover, land managers can be deterred from prescribed burns due to existing environmental penalties. Yet, by avoiding these controlled burns, catastrophic wildfires become practically guaranteed and emit far more carbon than proactive management ever would.

The Wildfire Emissions Prevention Act would:

Make it easier for states and communities to use prescribed fire to prevent wildfire emissions;

Protect ecosystems and wildlife habitat;

Provide certainty that states won’t be penalized for taking action to prevent wildfires;

Promote the efficient use of state air quality resources; and

Make our forests and communities safer, healthier, and cleaner.

title: Curtis, Padilla, Tillis, Schiff Press Congressional Leaders to Pass Long-Term Disaster Recovery Funding
text:
WASHINGTON—U.S. Senators John Curtis (R-UT), Alex Padilla (D-CA), Thom Tillis (R-NC), and Adam Schiff (D-CA) urged Congressional leaders to include long-term disaster recovery funding in any supplemental appropriations package after the Administration’s recent emergency funding request did not include desperately needed resources for communities to rebuild and recover following catastrophic natural disasters.

In a letter to Senate Committee on Appropriations Chair Susan Collins (R-ME) and Vice Chair Patty Murray (D-WA), the Senators identified natural disasters that have severely devastated communities across the country, specifically the wildfires across Utah.

“This year alone, wildfires have already burned approximately 373,295 acres across 493 fires in Utah,” wrote the senators. “It is only the beginning of the peak dry season, with dangerous conditions persisting for months ahead, and Utah’s prevention and rebuilding efforts have barely begun as communities grapple with destroyed homes, damaged infrastructure, displaced families, and the looming threats of post-fire flooding, erosion, and watershed contamination. These devastating losses not only endanger lives and livelihoods but also impose enormous economic burdens through skyrocketing suppression costs, lost agricultural productivity, and long-term recovery needs. Immediate funding for wildfire protection, prevention, fuel reduction, and rebuilding are more critical than ever to safeguard the West before the season worsens further.”

“These disasters have caused widespread damage across California, North Carolina, and Utah, affecting federal and state highways, critical public infrastructure, homes, and buildings,” the senators continued. “The scale and complexity of these events will require sustained federal support to help communities rebuild damaged infrastructure, restore essential services, and meet long term recovery needs. Therefore, we strongly urge you to include long-term disaster recovery funding, like the Community Development Block Grant Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR), in any supplemental appropriations package to ensure communities have the resources needed to rebuild and recover.”

The senators urged that long-term disaster recovery funding be included in any supplemental appropriations package moving forward, emphasizing the critical need required to fully rebuild, as well as support needed for other natural disasters in Utah and North Carolina.

title: Daines to FERC: Reduce Red Tape, Build More Hydro and Natural Gas
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Steve Daines today spoke with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in a Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee hearing. They discussed the importance of streamlining the license and permitting processes for hydropower and natural gas.

Watch the full exchange HERE.

Daines on hydropower licensing reform:

Daines: There’s one source of energy that has bipartisan cooperation support, it’s hydropower. It’s a renewable source of energy, it’s great baseload power, it’s low cost. This week I introduced the “Hydropower Licensing Affordability Act” with Senators Risch and Murkowski. This bill makes a small but very important change to the “Federal Power Act,” because right now, resource agencies can put mandatory conditions on hydropower licenses. While FERC is the agency that grants the permits for non-federal hydropower projects, resource agencies like the Forest Service and Fish and Wildlife Service can set mandatory conditions on a license that FERC, you all, issue. This can also happen during a relicensing of an existing project. This process can be abused. Resource agencies can end up on a wish list of projects that have no direct connection to a hydropower dam. This bill is very simple. It requires all conditions to be directly related to a project. This just makes sense. In fact, this week I sent a letter to FERC, the Department of Interior, the Department of Ag, and the Department of Commerce asking them to initiate a rulemaking to address hydropower licensing, including mandatory conditions, under Section 4E and Section 18 of the Federal Power Act. For each of you, with 40% of the nation’s hydropower fleet being up for relicensing, 40 percent in the next four years, do you agree that we need to streamline and look for ways to simplify the hydropower licensing and relicensing process at a time when we are constrained as we look forward here? I’d just like to hear from each of you. Do you think we need to simplify and streamline it?

Commissioners: Yes, absolutely.

Daines: Chairman Swett, there are multiple large hydropower projects up for relicensing in Montana, including the Thompson Falls Dam. Will you work closely with resource agencies and push back against indirect or costly mandatory conditions imposed by agencies on existing projects?

Swett: Yes, we are spending an inordinate amount of time on hydro during this commission right now, more than this commission ever has focused on it, because it is so important.

Daines: Thank you. I mean, this ought to be the easy kind of licensing 101. There’s much more difficult and complicated issues in front of us, and thank you for your support to find ways to move this faster at time. We need more hydropower energy.

Daines: Chairman Swett, in May, President Trump signed my bill, it was Senate Bill 1020, to extend certain hydropower licenses for an additional six years. Could you give me the status of FERC’s implementation of that particular law?

Swett: Senator, I applaud your bill… We’ve received requests for extensions of construction deadlines under your statute, and we are processing them in accordance with the terms of your statute. We have not actually granted any requests under the new law yet, but that is simply a function of timing, and I believe that it is imminent.

Daines on expanding natural gas production:

Daines: I want to move to natural gas for a moment if I might. Montana recently built a brand new natural gas peaking plant in Laurel, Montana, just outside of Billings, to provide reliable and affordable electricity and maintain stability of the grid. This is the type of project we need to see installed across the United States. Unfortunately… We’re seeing long delays for permitting at the federal and even at the state level. I’ll keep working on the state level. You can help me on the federal level. Commissioner LaCerte, how do you see changes proposed by FERC, including updates to the blanket certificate program, helping to expand natural gas electricity production and leading to lower prices and a more reliable grid?

LaCerte: That’s a great question, Senator. I think the blanket programs, whether it be natural gas, whether it be hydro, I think that they’re going to allow us to focus on the hard issues so that the small issues don’t have to be litigated before us.

title: Daines to USTR Greer: Repeal Jackson-Vanik Trade Restrictions, Protect Montana Mining Jobs
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Steve Daines today spoke with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in a Senate Finance Committee hearing. They discussed repealing the Jackson-Vanik trade restrictions and the importance of countering Russian dumping of palladium and supporting Montana miners.

Watch the full exchange HERE.

Daines and Greer discussed Jackson-Vanik:

Daines: Ambassador Greer, welcome to the committee. Good to have you here. Last November, there was a historic dinner at the White House. We had all five Central Asian presidents and their corresponding foreign ministers. On one side of the table, I was there with the President, the Vice President, Secretary Bessent, Secretary Rubio, as well as Ambassador Sergio Gor. For a historic moment, they’re in the White House as these great Central Asian countries now are developing a much closer relationship with the United States. And as you know, geopolitically, it’s such an important part of the world in a very tough neighborhood surrounded by Russia, China, Afghanistan, Iran. And as we have discussed, and by the way, one of the top issues they brought up that night at that dinner was a repeal of the antiquated Jackson-Vanik provision. It is an embarrassment the United States maintains these trade restrictions associated with Jackson-Vanik on Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and now Azerbaijan. As of late last year, Azerbaijan is now officially part of what we call the C-6. What used to be the C-5 is now Azerbaijan as we’re pulling that group together as they work with the United States. This Jackson-Vanik restriction is an ancient relic of Soviet Union days. It long ago ceased serving any useful purpose. It’s become a barrier to deepening America’s relationship with this most strategic region. And again, it was the issue they brought up with President Trump when we had dinner in November. Ambassador Greer, I know you’ve been engaged in that part of the world. Very important. Would you support the efforts to repeal these antiquated trade restrictions?

Greer: My sense is that we’ll be supportive… I think if this process goes along with these countries agreeing to open their markets to us, then that’s a complementary effort that we could support.

Daines: Yeah, and this is tied to some Jewish immigration issues from the Soviet Union days. The embarrassing part of this is that there’s three countries that would remain after we get this bill through. And by the way, Chris Murphy is my Democrat co-sponsor on this. It’s bipartisan. But the remaining countries would be Cuba, Belarus, and North Korea. And this is the embarrassing part of the Jackson-Vanik provisions. We have these countries that are working closely with us now in Central Asian and South Caucasus. And yet they’re in the same list as North Korea, Cuba, and Belarus. So, we hope we can get this done before the end of the year, and I appreciate your support on that. I know Secretary Rubio supports this in the administration as well.

Daines and Greer on stopping the flood of Russian palladium into American markets:

Daines: Last, I wanted to talk briefly on palladium. There’s three chief producers of palladium in the world. It’s Russia, South Africa, and Montana. The Russians are dumping palladium below prices here in the United States. It caused 700 workers in Montana to lose their jobs at that mine. They’re under the assault of Russian market manipulation to knock them out of business. This brazen assault on U.S. national security and hardworking Montana miners can’t be allowed to stand. Ambassador Greer, would you support taking corrective action to end Russia’s market manipulation and ensuring we get Montana miners back on the job to supply this critical mineral, made in Montana mineral, no less, and support this industry?

Greer: I am supportive. Anywhere where there’s a distorted market, we want to get those fixed.

title: Duckworth-Hoeven-Durbin-Britt Bipartisan Bill to Strengthen Aviation Safety Passes Committee
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – Bipartisan legislation led by U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL)—a member of the U.S. Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation (CST) and Ranking Member of the Aviation Subcommittee—and U.S. Senators John Hoeven (R-ND), Dick Durbin (D-IL) and Katie Britt (R-AL) to strengthen aviation safety and support our aviation workforce by fostering transparency surrounding medication guidelines successfully passed committee today. The Aviation Medication Transparency Act would require the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to issue accessible, user-friendly guidance on medications that are safe for individuals holding, applying for or training for a position that requires an FAA medical certificate—helping ensure these individuals don’t unknowingly take medications that could put their careers in jeopardy.

“The careers of our pilots and air traffic controllers should never be in jeopardy because they weren’t properly informed about which medications they’re allowed to take,” said Duckworth. “This bipartisan, commonsense legislation would make it easier for members of our aviation workforce to take care of themselves without fearing for their job security—while also sending this important message to future recruits. Now that this critical bill has passed through committee, Congress must continue to show our pilots and air traffic controllers that we are invested in them by passing both the Aviation Medication Transparency Act and Mental Health in Aviation Act together. These companion bills would reform bureaucratic shortcomings within the FAA and put the health of these workers first, ultimately making our skies safer for the flying public.”

“Committee passage of the Aviation Medication Transparency Act marks an important step toward providing pilots, air traffic controllers, and other aviation professionals with greater clarity and transparency regarding FAA-approved medications,” said Hoeven. “By improving access to information and supporting timely treatment, this bill will help aviation professionals access the care they need while maintaining the highest standards of aviation safety.”

“No pilot or air traffic controller should be pushed out of their job because they unknowingly took a barred medication, especially as staffing shortages continue to persist at airports across the country, endangering our skies,” said Durbin. “This bill will bring about much needed clarity as to which medications are allowed to be taken by aviation professionals, ensuring they remain in these critical roles.”

“From our pilots to our air traffic control specialists, aviation professionals are working in a uniquely stressful, high-stakes environment. It is our role as legislators to help provide accessible information and resources for those seeking to enter the aviation workforce and individuals currently in these roles, which is why I’m pleased to see the Aviation Medication Transparency Act pass out of Senate committee,” said Britt. “I’m proud to champion efforts that support our tremendous aviation workforce and ensure that our air traffic controllers and pilots are provided with modern and accessible mental health resources.”

The FAA currently provides Aviation Medical Examiners with specific guidance on medications that are safe for individuals holding an FAA medical certificate to take—but confoundingly, this crucial information is not easily accessible to pilots, ATCs and other aviation professionals. As a result, pilots and ATCs with medical certifications may unknowingly take medications that could potentially jeopardize their careers.

To help make this information more accessible, the Aviation Medication Transparency Act would require the FAA to:

Publish within one year of enactment—and keep up-to-update—a comprehensive, user-friendly and accessible list of medications that are safe for pilots, air traffic control specialists and trainees, developed in consultation with various stakeholders.

Indicate what, if any, period of time individuals holding an FAA medical certificate must have limited or no duties while taking this medication.

Indicate a list of medications the FAA has designated as “Do Not Issue” and “Do Not Fly.”

Provide information for doctors to contact the FAA should they have any questions.

This legislation is also endorsed by the Airlines for America, Air Line Pilots Association, Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association, National Air Traffic Controllers Association, National Business Aviation Association, National Flight Training Alliance, NetJets Association of Shared Aircraft Pilots, Pilot Mental Health Campaign, Southwest Airlines Pilots Association and United Aerial Firefighters Association.

Full text of bill is available on Senator Duckworth’s website.

title: Duckworth Joins Blumenthal in Introducing Bill Strengthening Social Security
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) joined U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) and her colleagues in introducing the Social Security 2100 Act, legislation to increase Social Security benefits and make the critical system financially stable throughout the 21st Century. As our nation’s bedrock social insurance program, Social Security is the most important source of retirement income for 4 out of 5 seniors and provides vital protections for disabled workers and families who have lost a breadwinner.

“Protecting and expanding Social Security helps preserve Americans’ quality of life,” said Duckworth. “People who work their whole lives deserve the benefits they were promised. The Trump Administration cannot be allowed to further undermine essential programs that keep Americans afloat.”

“Social Security is a promise that must be kept. The Trump Administration’s threats to Social Security and skyrocketing costs require common sense steps to expand benefits and ensure financial stability,” said Blumenthal. “Bolstering Social Security guarantees all Americans a standard of living and protects the American dream.”

The legislation would increase benefits for current and new beneficiaries by eliminating the Social Security tax cap and by adding a tax on investment income for taxpayers making over $400,000. Additionally, the bill would utilize an improved cost-of-living adjustment to more accurately take into account true costs incurred by seniors and implement a stronger minimum benefit, so an individual who works their whole life will not retire into poverty.

The bill also includes provisions to fight back against the Trump Administration’s attacks on the Social Security Administration (SSA), including undoing staffing cuts made by the Trump Administration, blocking any future efforts by the Administration to close Social Security field offices and preventing DOGE and political appointees from accessing sensitive data systems at SSA.

Along with Duckworth and Blumenthal, the Social Security 2100 Act is cosponsored in the Senate by U.S. Senators Elissa Slotkin (D-MI), Ben Ray Luján (D-NM) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI).

The full text of the bill can be on Senator Duckworth’s website.

title: Duckworth, McCormick Lead Bipartisan Push to Renew ASAP Program Helping Make Transit Accessible for All
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – Ahead of the 36th Anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), U.S. Senators Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) and U.S. Senator Dave McCormick (R-PA) today introduced bipartisan legislation to renew the All Stations Accessibility Program (ASAP)—a program Duckworth championed in the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law—that is helping make public transit stations across the nation more accessible and inclusive for all Americans, including people with disabilities. Building on the progress made possible by Senator Duckworth’s program, today’s bipartisan legislation would reauthorize the first-ever grant program dedicated to improving accessibility at public transit stations, including elevator installations, ramps and accessible wayfinding, among other upgrades that make travel easier for Americans of all abilities and backgrounds. Companion legislation is being led in the House by Congressman Jesús “Chuy” García (D-IL-04) and Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA-01).

“For the last 5 years, the All Stations Accessibility Program has helped make our nation’s transit systems more accessible for all Americans,” said Duckworth. “Everyone benefits from more ramps, elevators and accessibility upgrades—and it’s long past time we help ensure Americans with disabilities don’t have to fight so hard just to go about their daily lives. Now, as the program is set to expire at the end of September, Congress must take action to renew this funding and ensure the program can continue doing what it was designed to do: make our transit stations live up to the promise of the ADA.”

“The All Stations Accessibility Program (ASAP) delivers federal transit dollars to a need that is too often overlooked: improving public transportation for those with disabilities,” said McCormick. “This is especially important for the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, home to legacy transit infrastructure in need of modernization. I’m proud to co-lead this legislation with Senator Duckworth.”

Before Senator Duckworth’s All Stations Accessibility Program was established by the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, more than 900 transit stations across the country still lack basic ADA-compliant access, such as elevators, accessible pathways and platform upgrades. Further, electronic ticketing, kiosks, notification systems and signage and mobile apps remain inaccessible to people with disabilities. The demand for ASAP funding remains substantially higher than available resources. Investments through ASAP consistently demonstrate that accessibility improvements are not niche upgrades, they are system-level mobility enhancements benefiting millions of riders and strengthening the economic and social fabric of communities.

Because of ASAP, Illinois received $185 million in funding for job creating Chicago Transit Authority and Metra projects to build ramps, install elevators and make other improvements to make the region’s public bus and rail system accessible.

Because of Senator Duckworth’s ASAP, the following transit stations have been awarded funding to improve accessibility, including:

Chicago Transit Authority, Blue Line Stations: $118.5 million to modernize the Irving Park, Belmont and Pulaski stations to make them fully ADA accessible and provide safe and convenient travel for millions of riders each year.

Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority, Station Improvements: $56 million to install elevators and ramps, upgrade general stations, and make path of travel improvements at the 11th Street subway station and Snyder station.

City of Seattle, Seattle Center Monorail Station: $15 million to make the Seattle Center Monorail Station fully ADA accessible, including installing ramps, making path of travel improvements for individuals with mobility devices and other station upgrades.

Metropolitan Transportation Authority, Station Upgrades: $254.5 million to make its Myrtle Avenue, Norwood Avenue and Avenue I subway stations in Brooklyn and the Burnside Avenue subway station in the Bronx fully ADA accessible, allowing safe and convenient travel to and through the stations.

Maryland Department of Transportation/Maryland Transit Administration, Martin Airport station: $7.1 million to develop plans and complete environmental work for the future renovation of the Martin Airport station on its Penn commuter rail line to make it safer and fully accessible. The station, located north of Baltimore, requires riders to cross multiple tracks to board the train.

Connecticut Department of Transportation, Metro-North Railroad Waterbury Branch: $29.6 million to retrofit three stations on its Metro-North Railroad Waterbury Branch commuter rail line, which provides service to New York City, to make them fully accessible to passengers with disabilities. Improvements to the century-old stations include building a high-level rail platform and installing handrails, which will provide more equitable service and increase access to jobs.

Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority, Green Line Improvements: $66.6 million to upgrade station platforms at 14 stops along the Green Line's light rail B and C branches that are not accessible to riders with disabilities.

Greater Cleveland Regional Transit Authority, Blue Line Improvements: $16 million to make the entire Blue Line accessible for people with disabilities.

This legislation is supported by: Access Living, AARP, American Council of the Blind, Access Ready Inc, American Association of People with Disabilities, American Foundation for the Blind, Chicago Transit Authority, Cure SMA, Disability Belongs, Disability Rights Education & Defense Fund, Easterseals, Epilepsy Foundation of America, Metra, Muscular Dystrophy Association, National Council on Independent Living, National Disability Rights Network, Paralyzed Veterans of America, Partnership for Inclusive Disaster Strategies, Pittsburgh Regional Transit, SMART Transportation Division Illinois Legislative Board, Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority and United Spinal Association.

Full text of the ASAP Reauthorization Act is available on the Senator’s website.

title: Durbin, Duckworth, Wyden, Sanders, Scanlon, Dingell, Simon Lead 100 Members Of Congress In Calling On DOJ To Rescind Opinion Undermining Olmstead
text:
Lawmakers to Acting AG Blanche: “We cannot return to a time when people with disabilities were denied basic civil rights, ripped away from their families, and institutionalized against their will… we urge the Department to honor both the letter and spirit of the ADA by rescinding this opinion.”

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee; U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL); U.S. Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR), Ranking Member of the Senate Finance Committee; U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; and U.S. Representatives Mary Gay Scanlon (D-PA-07), Debbie Dingell (D-MI-06), and Lateefah Simon (D-CA-12) today led 100 Members of Congress in a letter to Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche calling on the Department of Justice (DOJ) to rescind its June 18 Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) opinion that undermines decades of protections for disability rights that have ensured people with disabilities are not arbitrarily placed in segregated, institutionalized settings and instead can access services in integrated settings within their communities. DOJ’s opinion, titled “Application of the Rehabilitation Act and Americans with Disabilities Act to State Institutionalization of Patients with Severe Mental Illness or Disabilities,” would undermine both the scope and enforcement of the integration mandate under Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act.

“The opinion represents a dramatic departure from decades of federal law, regulations, and judicial precedent protecting the civil rights of people with all types of disabilities and must be withdrawn,” the lawmakers wrote.

In enacting the ADA, Congress explicitly found that “historically, society has tended to isolate and segregate individuals with disabilities” and determined that such segregation constitutes a serious and pervasive form of discrimination. The ADA was designed not merely to prohibit intentional exclusion, but to ensure that people with disabilities have meaningful opportunities to live, work, learn, and participate fully in community life as full members of their communities.

In 1999, the Supreme Court affirmed these principles in Olmstead v. L.C., holding that unjustified institutional isolation of individuals with disabilities is discrimination under the ADA. The Court recognized that institutionalization perpetuates harmful stereotypes about the capabilities of people with disabilities and severely diminishes opportunities for family relationships, employment, economic independence, educational advancement, and participation in community life.

“For more than 25 years, federal courts across the country, Republican and Democratic administrations alike, the Department of Justice, and Congress have interpreted and implemented the Olmstead decision to require states and public entities to provide services in integrated settings when appropriate,” the lawmakers wrote. “This long-accepted interpretation has enabled hundreds of thousands of Americans with disabilities to avoid harmful and unnecessary institutionalization and remain connected to their families, schools, workplaces, neighborhoods, and chosen communities.”

The lawmakers’ letter continues, “The Department’s recent opinion rejects this settled understanding and threatens to undermine one of the most important civil rights protections for people with disabilities. Notably, the opinion itself acknowledges that its interpretation is ‘out of step with common understanding of that decision within Federal courts.’ Such an admission should give serious pause before the Department reverses decades of enforcement efforts or undertakes further regulatory actions. In order to protect the civil rights of disabled people, DOJ must meaningfully enforce the integration mandate.”

The consequences of weakening the integration mandate would be profound. Millions of Americans with disabilities rely on home and community-based services supporting them to be among their families, maintain employment, pursue education, and participate in civic life. The Department’s new interpretation risks creating, supporting, and encouraging policies that steer individuals into segregated settings such as nursing homes, psychiatric facilities, segregated work programs, and segregated classrooms. Such a result would be inconsistent with federal law, contrary to congressional intent, and harmful to people with disabilities and their families.

“We cannot return to a time when people with disabilities were denied basic civil rights, ripped away from their families, and institutionalized against their will. The disability community has spent decades advancing the promise that disability should never be grounds for exclusion from community life. The integration mandate is a cornerstone of that promise, and weakening it would reverse decades of bipartisan progress,” the lawmakers wrote.

The lawmakers’ letter concludes, “The integration mandate has transformed the lives of countless Americans with disabilities by expanding access to community living, employment, education, and self-determination. We urge the Department to honor both the letter and spirit of the ADA by rescinding this opinion and reaffirming its commitment to the civil rights of people with disabilities.”

In the letter, the Senators request responses to a number of questions no later than August 5, 2026.

title: Durbin Questions Witnesses During Spotlight Forum On President Trump’s Nominee To Be Attorney General, Todd Blanche
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, today questioned witnesses during a spotlight forum hosted by U.S. Senator Cory Booker (D-NJ) examining President Trump’s pick to be the Attorney General, Todd Blanche. Durbin first questioned Professor of Law at the University of Pennsylvania, Claire Finkelstein, founder and faculty director of the Center for Ethics and the Rule of Law (CERL), about the conflict of interest involving Mr. Blanche’s cryptocurrency holdings. In April 2025, as then-Deputy Attorney General, he disbanded the National Cryptocurrency Enforcement Team and shut down ongoing crypto-crime investigations.

“Should Mr. Blanche have recused himself from the decision to issue his April 2025 memo regarding cryptocurrency enforcement?” Durbin asked.

Ms. Finklestein responded that he “absolutely” should have recused himself. At the time, he held more than $150,000 in cryptocurrency. Mr. Blanche denies that he should have recused himself.

Durbin then asked Perry Carbone, former Chief of the White Plains Division for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York, about the professional responsibility and ethical duties a DOJ attorney has regarding investigating industries if one has a vested financial interest in it. Mr. Carbone responded that proper procedure would be to divest or “get off the case.”

Durbin then asked Mr. Carbone about the “Anti-Weaponization Fund” and the lawsuit against the IRS in which Mr. Blanche signed an order providing President Trump, his family, and his businesses with immunity for any federal tax law violations prior to May 19, 2026.

“[Mr. Blanche] believes that he and he alone at DOJ can sign that immunity. What is your feeling?” Durbin asked.

Mr. Carbone noted that it’s “extraordinary” that any Attorney General would sign off on a settlement agreement.

“There’s going to be history written about this Administration and I think it will be extraordinary with its corruption,” Durbin replied.

Durbin then asked Liz Stein—a human trafficking survivor, advocate, and one of the most prominent public voices among survivors of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell—about the Epstein survivors’ meeting with Mr. Blanche last week.

Ms. Stein noted that they asked Mr. Blanche to speak about his interview of Ghislaine Maxwell and her transfer to a minimum-security camp, which is unheard of for a convicted sex offender. Ms. Stein noted they got “no substantive answers, he spoke in circles, and he evaded our questions.” She also noted “there seems to be no interest” from DOJ to pursue justice for survivors of abuse by Epstein’s associates.

Durbin concluded by asking Peter Carr, who spent nearly two decades at the Department of Justice, about Special Counsel Jack Smith testifying in front of the Senate Judiciary Committee. Mr. Carr is the public spokesperson for Special Counsel Smith’s investigation.

“He [Jack Smith] has agreed voluntarily to come before this Senate Judiciary Committee and answer questions under oath… [Republicans] owe it to him to tell his story under oath and [Republicans] refused to [bring him before the Committee]. The conclusion I draw is that they are afraid of what he has to say… would you comment on it?” Durbin asked.

Mr. Carr reiterated Durbin’s point that Mr. Smith has said publicly he is willing to come before the Senate Judiciary Committee and testify. He continued to say, “I encourage the Senate to take him up on it.”

title: Following Alarming Reports Social Security Will Face Insolvency By 2032, Durbin Calls On Congress To Strengthen Social Security Before End Of The Year
text:
Durbin: “The longer Congress waits to act on Social Security, the more expensive it will be [and] the more difficult the policy choices will be.”

WASHINGTON – In a speech on the Senate floor today, U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL) raised alarms that the Social Security Trust Fund will face insolvency in 2032 unless Congress acts and called on his colleagues to pass his new bipartisan legislation, the Protecting Retirement Opportunities and Maintaining Income Security for Everyone (PROMISE) Act, to initiate Congressional action on extending Social Security’s solvency.

“In 1983, we [Congress] faced a possibility where we couldn’t make the promised Social Security payments to beneficiaries across America… And so, [Congress] proposed a commission to take a look at it... In 1983, we raised the retirement age, raised the amount of money paid by employers and employees into Social Security, and taxed income from Social Security for the first time. These changes were not easy, and some were controversial, but we knew we had to do it. Our goal was to buy 50 years of solvency for Social Security with the changes in 1983. And you know what? It worked,” Durbin said. “It worked to the point where we just had an announcement last week by the trustees that the system will make every payment promised until the end 2032—50 years after the 1983 changes were made.”

The Social Security Board of Trustees’ annual report found that the Social Security Trust Fund will only be able to cover 78 percent of benefits in 2032—meaning that Americans who rely on the program will have their benefits reduced by 22 percent. In just six short years, the 70 million Americans who rely on Social Security will see their monthly benefits cut by an average of $450. Many beneficiaries have no other source of income, and they depend on Social Security.

“The obvious question from the American people—just those receiving Social Security today as well as those that will in the future—is what is Congress going to do about it now? … If you look at the agenda of the United States Senate and the U.S. House of Representatives this year, we’re going to do little or nothing… the bottom line is: the longer Congress waits to act on Social Security, the more expensive it will be [and] the more difficult the policy choices will be,” Durbin said.

That’s why Durbin introduced the bipartisan PROMISE Act—legislation that would create a transparent, fair, and bipartisan process to ensure Congress finally debates—and votes—on the future of Social Security. Under the bill, the independent Social Security Advisory Board would collect public input and send a proposal to Congress that would keep the Trust Fund solvent for the next 50 years, at least. That would begin a process in both the House and Senate to hold Committee hearings, offer germane amendments, debate competing proposals, and ultimately vote on them.

During his speech, Durbin noted that there have been various bipartisan proposals to strengthen Social Security but unfortunately none have come to fruition.

“If they [the Republican majority] believe Social Security is important enough to make it a priority, let’s put it on the legislative agenda when we return this year. Let’s give peace of mind to the millions of Americans who currently live on Social Security benefits and those that work every week and every month paying into Social Security for their own retirement in the future. This is not easy, but it is doable. I was part of that process many years ago and want to be part of it again before I retire at the end of this year,” Durbin said.

Durbin concluded, “We have the bipartisan starting point, the PROMISE Act—I want to see, I hope, a bipartisan vote to set up that procedure when we return in September [or] October of this year so that we get something done and give peace of mind to the people who are depending on Social Security for their future.”

title: Fischer on Senate Floor: Pass the Sanctioning Russia Act
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senator Deb Fischer (R-NE), a senior member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, spoke on the Senate floor in support of the Sanctioning Russia Act, which she is an original cosponsor of. The legislation will impose mandatory sanctions on Russia’s political leadership, financial institutions, and energy sector — putting economic pressure on Moscow to end Putin’s war against Ukraine.

Click the image above to watch a video of Fischer’s remarks.

Click here to download audio.

Click here to download video.

Fischer’s Senate floor speech as prepared for delivery:

M. President,

Lindsey Graham. Friend. Colleague. Tireless national security advocate.

He was a true leader in strengthening our military and our country’s defense.

I miss him dearly.

I am so pleased his beloved sister, Darline, now serves here in this institution.

She is carrying on his legacy and honoring his commitment to the people of South Carolina and this country.

M. President, I rise here today to, yes, pay tribute to Lindsey Graham – but to also call on my colleagues to help us carry on one of his greatest efforts: ending Putin’s barbaric and unjust war against sovereign Ukraine.

For more than four years, the Ukrainian people have shown extraordinary resilience and resolve. They have defended their homeland with courage that has inspired the world.

In 2022, Vladimir Putin thought he could seize eastern Ukraine in days.

He thought he could drag Europe back into the dark shadow of the Soviet Union.

He thought he would be feared and respected.

But he is neither strong nor powerful. He is a war criminal.

Putin has made clear his intentions to push beyond Ukraine and into NATO territory.

Russian drones have encroached on Polish, Finnish, Lithuanian, Latvian, Estonian, and Romanian airspace.

These were deliberate provocations to test NATO’s resolve.

Putin seeks to push deeper into Europe, to see just how far he can go before we push back.

That is why the United States and our allies must raise the stakes through tougher sanctions and a stronger U.S. deterrence posture along NATO’s eastern flank.

I commend the Polish, Dutch, German, and Italian Armed Forces for their swift and professional response in intercepting drones that could have killed innocent civilians during these incursions.

Their actions remind us that NATO’s strength lies in unity and readiness.

President Trump has made clear that Europe must carry more of the burden for its own security.

Poland, in particular, has answered that call, committing 5 percent of its GDP to defense. Other allies are stepping up as well.

This is the path forward: a stronger, more capable NATO prepared to deter and defeat any threat.

But make no mistake — Putin understands only one language: power.

And the surest road to peace in Europe lies in NATO’s strength and Ukraine’s survival.

Yet strength must also be economic.

The Kremlin’s war machine runs on the money it makes from selling cheap oil and gas to countries like China, India, and Brazil.

Those nations then profit by reselling Russian energy at a markup.

That must end.

It is long overdue for the financial enablers of Russia’s atrocities to pay a price.

They cannot keep fueling Putin’s war and expect business as usual with the United States.

That is why Congress must pass the Sanctioning Russia Act.

This legislation would impose mandatory sanctions on Russia’s political leadership, financial institutions, energy sector, and sanctions evasion networks.

By employing targeted tariffs, this policy would pressure the world’s largest purchasers of Russian energy to reduce their dependence on Moscow.

This bill gives the president maximum flexibility to enforce these measures, ensuring both legal strength and political durability.

I am grateful to Senator Blumenthal, who worked closely with Lindsey on this important bipartisan legislation.

And I am encouraged to see him carry this effort forward.

I was proud to be an early supporter of this bill, and I am proud to support this updated version now.

The Sanctioning Russia Act is the sledgehammer we need: decisive economic pressure that cripples Putin’s lifeline and hastens the day his war with Ukraine finally ends.

Peace will not come from weakness or hesitation. It will come from strength — military, economic, and moral strength — wielded together by the free nations of the world.

I ask my colleagues on both sides of the aisle to join our broad coalition in supporting this bill.

Let us carry on Lindsey’s mission.

Let us stand up to evil.

Let us bring freedom and security to the people of Ukraine.

Thank you, M. President. I yield the floor.

###

title: Fischer Questions Hegseth, Caine on Munitions Stockpiles
text:
WASHINGTON –U.S. Senator Deb Fischer (R-NE), a member of the Senate Appropriations Committee, questioned U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine on the importance of replenishing munitions expended in Operation Epic Fury and expanding domestic production capacity.

Click here to download video of Fischer’s remarks

Fischer’s exchange with Caine:

FISCHER: If we want to support Ukraine going forward, I think the best way to do that is to dramatically increase munitions production, and we need more interceptors. We have to be able to move forward.

Let me emphasize that this supplemental does that. This is what we're talking about here today. It's one of the things that we're talking about. As a member of the Armed Services Committee, one of my priorities for over five years now has been on munitions production. General Caine, what happens if Congress doesn't fund this $21 billion request for additional munitions?

CAINE: Well, ma'am, there's been a lot of work done by the department to partner with the private sector. I'll acknowledge some of the efforts that the private sector is doing to utilize their own capital to facilitate factories. If we don't, as a team, figure out how to properly fund the department, then we're not going to get the munitions, and there's going to be a lack of shared risk between the federal government and the private sector.

I think we're at a point in time in our history where we need to partner. We need to find an ability to share risk. We need to be better sellers and buyers on both sides in order to make sure that the young, all volunteer force has the weapons that they need before they are asked to go do something.

FISHER: You're saying we need to be prepared as a country?

CAINE: Yes, ma'am, and I hope, as I said in my opening statement, that we will find a way to make sure that we seize this moment in this time in history to ensure that we've got the right mix of munitions—high, low scale, autonomous.

FISCHER: What's your plan B if the supplemental doesn't pass?

CAINE: Ma'am, we will always figure things out. We will always have contingencies. We will always determine a way to create multiple simultaneous dilemmas for adversaries around the world in order to create time for us to do the work that the Congress and the department needs to do together.

FISCHER: As you've heard me say a number of times in our posture hearings on Armed Services and also in classified briefings, we don't have a lot of time, do we, sir?

CAINE: No, ma'am. That's why I said, if not now, then when, and if not us, then who. I truly believe we're at one of those moments in history where we have a choice to make, just given what I see on the next couple of ridge lines, and I encourage us to move forward.

Fischer’s exchange with Hegseth:

FISCHER: Mr. Secretary, how would this request scale munitions production and be able to accelerate our delivery times?

HEGSETH: In the past, previous administrations would sort of send the same amount of dollars into trying to encourage companies to build another factory and add an additional shift. What this munitions request does is fulfills deals that our department has cut with these companies. First, multi-year procurement, where these companies that make SM-3s or Patriots or THAADs [Terminal High Altitude Area Defense] or Tomahawks...

FISCHER: A priority for our NDAA a couple years ago.

HEGSETH: Absolutely, and you have provided that authority, multi-year procurement, and now those companies are spending $4 billion, $5 billion, $3 billion on building their own new factories, that then produce 2x, 3x, or 4x the amount of munitions than they did in the past, and they paid for it.

So actually, in this budget, which is $21 billion, as you mentioned, it saves $18 billion over the FYDP on munitions because we're buying munitions at today's cost and not five or seven years from now when we will also get them.

FISCHER: I hate to interrupt, but we're running out of time. We also have the request includes $4.1 billion for our space-based capabilities, and that includes the AMTI and our space data network capabilities, and these really underpin the long-range kill chains and allow our warfighters to detect and also then to track the airborne threats. So, Mr. Secretary, what's the risk to the joint force if we delay these programs until FY28 or beyond?

HEGSETH: Senator, not being able to see, not being able to sense before an adversary is able to engage one of our capabilities, which means falling behind in the domain of space, which means falling behind at every other domain.

This hearing titled “A Review of the President’s Supplemental Funding Request of June 24, 2026” was convened by the Senate Appropriations Committee.

title: Gallego, Cramer Introduce the CLAIM Act
text:
WASHINGTON – Cannabis has been legalized in 42 states, but not federally. This legal disparity has created a haphazard regulatory environment for marijuana and cannabis-related businesses and services. Federal prohibitions conflict with state laws, leaving legal enterprises in limbo and requiring them to exist in the shadows, unable to access tools necessary for their success. For example, insurance companies wishing to serve cannabis-related businesses face legal liability for providing the insurance those businesses need to operate.

As members of the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, U.S. Senators Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) and Kevin Cramer (R-ND) introduced the Clarifying Law Around Insurance of Marijuana (CLAIM) Act to ensure legal, law-abiding cannabis businesses in compliance with their state’s relevant regulations have access to insurance products. Specifically, the CLAIM Act ensures safe harbor for any insurance company that provides insurance products to cannabis-related businesses.

“In states that have legalized marijuana, including Arizona, legitimate cannabis businesses should have the same access to insurance coverage as any other business,” said Gallego. “I’m proud to partner with Senator Cramer to introduce this commonsense, bipartisan fix.”

“Much like marijuana businesses are barred from using bank accounts, they are also locked out of insurance markets,” said Cramer. “Businesses, as we know, obviously assume risk [because] that’s part of being in business. But the risk for cannabis companies that operate in states where it’s actually legal is especially high. The CLAIM Act makes sure insurers can offer their commercial products to regulated marijuana-related businesses without fear of federal prosecution.”

title: Gillibrand Holds Virtual Press Conference Celebrating Senate Passage Of Her Bipartisan Legislation To Support Seniors
text:
Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) held a virtual press conference to celebrate unanimous Senate passage of her bipartisan Older Americans Act (OAA) Reauthorization Act. The OAA Reauthorization Act renews funding for the essential services provided by the OAA, including programs that provide nutrition assistance, meal deliveries, transportation services, caregiver support, long-term care, and more.

“The OAA is a lifeline for American seniors, and I am proud to have successfully led the charge for its reauthorization in the Senate,” said Senator Gillibrand. “Our seniors have spent their lives building our communities, raising families, and serving our country. They have earned the right to age with health, dignity, and independence in the settings of their choice—and OAA programs help them do just that. I am proud to see this legislation pass the Senate with unanimous support, and I am calling on the House to take up and pass this legislation immediately.”

The OAA has been a lifeline for American seniors since its passage in 1965. Every year, OAA programs deliver over 250 million meals, provide more than 14 million rides, and offer 30 million hours of caregiver support and in-home assistance with daily tasks like bathing and dressing. In total, about one in six older adults across the country rely on OAA-funded services every year.

However, authorization of the OAA expired at the end of 2024, jeopardizing OAA programs’ long-term future.

Specifically, this year’s OAA Reauthorization Act reauthorizes the following programs through fiscal year 2030:

the national eldercare locator service;

regional aging and disability resource centers;

grants to support counseling and assistance on pensions and other retirement benefits;

grants to support home-delivered nutrition services like Meals on Wheels;

programs to facilitate the delivery of supportive services to tribal organizations; and

programs to prevent elder abuse, neglect, and exploitation.

The bill also modifies existing programs for older individuals to promote innovation and flexibility, strengthen program integrity, and better support family caregivers and direct care workers.

title: Grassley Probes Meta on Disclosures Alleging Company Disregarded Child Safety Risks and Retaliated Against Whistleblowers
text:
WASHINGTON – Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) is raising concerns about allegations that Meta has engaged in a longstanding campaign to discredit and malign whistleblowers as “leakers” for raising concerns about child safety and product development.

Whistleblowers Joshua DeFriez and William Sevedge, along with four of their colleagues, provided lawful disclosures to Congress as part of a September 2025 Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing. While two whistleblowers testified publicly, the other four remained anonymous. DeFriez and Sevedge have now decided to become public.

In a letter to Meta, Instagram and Facebook leaders, Grassley outlined the whistleblower retaliation alleged by DeFriez and Sevedge.

“On July 1, 2026, my office received a letter alleging that Meta ‘recently terminated two anonymous whistleblowers following their cooperation with Senator Grassley’s office and the Senate Judiciary Committee, in furtherance of [the] Committee’s oversight mission.’ The disclosure notes that each whistleblower ‘consistently received exemplary performance evaluations during their time at the Company.’ If you disagree, please let me know,” Grassley wrote.

Grassley is also asking for a full response to his April 2025 letter questioning Meta’s deployment of harmful targeted ads to young and vulnerable users, and is following up on recent allegations from Meta whistleblower Sarah Wynn-Williams that the company sent a representative to surveil her in Wales during a literary and arts festival appearance.

Full text of the letter can be found HERE and below:

July 22, 2026

VIA ELECTRONIC TRANSMISSION

Mr. Mark Zuckerberg

Founder, Chairman, and Chief Executive Officer

Meta Platforms, Inc.

Mr. Adam Mosseri

Head of Instagram

Meta Platforms, Inc.

Mr. Tom Alison

Head of Facebook

Meta Platforms, Inc.

Mr. Andrew Bosworth

Chief Technology Officer

Meta Platforms, Inc.

Dear Mr. Zuckerberg, Mr. Mosseri, Mr. Alison, and Mr. Bosworth:

On April 14, 2025, I sent Meta a letter with respect to reported efforts by the company to silence whistleblower Ms. Sarah Wynn-Williams.[1] My letter requested information regarding the number of requests Meta and its subsidiaries received by employees to disclose information to federal authorities and Congress, as well as information about how many Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) investigations Meta and its subsidiaries have been subject to.[2] To date, Meta has failed to fully and completely respond to my questions and document requests from that letter.

More recently, according to reporting, Ms. Wynn-Williams filed a lawsuit against Meta in federal court. The suit contains an allegation that Meta sent a representative to Wales to surveil Ms. Wynn-Williams during an appearance at a literary and arts festival, where she was on a panel on digital technology and public policy.[3] Ms. Wynn-Williams alleges that at the event, she did not speak about the book nor did she publicly speak at all.[4]

On July 1, 2026, my office received a letter alleging that Meta “recently terminated two anonymous whistleblowers following their cooperation with Senator Grassley’s office and the Senate Judiciary Committee, in furtherance of [the] Committee’s oversight mission.”[5] The disclosure notes that each whistleblower “consistently received exemplary performance evaluations during their time at the Company.”[6] If you disagree, please let me know.

These two whistleblowers, along with four of their colleagues, provided lawful disclosures to the Committee and Senator Blackburn’s office as part of the September 9, 2025, Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, and the Law hearing entitled, “Hidden Harms: Examining Whistleblower Allegations that Meta Buried Child Safety Research.”[7] Two of these six whistleblowers, Jason Sattizan and Cayce Savage, testified before the subcommittee; however, the other four whistleblowers decided to remain anonymous at that time.[8] Joshua DeFriez and William Sevedge have now decided to become public through their disclosure of whistleblower retaliation to my office.[9]

According to Joshua DeFriez and William Sevedge, they disclosed concerns “over the Company’s disregard for child safety risks.”[10] Specifically, according to their letter, DeFriez and Sevedge made whistleblower disclosures to Congress “regarding harmful and deceptive practices at Meta with regard [to] the dangers posed to the public by Meta’s platforms and products—including its VR headsets, augmented reality glasses, and its ‘Metaverse,’ as well as its more popular products like Instagram and Facebook.”[11] The letter further states that when the whistleblowers raised concerns to their managers at Meta, “they were met with opposition, censored when raising concerns to fellow employees, and expressly instructed to avoid pursuing research that could subject Meta to liability for failing to adequately [comply] with the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA).”[12] The letter also raises concerning issues that Meta has engaged in a “longstanding campaign to discredit and malign whistleblowers as ‘leakers’” for reporting misconduct to Congress or enforcement agencies.[13] The letter specifically cites to an article which highlighted comments from Meta’s Chief Technology Officer (CTO) Andrew Bosworth, and that Meta created a team to “hunt for insider threats,” which reporting attributes to the “heavy scrutiny” Meta received from disclosures by concerned employees to Congress and superiors at the company.[14] According to the reporting:

“There’s a funny thing that’s happening with these leaks,” Bosworth said during his Q&A earlier this week (a recording of which I obtained). “When things leak, I think a lot of times people think, ‘Ah, okay, this is leaked, therefore it’ll put pressure on us to change things.’ The opposite is more likely.”[15]

As the Co-Chairman of the Senate’s Whistleblower Protection Caucus, I am concerned about the allegations my office has received of Meta’s alleged continued retaliation of whistleblowers. To provide your organization with an opportunity to respond, and so that Congress may conduct objective and independent oversight, please provide answers to the following no later than August 4, 2026:

Provide a full and complete response, including all responsive records, to my April 14, 2025, letter.[16]

Does Meta[17] have an office policy to retaliate against whistleblowers? If not, how do you explain the recent terminations?

Has Meta ever terminated an employee because they disclosed information to Congress? If so, how many, who and when?

Are the allegations raised in The Verge reporting accurate? Please address each allegation and its accuracy, or lack thereof. In your answer, specifically address the reported quote from Andrew Bosworth. Provide all records.

Are the allegations raised by Mr. DeFriez and Mr. Sevedge accurate?[18] Please address each allegation and its accuracy, or lack thereof. Provide all records.

Are the allegations raised in the Wynn-Williams v. Meta case accurate?[19] Please address each allegation and its accuracy, or lack thereof. Provide all records.

Thank you for your prompt review and response. If you have any questions, please contact Tucker Akin of Chairman Grassley’s Committee staff at (202) 224-5225.

Sincerely,

Charles E. Grassley

Chairman

Senate Committee on the Judiciary

-30-

[1] Letter from Sen. Charles E. Grassley, Chairman, Senate Judiciary Committee, to Mark Zuckerberg, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Meta Platforms, Inc., (April 14, 2025), https://www.grassley.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2025-04-14_grassley_to_meta_-_wb_retaliation.pdf.

[2] Id.
