title: Grassley Questions Trade Ambassador Greer on Increasing Access to Fertilizer, Supporting Iowa Pig Farmers and USMCA
text:
WASHINGTON – Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), a senior member and former chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, questioned U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer about the need to expand access to fertilizer and the benefits of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).

Grassley urged Greer to work with America’s trade partners to increase fertilizer supply and to remove any tariffs on anhydrous ammonia. On USMCA, Grassley called on Greer to ensure Iowa pig farmers are not caught up in a crossfire of trade retaliation. Iowa leads the nation in pork production.

Video and excerpts follow.

VIDEO

On increasing fertilizer access:

I want to compliment the president for delaying the 18% duties on Moroccan phosphate coming into our country so that Mosaic has some competition. They’ve got 85% of the market already. We have two suppliers of anhydrous ammonia in America.

So, can we get a commitment to working with our trading partners to increase the availability of fertilizers generally for U.S. farmers, but most importantly, removing any tariffs on anhydrous ammonia? In other words, we need to get a bigger supply. You can’t just have two companies dominating the whole market of nitrogen for corn farmers.

…

Well, if you want to increase supply, get Mosaic to quit shutting down plants they have with their phosphate production.

On removing Chinese export restrictions:

Let’s go to China. They have placed unfair export restrictions on fertilizer products, upsetting the global markets for fertilizer. What can you do to get the Chinese to remove these export restrictions in future trade negotiations with China?

On USMCA and supporting Iowa pork producers:

USMCA has shown its value to the economies of all three countries because it’s dramatically improved the economies of the countries and the increased trade that’s happened. [For a]ll segments of the economy in all [three] countries, but particularly for agriculture, it’s been very good.

And so, the United States and Mexico failed to reach an agreement on Mexican tomato exports. The Mexican government then launched an investigation into unfair trade practices of the U.S. pork industry.

Ahead of further negotiations with Mexico this week, what is USTR doing to ensure Iowa pig farmers – because we’re number one in the production of pork – so we don’t get caught up in the crossfire of trade retaliation?

title: Hawley Announces Legislation to Ban Bonuses for Postal Service Leadership Until Mail Is Delivered on Time
text:
WASHINGTON — Today, U.S. Senator Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) announced he will introduce the No Bonuses for Bad Service Act to prohibit United States Postal Service (USPS) leadership from receiving bonuses or additional compensation until mail service and delivery meet the standards that the American people deserve. The bill comes after Senator Hawley launched an investigation into USPS’ failure to deliver Missourians’ mail on time.

“While Missourians don’t receive their mail on time, the Postmaster General receives a hefty bonus each year. I am introducing the No Bonuses for Bad Service Act to ensure postal service leadership isn’t receiving bonuses while Americans’ mail goes undelivered. It’s time for the Postmaster General to do his job and put Americans first,” Senator Hawley said.

The No Bonuses for Bad Service Act would:

Prohibit the USPS Board of Governors from approving any additional compensation for the Postmaster General and Deputy Postmaster General for a fiscal year in which the Postal Service does not meet or exceed an on-time delivery rate of 95% for all market dominant mail products.

Require the Postal Service to submit its annual delivery rate report to the Postal Regulatory Commission.

The United States Postal Service (USPS) has posted staggering financial losses in recent years, including $25 billion over the last three fiscal years, more than $6 billion beyond USPS’s own internal projections. At the same time, USPS has repeatedly raised postage rates on American households and businesses while consistently missing its own service standards. On-time delivery has continued to slip. Residents in rural areas wait weeks to receive mail. Recently in Missouri, a massive pile of undelivered mail was discovered in a vacant lot without explanation from the Postal Service. These delays and missing mail are becoming a real financial burden for those Americans who don’t receive their bills or paychecks.

Despite these failures, Postal Service executives have been rewarded with lavish bonuses. Over the past ten years, Postmasters General have received more than $2 million in additional compensation, even as delivery performance declined and the budget numbers got worse. During the last three years of Louis DeJoy’s tenure alone, the Board of Governors approved more than $567,000 in additional bonus compensation. Postmaster General David Steiner, who assumed office just a year ago, has already pocketed a $170,000 bonus. Senator Hawley directly confronted Steiner about these bonuses in a recent committee hearing, and the Postmaster refused to forgo bonuses until the mail is delivered on time.

Read more about Senator Hawley’s ongoing investigation here.

title: Hawley Requests Additional Disaster Relief Funds for Missouri Following 2025 Tornadoes
text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) requested that the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Transportation, Housing and Urban Development fully fund the Community Development Block Grant-Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) program to provide much-needed relief to Missourians. This program can provide additional, flexible resources for long-term rehabilitation and recovery for the St. Louis region following the 2025 tornadoes.

Senator Hawley wrote, “I write to urge the subcommittee to allocate robust funding in the next funding vehicle for long-term disaster relief. As you may know, on May 16, 2025, a devastating tornado struck the City of St. Louis, killing at least five people and destroying hundreds of homes and businesses. President Trump rightly approved a major disaster declaration for the incident. One year later, further federal resources are still required to help this community rebuild.”

He continued, “Local officials in Missouri estimate the outstanding federal needs for full rehabilitation and recovery are between $1 billion and $1.5 billion. The Community Development Block Grant-Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) program can provide the flexible, long-term recovery funding that the region requires for housing, infrastructure, and economic revitalization. This program has historically been used for such purposes, and Missouri has received substantial allocations for major disasters in the past. However, there have been no additional appropriations for this program since the end of 2024.”

Senator Hawley concluded, “I request that the CBDG-DR program be fully funded to provide adequate resources to meet these outstanding needs in Missouri.”

Read the full letter here or below.

July 21, 2026

Senate Committee on Appropriations

Subcommittee on Transportation, Housing and Urban Development

The Capitol,

Room S-128,

Washington, D.C. 20510

Dear Chair Hyde-Smith and Ranking Member Gillibrand,

I write to urge the subcommittee to allocate robust funding in the next funding vehicle for long-term disaster relief. As you may know, on May 16, 2025, a devastating tornado struck the City of St. Louis, killing at least five people and destroying hundreds of homes and businesses. President Trump rightly approved a major disaster declaration for the incident. One year later, further federal resources are still required to help this community rebuild.

While the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) has now disbursed short-term relief in both individual and public assistance, there remain gaps in federal aid. Local officials in Missouri estimate the outstanding federal needs for full rehabilitation and recovery are between $1 billion and $1.5 billion. The Community Development Block Grant-Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) program can provide the flexible, long-term recovery funding that the region requires for housing, infrastructure, and economic revitalization. This program has historically been used for such purposes, and Missouri has received substantial allocations for major disasters in the past. However, there have been no additional appropriations for this program since the end of 2024.

As you work on appropriations legislation for both outstanding disaster needs and the upcoming fiscal year, I request that the CBDG-DR program be fully funded to provide adequate resources to meet these outstanding needs in Missouri. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Sincerely,

Josh Hawley

United States Senator

title: Heinrich Demands Answers from Trump Admin on U.S. Park Police Vehicle Pursuit Policy After Killing of Nolberto Armando Sanabria Meza
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, sent a letter to U.S. Department of the Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and U.S Park Chief of Police Scott Brecht demanding answers and transparency about the U.S. Park Police’s new vehicle pursuit policy following news reports that an innocent bystander, Nolberto Armando Sanabria Meza, 46-year-old food delivery driver, was hit and tragically killed in D.C. by a driver being chased by U.S. Park Police.

Under President Trump’s Executive Order 14339, “Additional Measures to Address the Crime Emergency in the District of Columbia,” there has been an increase in USPP car chases spurred by nonviolent actions ending in collisions.

“I write to express serious concern about U.S. Park Police’s (USPP) new vehicle pursuit policy. Following the fatal accident of a Venezuelan delivery driver during a USPP police pursuit in June 2026, I request that your Department provide full transparency and answers concerning the Departments revised pursuit policy, and the measures being implemented to reduce the risk of future accidents and fatalities,” the Senator began.

The Senator continued, highlighting the change to USPP’s vehicle pursuit policy, “Prior to President Trump’s Executive Order, USPP operated under General Order 2205, which placed firm limits on when officers could initiate vehicular pursuits. Under the order, officers could initiate a vehicular pursuit only if the suspect was wanted for or suspected of committing a violent felony offense, or if they were known to be carrying a firearm and had explicit approval from a supervisor prior to initiating a pursuit. However, since then, Executive Order 14339 has directed the National Park Service to hire additional USPP officers and instructed NPS to “ensure enforcement of all applicable laws within their jurisdiction” as part of the administration’s broader response to the “crime emergency” in Washington, D.C.”

The Senator continued, highlighting the tragic killing of Nolberto Armando Sanabria Meza, “On August 14, 2025, USPP formally issued an “emergency modification” to General Order 2205... Weeks after Trump’s Executive Order, reports indicated an increase of USPP car chases ending in collisions and chases being initiated over nonviolent offenses, such as traffic violations or suspected stolen vehicles. Last month, Nolberto Armando Sanabria Meza, a 46-year-old food delivery driver, was tragically killed on the William Howard Taft Bridge in Northwest D.C. when a stolen vehicle being chased by USPP crossed into oncoming traffic and struck Nolberto’s moped. Mr. Meza was an innocent bystander who tragically lost his life. His death is the second reported death caused by a USPP car chase since the change in policy last August.”

“Nearly a year after the change in USPP’s pursuit policy, there is little to no evidence that it has reduced crime or improved outcomes. The public deserves answers as to whether this policy change is working as intended,” the Senator continued.

Heinrich concluded the letter by requesting information on the oversight of USPP’s revised pursuit standard, officer training, and the number of vehicle pursuits that have led to injury or fatality.

title: Heinrich Presses Top Trump Administration Officials on Strategy to Reopen the Strait of Hormuz, Lower Energy Costs, & Provide Relief for American Producers and Farmers
text:
VIDEO HERE

WASHINGTON — This week, at a U.S. Senate Appropriations Committee hearing to review President Trump’s supplemental budget request, U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) pressed top Trump administration officials on the need for a strategy to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and protect American families from rising energy costs, while demanding that U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) relief funds support American producers and farmers — not foreign meatpacking corporations.

VIDEO: U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), a member of the U.S. Senate Appropriations Committee, presses top Trump administration officials on the president’s supplemental budget request, July 21, 2026.

On the Need for a Strategy to Reopen the Strait of Hormuz and Protect American Families from Rising Energy Costs:

Senator Heinrich: “General Caine, our military is the best in the world. And so, I don't think any of us should be surprised with the technical execution of its attacks on the Iranian regime's forces. They've been flawless. What I don't want [is] us to confuse flawless technical execution with long-term strategic success. And I think one objective that is relatively modest, because it puts us back to where we were when we started this, but nonetheless is incredibly important as a critical objective, is that I want to see the Strait open again. And I want to see it open where shippers can transit that Strait without being extorted by Iran. And I would love to see that before our commercial and other oil reserves are exhausted because of the impacts that will then have on the pocketbooks of American families. Is that a reasonable objective, and is one — is it one that you share?”

Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman General John Caine: “I'll defer on the military objectives to the political leaders who set them. What I can tell you is, U.S. Central Command is working hard to ensure that Iran cannot terrorize the southern flank down there. And they're doing so every single day and night. And you and the rest of the Senate would be proud of the actions and activities for the forces that are down there. The character of war is changing, though, like I said in my opening statement. And so, there's a variety of mixed ammunitions that are down there coming at the commercial traffic. But I would like to be clear and unambiguous with you and the rest of the Senate, and the Iranian forces. They have a choice to make, and they should knock it off.”

Heinrich: “I have no doubt I would be incredibly proud of the actions of our service members in this conflict. And I hope we can achieve that kind of strategic objection on the timeline that obviously avoids the worst impacts of the limitations of commercial oil supplies right now.”

On Ensuring USDA Relief Funds Support American Producers — Not Foreign Meatpacking Corporations:

Heinrich: “Secretary Rollins, I want to shift gears. One of the things that you mentioned in your opening statement, that we appear to agree on, is that there is simply too much consolidation in a number of agricultural sectors. You mentioned fertilizer and seeds, but in particular, I want to talk about the meatpacking industry. Because in a previous Trump administration bailout, about $90 million went to the corrupt Brazilian meat packer JBS. I think that Congress really intended those funds to go to American ranchers. So, I want to ask you, what are you going to do this time around to ensure that the proposed relief dollars that we're talking about today, that those funds go to American producers — instead of to the very foreign corporations who have created the business model where ranchers bear the risk and meat packers reap the profits?”

USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins: “Well, that's right, and we're obviously at a seventy-five-year herd low. There are a lot of reasons for that but we’re working to solve for that. Number one, the Department of Justice is investigating right now, significantly the four, but especially the two foreign owned. Number two, USDA is investing significant funds in deconsolidating packing and supporting mid-sized and smaller packers around the country. I know that wasn't your question, but just to answer the bigger question, which is a really important one. But from my perspective, what the Trump USDA 2.0 has been hyper-focused on small and mid-sized farmers and ranchers. We have worked really hard on the $40 billion that has already moved through to make sure that goes to where it is intended, which is not multinational foreign agricultural corporations.”

Heinrich: “I very much support the efforts of the Department of Justice. I think there is a very important antitrust case to be made here. At the same time, I've watched as your Department has rescinded three important rules that were put in place to protect farmers and ranchers from unfair practices by the large meat packers. Those rules were supported by the American Farm Bureau and the National Farmers Union. Explain that discrepancy to me?”

Rollins: “Which rules? I’m not tracking.”

Heinrich: “Inclusive Competition and Market Integrity rule, the Transparency in Poultry Grower Contracting and Tournaments rule, and the Poultry Grower Payment Systems and Capital Improvement Systems rules.”

Rollins: “The packers and stockyards, I think, is what you're talking about. So, we are executing an additional review on that. I think that the point is very well made that sometimes that inures to the benefit of the larger corporations. As I have begun to make a larger case, and a more vigorous case, in the importance of deconsolidation. We'll be taking a second look at that. And I would love your input.”

Heinrich: “And I would very much support deconsolidation. Thank you.”

###

title: Heinrich: Trump Admin’s War on Renewables is Raising Families’ Energy Costs as Demand Surges
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, during a U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee hearing to conduct oversight of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the Committee, criticized the Trump administration’s efforts to block renewable energy projects that could increase electricity costs for consumers, highlighted his Grid for Growth initiative to meet surging electricity demand, and emphasized the importance of preserving FERC’s independence as the nation faces growing energy needs.

VIDEO: U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, delivers opening remarks during a Committee hearing to conduct oversight of FERC, July 22, 2026.

“Electricity prices are rising, and electricity supply cannot keep up with demand,” said Heinrich. “We are seeing a rapid increase in electricity demand and are being hampered by not getting enough power from generators to end-users and struggling to quickly add new, needed generation sources.”

Heinrich criticized the Trump administration for stalling renewable energy projects that could help meet growing electricity demand and keep costs down.

“The administration is slow walking and stalling 73 GW of solar, 43 GW of storage, 30 GW of onshore wind, and 16 GW of offshore wind. Constraining the renewable buildout would increase economy-wide utility costs by approximately $11.6 billion per year,” continued Heinrich.

Heinrich also commended FERC for taking steps to address the growing electricity needs of large energy users, including data centers and advanced manufacturing facilities. Last month, FERC issued six show cause orders requiring grid operations and transmission owners to justify or propose changes to their tariffs governing large load customers.

“FERC choosing to address major electricity users, like data centers and advanced manufacturers, is an important step in the right direction,” said Heinrich. “Now, more than ever, FERC’s mission to ensure that utility rates remain just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential is critical to making sure millions of Americans can keep their lights on. During this once in a generation moment, I continue to believe that regulatory certainty, and the freedom for commissioners of independent agencies like FERC to act in a way to provide that certainty, will be critical in meeting the energy challenges of today.”

A video of Heinrich’s opening remarks is here.

A transcript of Heinrich’s remarks as delivered is below:

Thank you, Chairman Lee, and special thanks to all five of our FERC Commissioners for attending this hearing today. We very much appreciate having you here.

The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has long been an important independent agency. It serves the public interest by regulating electricity, hydroelectric dams, natural gas, and oil in a manner that is both fair and impartial from the president and Congress, as required by statute.

Historically considered by some to be bit of a “sleepy” agency, FERC faces a pivotal time in our nation’s history right now.

Electricity prices are rising, and electricity supply cannot keep up with demand.

According to a recent report, 75% of U.S. adults say that they’ve noticed their home energy costs increasing in recent years.

Some of that blame can be squarely placed on our current president.

I recently released a report on how this administration is waging a war on renewables that is raising energy costs. The Administration is slow walking and stalling 73 GW of solar, 43 GW of storage, 30 GW of onshore wind, and 16 GW of offshore wind.

Constraining the renewable buildout would increase economy-wide utility costs by approximately $11.6 billion per year.

But that is not the only reason costs are rising. We are seeing a rapid increase in electricity demand and are being hampered by not getting enough power from generators to end-users and struggling to quickly add new, needed generation sources.

Luckily, we can take steps to improve our grid to help move electricity more efficiently and bring new power sources online.

I recently launched an initiative called Grid for Growth, a plan to meet surging electricity demand without shifting the cost of that to consumers. This effort complements ongoing efforts to pass a bipartisan permitting reform.

As part of the effort, last week I introduced the Grid Connection and Congestion Management Act to create a faster path for generator interconnection. Modeled after ERCOT’s connect and manage process, projects are rewarded for being flexible in their output by getting onto the grid faster.

Other bills will follow in the next few weeks and months, but our ability to meet the rising needs of the grid are based, in large part, on our ability to build more interregional transmission lines.

That is why permitting reform is so important.

Interregional transmission lines can be the best line of defense against extreme weather conditions, improving reliability, and reducing consumer costs.

While FERC requires some interregional transmission planning under Order Numbers 1000 and 1920, this coordination has not produced a substantial number of interregional transmission projects in the last decade.

We need to find a way to build more high voltage transmission lines in the next decade—our ability to grow our economy depends on it.

To FERC’s credit, the agency has taken active steps to confront energy challenges.

Last month, FERC issued six “show cause” orders, requiring grid operators and their transmission owners to justify or propose changes to their current tariffs with respect to large load customers.

These steps by FERC can help protect consumers and encourage grid operators to integrate new advanced technologies when adding new large loads to the grid.

FERC choosing to address major electricity users, like data centers and manufacturers, is an important step in the right direction.

Nevertheless, more action can, and should be, taken to ensure that consumers are protected from sky-high costs associated with data centers, manufacturers, and other large loads. I have been working on a bill intended to do just that and hope to speak more about that soon.

However, all of these efforts that I mentioned will be meaningless if the independence of FERC is erased.

The Supreme Court’s recent decision has put the impartiality of independent agencies at risk.

Now, more than ever, FERC’s mission to ensure that utility rates remain just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential is critical to making sure millions of Americans can keep their lights on.

During this once in a generation moment, I continue to believe that regulatory certainty, and the freedom for commissioners of independent agencies like FERC to act in a way to provide that certainty, will be critical in meeting the energy challenges of today.

I hope to discuss these issues with each of you during this hearing and look forward to it.

Thank you.

title: N.M. Delegation Joins Pueblo Governors to Push for Permanent Protections for Chaco Canyon
text:
N.M. Delegation’s push occurs during a 14-day public comment period set by the Trump administration in their effort to fully revoke a 20-year mineral withdrawal that has protected public lands within Chaco Canyon

VIDEO HERE

WASHINGTON — Today, U.S. Senators Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), and U.S. Representatives Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.), Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.), and Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) joined the All Pueblo Council of Governors (APCG) at a press conference to call for permanent protection of Chaco Canyon.

Located in northwestern New Mexico, the Greater Chaco landscape is a region of great cultural, spiritual, and historical significance to many Pueblos and Tribes and contains living sacred sites. Chaco was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987 and is one of only 24 such sites in the United States.

Last week, the Trump administration announced a proposal to fully revoke a 20-year mineral withdrawal that has protected public lands surrounding the Chaco Culture National Historic Park, and only allowed 14 days for public comment. The N.M. Delegation released a statement strongly condemning the Trump administration’s actions.

This week, Heinrich, Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee,led a N.M. Delegation letter urging U.S. Department of the Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to extend the public comment period to 90-days and conduct genuine Tribal consultation and extensive public engagement before revoking protections for the Chaco region. Most importantly, the Delegation urged Secretary Burgum to withdraw this proposal and leave Public Land Order No. 7923 in place. The Delegation also, once again, invited Secretary Burgum to visit Chaco before taking any action that would put this irreplaceable cultural landmark at risk.

VIDEO: The N.M. Delegation joins the All Pueblo Council of Governors to call for permanent protection of the Chaco Canyon Cultural Protection Zone, July 22, 2026.

“Chaco Canyon is not for sale. New Mexico has an important role to play producing energy for the nation. We're the second largest producer of oil in the country, we produce far more electrons than we consume, and we have never had to sacrifice our most sacred places to do that — and we should not do that going forward,” said Heinrich, Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. “Chaco Canyon is not just a place on a map. It is not a museum. It is not about what happened 1,000 years ago. It is about the future. It is about these governors and their communities, their identity, and their relationship to this sacred place that they use now. This is about our state's ability to stand up for what is right and moral. Our New Mexico Delegation stands arm in arm and shoulder to shoulder with these Tribal governors and their communities in standing up to protect this place. And we will fight that fight until we win.”

“Chaco Canyon is more than a place on a map — it is thousands of years of culture, history, and the enduring spirit of the Pueblo peoples. Protecting Chaco is our sacred responsibility. Once Chaco is damaged, it cannot be undone. That’s why we are standing together to make our voices heard,” said Luján. “I am deeply grateful for the Pueblo leaders whose leadership and tireless advocacy are at the heart of the fight to protect Chaco Canyon. Now is your turn to make your voice heard. Submit your comment today to tell the Trump administration to keep its hands off Chaco.”

“There is not a single molecule of gas worth sacrificing a landscape that holds more than 4,700 archaeological sites, the prayers and history of generations, and the living culture of Chaco Canyon,”said Leger Fernández, Ranking Member of the House Indian and Insular Affairs Subcommittee. “Secretary Burgum lied when he promised meaningful, in-person tribal consultation before any decision was made. Our Chaco Cultural Heritage Area Protection Act will permanently protect Chaco. In the meantime, we will use every tool at our disposal to stop the bulldozers from tearing up living history.”

“Chaco Canyon is not for sale! As one the most sacred places on the planet — the Greater Chaco Landscape has been a sacred landscape for Pueblo and Diné people since time immemorial,” said Stansbury, Democratic Vice Chair of the Congressional Native American Caucus. “The Trump Administration's plan to open these sacred places to oil and gas drilling is a direct attack to Tribal Sovereignty and New Mexico's history, cultures, and living traditions. I am proud to stand today and every day with the entire New Mexico delegation, the All Pueblo Council of Governors, Tribal leaders, advocates, and communities across our state to protect this irreplaceable landscape for generations to come. We ask the American people to stand with us — and please submit a public comment and help save Chaco Canyon.”

“Chaco is central to New Mexico’s identity — a living cultural landscape, a sacred place and an irreplaceable unit of our national public lands. The Administration’s attempt to revoke the protections of this landscape, built through years of consultation and community engagement, with just 14 days of public comment is disingenuous and disrespectful,” said Vasquez. “Secretary Burgum must withdraw this proposal and come to New Mexico to hear directly from Pueblo leaders. He has an open invitation to come to Chaco and meet with Pueblo leaders. We can support responsible energy development without sacrificing places like Chaco that, once damaged, will be lost forever.”

The New Mexico Congressional Delegation has worked tirelessly to permanently protect Chaco Canyon.

Last week, the N.M. Delegation released a statement in response to the news that the Trump administration is proposing to fully revoke a 20-year mineral withdrawal that has protected public lands surrounding the Chaco Culture National Historic Park, and only allowing 14 days for public comment.

In April, the N.M. Delegation submitted a comment letter to the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) urging the Trump administration to reverse course on its decision to initiate the process to undo a 20-year mineral withdrawal that has kept public lands in the Chaco Canyon Cultural Protection Zone off-limits to new oil and gas leasing. Earlier that month, the N.M. Delegation sent statements in opposition to the Trump administration only granting seven days to submit scoping comments.

Last November, Heinrich, Luján, and Stansbury hosted a press conference with Pueblo leaders on the actions needed to permanently protect the landscape.

Last September, the N.M. Delegation hosted a press conference in front of the U.S. Capitol with 20 Governors and leaders from the Santa Ana, Picuris, Cochiti, Zia, Tesuque, Acoma, Santo Domingo, and Laguna Pueblos to demand the Trump administration permanently protect Chaco Canyon, and to invite U.S. Department of the Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to visit the Greater Chaco landscape before deciding its fate. Watch the video of the full press conference here.

In June 2025, the N.M. Delegation sent a letter initially inviting Secretary Burgum to visit Chaco Canyon and engage directly with Tribal leaders and local communities to hear about the profound cultural and spiritual significance of this sacred landscape. Secretary Burgum issued the directive to begin revoking the Chaco protections without experiencing it firsthand. Following Secretary Burgum’s directive, the N.M. Delegation sent a letter urging the Trump administration to reverse course on its decision to initiate the process to fully revoke Chaco Canyon’s protections.

In April 2025, the N.M. Delegation reintroduced legislation to protect Chaco Canyon and the greater sacred landscape surrounding the Chaco Culture National Historic Park. The legislation is led by Luján in the U.S. Senate and Leger Fernández in the U.S. House of Representatives.

title: N.M. Delegation Urges Trump Admin to Extend Comment Period for Chaco Canyon Protection, Calls for Genuine Tribal Consultation, Invites Burgum to Visit Chaco Canyon Before Taking Further Action
text:
WASHINGTON – This week, U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, U.S. Senator Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), and U.S. Representatives Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.), member of the U.S. House Natural Resources Committee, Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.), member of the U.S. House Natural Resources Committee, and Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) sent a letter to U.S. Department of the Interior (DOI) Secretary Doug Burgum expressing deep concern and opposition to the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) only allowing 14 days for public comment in response to the Trump administration’s proposal to fully revoke a 20-year mineral withdrawal that has protected public lands surrounding Chaco Culture National Historical Park.

The lawmakers requested that the Department immediately extend the comment period to no fewer than 90 days and withdraw their proposal to gut protections for Chaco Canyon. The Delegation additionally invited Secretary Burgum to visit Chaco Canyon before taking any action that would put this irreplaceable landscape at risk.

“Since your confirmation, we have written numerous letters and spoken to you directly expressing why protections for the greater Chacoan landscape are important and popular in New Mexico. Yet the process to revoke the protections continues to move at a rapid pace... We would like to register immense concern and frustration with the fourteen-day public comment period. Fourteen days does not represent the scope of this action, is arbitrary, and not representative of the work that went into implementing PLO No. 7923,” the lawmakers began.

“The Chacoan region is a natural and cultural landscape and not represented by isolated individual sites. The withdrawal you are proposing to erase was built from over a decade of community and Tribal input... The previous public process was robust and ended in protection of the Chacoan landscape. In contrast, the current process to remove protections is based on an inadequate and incomplete review. It certainly does not constitute full and meaningful Tribal consultation,” the lawmakers continued.

“You committed before the House Natural Resources Committee to send an official with decision-making authority to conduct in-person consultation with every Tribe with an interest in Chaco. The draft assessment itself shows that commitment has not been met. Several Pueblos received nothing more than an invitation, others received only ‘informational meetings.’ No Secretarial-level official appears anywhere in its consultation record. An informational briefing or a group meeting in D.C. is not consultation. And despite repeated invitations from Pueblos and from every member of this delegation, you have not yet visited Chaco,” the lawmakers continued.

The lawmakers concluded by urging Secretary Burgum to extend the review process on his proposal to revoke protections for the Chaco Canyon Cultural protection zone, meaningfully engage with Tribes in good faith, extend the comment period to 90 days, visit Chaco Canyon, and, ultimately, reverse the proposal to fully revoke a 20-year mineral withdrawal protecting Chaco Canyon from drilling.

Read the full letter here and below:

Since your confirmation, we have written numerous letters and spoken to you directly expressing why protections for the greater Chacoan landscape are important and popular in New Mexico. Yet the process to revoke the protections continues to move at a rapid pace. Today, we write in response and in strong opposition to the Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM) draft environmental assessment proposing the full revocation of Public Land Order No. 7923, which protects approximately 336,404 acres surrounding Chaco Culture National Historical Park. We would like to register immense concern and frustration with the fourteen-day public comment period. Fourteen days does not represent the scope of this action, is arbitrary, and not representative of the work that went into implementing PLO No. 7923.

The Chacoan region is a natural and cultural landscape and not represented by isolated individual sites. The withdrawal you are proposing to erase was built from over a decade of community and Tribal input. Over the span of a year-and-a-half, the BLM conducted 150 days of public comment, eight public meetings, full and meaningful Tribal consultation, and a full environmental review to implement the existing withdrawal. BLM is now proposing to completely undo it after a seven-day scoping period and a fourteen-day comment window, while characterizing the revocation as a mere “continuation” of the original process. The previous public process was robust and ended in protection of the Chacoan landscape. In contrast, the current process to remove protections is based on an inadequate and incomplete review. It certainly does not constitute full and meaningful Tribal consultation.

Two months ago, the National Trust for Historic Preservation named the Greater Chaco Cultural Landscape as one of America’s Eleven Most Endangered Historic Places. There are 4,730 documented cultural sites within the 10-mile withdrawal radius and there could be countless more needing protection. This is a process that should not be rushed.

On June 12, 2025, you committed before the House Natural Resources Committee to send an official with decision-making authority to conduct in-person consultation with every Tribe with an interest in Chaco. The draft assessment itself shows that commitment has not been met. Several Pueblos received nothing more than an invitation, others received only “informational meetings.” No Secretarial-level official appears anywhere in its consultation record. An informational briefing or a group meeting in D.C. is not consultation. And despite repeated invitations from Pueblos and from every member of this delegation, you have not yet visited Chaco.

We, therefore, call for an actual review process regarding revoking protections for the Chaco region, with genuine Tribal consultation, as with the previous public process included. We request that the Department immediately extend the comment period to no fewer than 90 days. And, most importantly, we urge you to stand down, withdraw this proposal and leave Public Land Order No. 7923 in place. Further, we once again invite you to come to Chaco before taking any action that would put this irreplaceable landscape at risk.

Sincerely,

title: Hickenlooper, Marshall Celebrate Committee Passage of Bipartisan Bill to Make Health Care Costs Transparent
text:
Transparency for medical services will lower cost of health care and help Coloradans compare prices

Bill now heads to Senate floor for final passage

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senators John Hickenlooper and Roger Marshall celebrated passage of their bipartisan Patients Deserve Price Tags Act, which would make health care costs transparent, out of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions. The bill requires providers to publish the costs of services so Americans understand what a specific visit or procedure will cost, and have the opportunity to compare prices and get the best deal. The bill now heads to the Senate floor for a final vote.

“Right now, Americans walk into a hospital blind and walk out with a bill nobody could have predicted. That’s not a health care system — it’s a gamble,” said Hickenlooper, who sits on the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee. “Our bill makes hospitals and insurers publish their prices and backs it up with real fines, not empty threats. If we’re serious about getting universal coverage and lowering costs, we start by following the money.”

“Patients deserve price tags, not surprise bills. This is the only bipartisan healthcare reform before Congress today that can begin lowering the cost of living immediately by bringing real competition to our healthcare system,” said Marshall. “Americans have waited far too long to know what their care will cost before they receive it, and I’m proud this commonsense legislation passed out of the HELP Committee today with overwhelming bipartisan support. It’s time to put patients back in charge – not the big hospital systems and insurance companies.”

“The Patients Deserve Price Tags Act would replace healthcare’s blank checks with actual prices, empowering patients and employers to compare options, avoid the risk of surprise bills and reap the benefits of competition found elsewhere across the economy,” said Cynthia Fisher, founder and chair of PatientRightsAdvocate.org. “At a time when health insurers are planning massive premium increases, this bipartisan legislation will expose for the first time how exactly they set their prices.”

Americans are being crushed by the high cost of health care. Most Americans go to the hospital with no idea what services will cost beforehand. As a result, 41% of Americans, more than 100 million people, owe a staggering $220 billion in medical debt. And in Colorado, 700,000 people are at risk of losing their wages or their homes due to unpaid medical bills. In addition, the historic cuts the Trump administration made to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act have only increased the cost of health care and forced millions of Americans off their insurance.

The Patients Deserve Price Tags Act would create true transparency for health care pricing by requiring all negotiated rates and cash prices between plans and providers to be accessible.

Specifically, the bill would require providers and insurers to:

Publish machine-readable files of all negotiated rates and cash prices between plans and providers, not estimates.

Publish actual prices for 300 shoppable services in a readable, consumer-friendly format.

Provide the right to a detailed itemized bill with plain-language descriptions and billing codes of each distinct item or service, or an all-in total price for bundled items if offered to the patient as an option.

Provide each patient with an Explanation of Benefits statement.

Hold the patient harmless for medical claims that are substantially in excess of the initially quoted cost, absent documented and unforeseen medical circumstances.

Previous efforts to enact price transparency in the Trump and Biden administrations fell short because enforcement was limited. The PatientsDeserve Price Tags Act goes further by codifying price transparency into law and strengthening enforcement mechanisms. Specifically, the bill:

Expands transparency to corporate ownership: the bill requires hospitals, insurers, labs, imaging centers, ambulatory surgical centers, and health plan service providers like Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs) to publish information on provider ownership or investment interest in the entity. This helps shine a light on corporate structures and financial interests that can influence health care costs. Puts real teeth into penalties: The bill requires hospital executives to formally verify that all prices are accurate and complete. A hospital that has failed to comply will be subject to civil monetary penalties. Fines become steeper the longer the provider is not in compliance. Strengthens patient billing protections: if a hospital isn’t following the pricetransparency rules, it’s barred from going after patients with aggressive debt collection tactics for bills tied to the period when the hospital was out of compliance. Protects against add-on charges: The bill requires providers to publish facility fees or add-on charges that’ll be tacked onto the final bill, plus a plain-language explanation of when that fee applies and how to avoid it. title: Husted op-ed: Ohio’s long road from economic decline to No. 1
text:
“I have been fortunate to play a role in many of those reforms during my years in public service, and I have witnessed firsthand the difficult decisions that helped Ohio climb from near the bottom of the pack to the top.”

WASHINGTON – Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) penned an op-ed in the Cincinnati Enquirer tracing Ohio’s transformation from the nation’s 34th-ranked state for business in 2010 to the No. 1 state for business in 2026.

In the piece, Husted reflects on the policy decisions, long-term investments and collaborative leadership that helped fuel Ohio’s economic resurgence and position the state as a national leader.

Key excepts include:

“When CNBC published its Top States for Business rankings in 2010, Ohio ranked 34th. In its latest rankings, Ohio is number one.”

. . .

“That recognition is gratifying because I remember just how difficult things were for Ohio families not all that long ago.”

. . .

“I grew up in northwest Ohio during a time when our state was in economic freefall. Around the time I graduated from high school, the company where my father worked was failing. My dad and my uncle lost their jobs in our hometown of Montpelier, and my family ultimately had to leave Ohio to find work.”

. . .

“I loved Ohio, so I stayed. I went to work in economic development at the Dayton Area Chamber of Commerce because I believed our state could compete again, and I’m not a quitter.”

. . .

“Those were difficult years. Companies were leaving Ohio, and manufacturing communities were suffering.”

. . .

“Our state had one of the nation’s highest income tax rates, three burdensome business taxes, and even taxed the machinery and equipment companies needed to modernize and compete. We had become a harder place to invest, build, hire and grow.”

. . .

“Fortunately, leaders in both the public and private sectors began the long work of turning Ohio around.”

. . .

“I have been fortunate to play a role in many of those reforms during my years in public service, and I have witnessed firsthand the difficult decisions that helped Ohio climb from near the bottom of the pack to the top.”

. . .

“Governors and legislators from both parties made important contributions.

“Governor George Voinovich restored fiscal discipline and reformed workers’ compensation.

“Governor Bob Taft championed tax and tort reform.

“Governor John Kasich created JobsOhio and signed a law eliminating the death tax to make Ohio more competitive.

“Governor Mike DeWine has built on that foundation with major investments in infrastructure, career and technical education, workforce development and transformational economic development projects.”

. . .

“At the turn of this century, Ohio was losing people, jobs, and confidence. Today, Ohio has more people employed than at any time in our state’s history, and unemployment remains near historic lows.”

. . .

“Of course, being No. 1 doesn’t mean our work is finished. The best organizations − and the best states − never stop improving. Every day presents another opportunity to become more competitive.”

. . .

“My goal has always been simple: to help make Ohio a place where our children and grandchildren can build successful careers close to the communities that raised them − if that’s where they choose to live.

“They may still pursue opportunities across the country or around the world, and that’s part of the American dream.

“But they should never have to leave because Ohio failed to provide one.”

. . .

“We’ve come a long way, and while there is still more to do, Ohio has proven that decline is not destiny.”

title: HYDE-SMITH, COMMITTEE REVIEW TRUMP SUPPLEMENTAL FUNDING REQUEST FOR AGRICULTURE, DEFENSE
text:
Senate Appropriations Committee Assesses $11.1B Request for Ag Assistance, $70B for Defense Readiness

VIDEO: Senator Hyde-Smith Questions Agriculture Secretary Rollins About Continued Assistance Payments for Farmers.

VIDEO: Senator Hyde-Smith Questions Defense Secretary Hegseth on Supplemental Funding Request and FY2027 Shipbuilding Budget.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) on Tuesday questioned Trump administration officials on the utility of Congress providing supplemental appropriations this year to bolster national security and continue agricultural assistance for row and specialty crop producers.

As a member of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Hyde-Smith participated in a hearing to review President Trump’s request for supplemental funding, including $11.1 billion for temporary economic assistance for farmers and approximately $70 billion to sustain military readiness and critical capabilities upgrades.

Regarding assistance to farmers, Hyde-Smith signaled her support for continuing to provide bridge payments to help producers overcome low commodity prices and escalated input costs.

“Our row crop producers, as you’ve mentioned in your opening remarks, are truly in a serious situation. I’ve talked to multi-generation farmers back home who are the best of the best that did not even plant this year because they could not make the numbers work. And producers in Mississippi and nationwide continue to face these economic conditions,” Hyde-Smith told Rollins. “If we want the next generation to stay on the land, we’re going to have to take this opportunity to provide this critical market assistance for our farmers and enact policies that build structural demands for commodities, like the Buying American Cotton Act and year-round E15. All of which would make the paths better, more favorable for these producers going forward.”

Rollins discussed the need for bridge payments and administration actions to bring down input costs.

“As of today, ensuring that we can keep these farmers farming while we’re opening the markets, while we’re bringing down the cost of inputs is paramount for a secure America. And that’s why this is so important today,” Rollins said.

On the Department of Defense request, Hyde-Smith also said the supplemental request lines up with her support for the nation’s warfighters. She also sought Hegseth’s input on the future of domestic shipbuilding.

“I, as well, am committed to ensuring that our war fighters have all the tools necessary to accomplish the mission in Iran and whatever else that they need to defend our nation’s interests. The supplemental request is in line with that goal,” Hyde-Smith said.

Hyde-Smith questioned the Defense Department’s FY2027 budget request for a single DDG 51 destroyer instead of the two destroyers desired by naval leadership, as well as the long-term impact on U.S. shipbuilding as the Navy explores using allied shipbuilders and foreign fabricators.

“The department is exploring options for using allied shipyards and overseas fabrication in future naval construction, which raises questions about the long-term role of the American naval industrial base or shifting work away from domestic ship builders – shipyards like Ingalls in Mississippi,” Hyde-Smith said. “They need the confidence that the work will be there so they can invest in new facilities, hire and train skilled workers, and expand capacity that we will need in the future.”

Hegseth pointed to his earlier testimony about the need to accelerate mission capabilities overall to overcome past funding shortfalls and lack of investment in the military during previous administrations. The Trump administration has requested a more than $1.5 trillion defense budget in FY2027.

“You just you just made the case for this generational investment because of the underinvestment, Senator, in shipbuilding in the previous administration – just static flat bureaucratic, slow. We’re having to revitalize that industry and one DDG is a reflection of a backlog in capability. So, as we ramp on more CA [Contract Administration] capacity, those numbers of DDGs, the workhorse of our Navy, will go up as we grow that force,” Hegseth told Hyde-Smith.

title: HYDE-SMITH, MERKLEY BILL WILL IMPROVE FOREST HEALTH, EXPAND MARKET FOR FORESTRY BIOMASS BYPRODUCTS
text:
‘Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act’ Would Broaden Renewable Fuel Standard Definition of Eligible Renewable Biomass

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.), with U.S. Senator Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), today introduced bipartisan legislation to improve forest health and management by creating new market demand for timber and forestry biomass byproducts.

The Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act (S.5087) would expand the definition of renewable biomass materials that qualify under the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) program within the Clean Air Act. Importantly, the legislation covers both non-federal private land and federal lands, which broadens its appeal beyond regional interests.

“This bipartisan bill creates avenues to help reduce the wildfire threats in the West but also clears the way for biomass produced from non-federal lands in heavily forested states like Mississippi to contribute to the nation’s renewable fuels resources,” Hyde-Smith said. “With this bill, we will make it easier to develop a new revenue stream for the thinnings, logging residuals, and mill byproducts that Mississippi landowners and forest products manufacturers already generate, without requiring them to change how they manage their timberland.”

“Reducing wildfire risk demands innovative solutions and using all the tools at our disposal to invest in wildfire prevention efforts,” said Merkley. “Woody biomass that comes from responsible forest management activities—like hazardous fuels reduction—presents a huge opportunity for communities in Oregon and across the nation. By updating the definition for these materials to qualify as renewable fuels, we can harness their power to create new markets for these materials, reducing wildfire risk and supporting healthier public, private, and Tribal lands.”

A key barrier to proactive forest management is the lack of viable markets for the woody material removed during fuel reduction treatments, thinning operations, and defensible space clearing. Without an economic outlet for this material, the cost of forest management remains prohibitively high for landowners and land managers, leaving forests untreated and vulnerable to wildfire, insects, disease, and habitat degradation. This bill is designed to create new value for forestry residuals and byproducts, helping offset the cost of proactive forest management.

The Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act addresses this by expanding the definition of renewable biomass under the RFS, making a broader range of forest-derived material – including thinnings, harvest residuals, wood chips, sawdust, bark, and manufacturing byproducts from private, federal, and tribal lands – eligible to generate Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs). RINs are the tradeable credits that track renewable fuel volumes under the RFS program, giving refiners more compliance flexibility and expanding the supply of qualifying feedstock.

Mississippi has more than 18.9 million acres of forested land, and the bill’s streamlined certification process would let private landowners make woody biomass from that land RFS-eligible by self-certifying as part of the RIN generation process with no new federal permitting layer required.

U.S. Senators John Kennedy (R-La.), Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), and Angus King (I-Maine) are original cosponsors of S.5087. U.S. Representatives Cliff Bentz (R-Ore.) and Bennie Thompson (D-Miss.) introduce a House companion bill, which is cosponsored by U.S. Representative Mike Ezell (R-Miss.).

A summary of the Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act is available here.

More than 80 stakeholder organizations support the legislation, including the Mississippi Department of Agriculture and Commerce, Mississippi Farm Bureau Federation, Mississippi Forestry Association, Mississippi Loggers Association, Mississippi Lumber Manufacturers Association, Wildlife Mississippi, Alliance for Wildfire Resilience, American Forest Fuels Alliance, American Biomass Energy Association, American Farm Bureau Federation, American Forest Resource Council, American Loggers Council, Bipartisan Policy Center Action, Boone and Crockett Club, Congressional Sportsmen’s Foundation, Forest Landowners Association, National Alliance of Forest Owners, National Association of State Foresters, National Deer Association, National Wild Turkey Federation, Pellet Fuels Institute, Pheasants Forever, Quail Forever, Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation, and Southeastern Lumber Manufacturers Association.

“NAFO thanks Senator Merkley and Senator Hyde-Smith for their leadership in introducing the Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act of 2026. Supporting this legislation is an easy call. The bill creates a powerful new tool for addressing the wildfire crisis and the ongoing closures of wood-consuming paper mills by unlocking practical markets for low-value wood and mill residuals. It supports forest health and resilience through active forest management, strengthens the sawmills that supply our housing sector, bolsters rural economies, and helps America meet growing demand for renewable fuels. At a time when forest owners, mills, and rural communities are facing real economic peril, this targeted fix to the definition of wood in the Renewable Fuel Standard is exactly the kind of commonsense solution Congress should advance,” said Dave Tenny, President and CEO, National Alliance of Forest Owners.

“Farm Bureau appreciates the introduction of bipartisan legislation that supports farmers, foresters and both public and private forest lands across the United States. Updating the definition of renewable biomass for the Renewable Fuel Standard will support active land stewardship and reduce wildfire risk through improved management of public lands. Farm Bureau encourages the Senate to swiftly consider the Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act of 2026,” said Dr. John Newton, Vice President of Public Policy and Economic Analysis, American Farm Bureau Federation.

“The Forest Landowners Association applauds Senators Jeff Merkley and Cindy Hyde-Smith for introducing the Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act of 2026. Family forestry businesses need an all-of-the-above approach to market opportunities, and low-value wood products, manufacturing residuals, and woody biomass should be part of that conversation. While no single policy will address every challenge facing working forests, expanding potential markets for these materials can help provide additional certainty and opportunity for private forest landowners, rural communities, and our nation's forest products supply chain,” said Scott Jones, CEO, Forest Landowners Association.

“The National Wild Turkey Federation proudly supports the Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act of 2026. A major barrier to achieving healthy, fire-resilient forests is the lack of viable markets for materials generated through forest-management activities, including small-diameter trees, treetops, limbs, and other woody residues. Enabling these materials to be used for biodiesel and sustainable aviation fuel creates a critical economic incentive that supports active forest management, strengthens rural wood products infrastructure, and advances forest health,” said Matt Lindler, Director of Government Affairs, National Wild Turkey Federation.

At an oversight hearing in June, Hyde-Smith focused on the risks posed by the delayed cleanup of significant damage to privately owned and national forest property caused by the May 6-7 tornadoes and Winter Storm Fern.

title: HYDE-SMITH NAMED TO DEFENSE APPROPRIATIONS SUBCOMMITTEE
text:
Senate Appropriations Committee Reorganizes Subcommittee Memberships Following the Death of Senator Lindsey Graham

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) today accepted an appointment to serve on the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, giving Mississippi added prominence in Congress when developing funding for the nation’s national security interests.

The appointment was made as the Senate Appropriations Committee reorganized its subcommittee makeup following the passing of U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) on July 11. The new assignments were announced Wednesday by Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine).

“I undertake this new assignment on the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee with a measure of sadness for my dear colleague Lindsey Graham, but I am also resolved to serve as he did in support of our men and women in uniform,” Hyde-Smith said. “I am proud to follow in the footsteps of our own Senator Thad Cochran, who chaired and served on this subcommittee so well, ensuring that states like Mississippi can contribute ably to our nation’s defense.”

Hyde-Smith retains her chairmanship of the Senate Transportation, Housing and Urban Development, and Related Agencies Appropriations Subcommittee, as well as her memberships on the subcommittees on: Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies; Energy and Water Development; Homeland Security; and Labor, Health and Human Services, Education and Related Agencies.

As part of the reorganization, Hyde-Smith relinquished her membership on the Military Construction and Veterans Affairs Appropriations Subcommittee. Links to Hyde-Smith’s overall committee assignments in the 119th Congress are available here.

title: Kaine Applauds Committee Passage of Bipartisan Legislation, Including Bill to Cap Insulin Costs
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Tim Kaine (D-VA), a member of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee, applauded committee passage of the INSULIN Act, legislation that would cap the cost of insulin at $35 per month for those with private insurance and create a pilot program to make insulin more accessible for those without insurance. Kaine, a cosponsor of the legislation, made a statement to the chair during the June 2026 HELP Committee markup urging passage of the bill.

“Far too many Virginians and people throughout the country have to ration their insulin, or even go without it, because of how expensive it is. I am glad that the HELP Committee passed this bipartisan legislation, which will cap insulin prices at $35 a month for people with private insurance and take strides toward making sure those without insurance can afford the insulin they need. I urge all of my colleagues to vote for final passage of this legislation when it comes before the full Senate,” said Kaine. “I am also pleased that the HELP Committee passed my bipartisan bill with Senators Cassidy and Tuberville to make the food supply chain safer; legislation containing provisions of my bill with Senator Collins to reauthorize crucial programs that train and prepare health care providers who care for older Americans; and a bill I cosponsored that will marshal the federal government’s resources to improve research into epilepsy.”

In addition to the INSULIN Act, the HELP Committee passed several other pieces of legislation led or cosponsored by Kaine. The committee passed the:

Educating Medical Professionals and Optimizing Workforce Efficiency and Readiness (EMPOWER) for Health Act, which contains the text of the Kaine-led Geriatrics Workforce Improvement Act, legislation that would reauthorize programs to train the next generation of providers who care for older adults and help improve access to high-quality care.

Making America’s Food Safer Act, legislation Kaine introduced alongside Senators Bill Cassidy (R-LA) and Tommy Tuberville (R-AL) to increase efficiency in the food supply chain auditing process, improve coordination about risks to food safety between regulators at the federal and state/local levels, and expand the authority of the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) to order the destruction of goods that pose a public health risk (e.g., contaminated foods, illegal vaping products).

National Plan for Epilepsy Act, of which Kaine is a cosponsor, which directs HHS to establish and carry out a National Plan for Epilepsy to pursue a cure for the disease and improve its prevention, treatment, and diagnosis.

###

title: Kelly, EPW Committee Colleagues Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Help Prevent Catastrophic Wildfires
text:
Today, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works members Mark Kelly (D-AZ), John Curtis (R-UT), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Alex Padilla (D-CA), and John Boozman (R-AR) introduced the bipartisan Wildfire Emissions Prevention Act (WEPA) of 2026.

The bill would make it easier for states and communities to use prescribed fires to prevent wildfire emissions, protect ecosystems and wildlife habitats, and make American forests and communities safer, healthier, and cleaner. The bill also promotes the efficient use of state air quality resources and provides certainty that states will not be penalized for taking action to prevent wildfires.

“Arizona knows the damage catastrophic wildfires can do to our communities and forests. Prescribed burns are one of the best ways to reduce that risk before a fire gets out of control, and states shouldn’t be penalized for taking action,” said Kelly. “This bipartisan effort will help prevent larger, more destructive wildfires, keep our forests healthier, and better protect families from the smoke and pollution they leave behind.”

“If we’re serious about reducing the size and severity of wildfires, we need to stop punishing local authorities for doing the right thing to improve forest health and remove hazardous fuels. By removing unnecessary regulatory burdens on prescribed burns, our legislation helps ensure states and localities can take proactive measures to help keep our forests and communities safe from the threat of wildfires,” said Curtis.

“When the 2020 Labor Day fires swept across Oregon, I drove over 600 miles and never once escaped the thick, dark smoke that blanketed our state. As Oregonians face yet another record-breaking fire season this year, we need to tackle this crisis at every stage. Our bipartisan bill supports more prescribed fire on the landscape—an essential forest management activity—while giving our communities the resources to plan and prepare for smoke events. Climate chaos is fueling more severe wildfires, and I’ll keep fighting to ensure Oregon and communities nationwide have the tools they need to protect public health and save lives,” said Merkley.

“I am very proud to cosponsor this legislation, which will help reduce the impact of wildfires on our land, our air, and our people. Wildfires have ravaged many parts of our country over the past several years, and change is necessary to ensure that states can successfully prevent the most dangerous and damaging fires. States should have the right to use known prevention practices, including prescribed fires, to mitigate potential catastrophes and care for their land. This bill gives states another tool in their toolbox, and will reduce barriers to successfully managing wildfires and protecting communities nationwide,” said Capito.

“We know prescribed burns help prevent catastrophic wildfires and save lives. This bipartisan bill cuts red tape so California and the whole country can make greater use of this proven, cost-effective tool to protect communities before the next major wildfire. It’s a commonsense step that prioritizes prevention instead of waiting to respond after disaster strikes,” said Padilla.

“In light of the devastating wildfires we now see far too often, Congress should do everything it can to encourage better forest management practices. Prescribed burns are an important way to prevent large-scale fires that threaten homes and property while damaging natural resources. I am proud to join colleagues on both sides of the aisle on this legislation to ensure controlled burns do not generate an adverse Clean Air Act impact or penalize states taking proactive mitigation steps,” said Boozman.

Background:

This builds on Kelly’s efforts to keeping Americans safe by reducing wildfire risk. This month, Kelly joined Senate colleagues in demanding the Federal Emergency Management Agency to ensure that all communities receive the federal resources they need to respond to and prevent wildfires.Kelly’s Wildfire Prevention and Recovery Act, which directs the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to conduct periodic wildfire risk assessments and study the impacts of wildfires on Corps-managed lands through a pilot program beginning in Arizona, passed the EPW) committee as part of the 2026 Water Resources Development Act (WRDA).

title: Luján, Cornyn Introduce Bipartisan Legislative Package to Increase Tax Transparency and Simplify the Tax System
text:
Washington, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senators Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas), members of the Senate Committee on Finance, introduced a bipartisan package of three bills to improve transparency, fairness, and simplicity in the federal tax system. The package includes the Small Tax Case Threshold Modernization Act, the Taxpayer Transparency and Notice Act, and the Tax Complexity and Fraud Prevention Review Act. Together, these bills would help taxpayers by simplifying Internal Revenue Service (IRS) disputes, increasing transparency around unpaid tax balances, and identifying opportunities to simplify the tax code.

“Families across New Mexico and the country deserve a tax system that is transparent, fair, and easy to navigate,” said Senator Luján. “By expanding access to small tax cases, requiring clear, regular communication from the IRS, and giving Congress better tools to understand and reduce unnecessary complexity, this legislative package will create a fairer tax system for all. I’m proud to partner with Senator Cornyn on this effort to help taxpayers avoid costly surprises, access the help they need, and strengthen trust in our tax system.”

“Hardworking Texans and small businesses are too often bogged down by financial stress, bureaucratic hurdles, or the repercussions of honest mistakes when trying to navigate the tax code in good faith,” said Senator Cornyn. “I’m proud to introduce these bipartisan bills with Senator Luján to unlock simplified Tax Court procedures, increase IRS transparency, and make it easier for Americans to meet their tax obligations.”

Small Tax Case Threshold Modernization Act: Updates the Tax Court’s “small tax case procedure” threshold by increasing it from $50,000 to $100,000 and indexing it to inflation, allowing more taxpayers to resolve disputes with the IRS through a faster, simpler, and cost-effective process. Full bill text is available here.

Taxpayer Transparency and Notice Act: Requires the IRS to send quarterly notices to taxpayers with unpaid tax balances, providing clear information on the amount owed, accrued interest and penalties, and available assistance programs. The Taxpayer Transparency and Notice Act helps taxpayers act earlier, avoid surprise debts, and make informed decisions before interest and penalties continue to grow. Full bill text is available here.

Tax Complexity and Fraud Prevention Review Act: Requires the Treasury Department to submit regular reports to Congress on tax law complexity, tax code implementation, and fraud prevention efforts, helping identify opportunities to simplify the tax code, improve oversight, and better protect taxpayers. The Tax Complexity and Fraud Prevention Review Act gives Congress the information it needs to identify unnecessary burdens in the tax code, reduce opportunities for fraud, and create a tax system that is more accessible and fairer for taxpayers. Full bill text is available here.

title: Luján, Warren, Wyden, Baldwin, Whitehouse Press Social Security Commissioner Bisignano on Misleading, Partisan Email Sent to Social Security Beneficiaries
text:
Unsolicited email from Social Security Administration misused government resources to praise President Trump, spread misleading information to Social Security recipients

“(F)ew presidents have done more than President Trump to damage Social Security — yet in an Orwellian twist, you are misusing official resources to heap praise on him.”

Washington, D.C. — U.S. Senators Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), Ranking Member of the Senate Finance Committee, Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.), and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) pressed Social Security Administration (SSA) Commissioner Frank Bisignano for answers on why the SSA earlier this month sent a misleading, partisan email to Social Security recipients.

On July 2, 2026, the SSA sent an unsolicited, highly politicized email to many Social Security recipients. The email referenced President Trump six times, wrongly credited him with “protecting and strengthening Social Security,” and presented misleading information about President Trump “providing meaningful and immediate relief to older Americans.” In July 2025, following the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), SSA similarly used official resources and channels to send a politically charged email.

“This was an unusual communication that served no legitimate purpose: rather than receiving necessary information about benefits or a critical communication from the SSA, recipients received a partisan, politicized message — containing multiple misleading statements — that heaped praise on President Trump,” wrote the senators.

The July 2 email, which celebrated the one-year anniversary of the OBBBA, included highly misleading information about the effects of the bill on seniors and claimed that it included a tax cut that “allows Americans 65 and older to keep more of their hard-earned Social Security benefits.” But the email’s claims were an overestimate of the impacts of the law. In reality, over half of households with seniors were projected to receive no benefit at all from the OBBBA’s Enhanced Deduction for Seniors.

“(N)ow you are abusing the millions of email addresses that may have been obtained through [enrollment in ‘my Social Security’ accounts] or other methods, bombarding Americans with blatantly partisan emails from SSA — misusing Americans’ personal information and jeopardizing the mission and integrity of SSA,” wrote the senators.

The senators ended the letter with a series of questions, including asking about how many Americans the email was sent to, the source of recipients’ email addresses and how they were compiled, the total cost to send the partisan message, and an explanation of how sending the July 2 email was consistent with Commissioner Bisignano’s promise to lead the SSA “in an independent and nonpartisan manner.” The senators demanded answers by August 11, 2026.

“(F)ew presidents have done more than President Trump to damage Social Security — yet in an Orwellian twist, you are misusing official resources to heap praise on him,” concluded the senators. “The decision to send this email raises fresh questions about your judgement and your ability to prioritize SSA beneficiaries.”
