title: N.M. Delegation Joins Pueblo Governors to Push for Permanent Protections for Chaco Canyon
text:
N.M. Delegation’s push occurs during a 14-day public comment period set by the Trump administration in their effort to fully revoke a 20-year mineral withdrawal that has protected public lands within Chaco Canyon

WASHINGTON — Today, U.S. Senators Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), and U.S. Representatives Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.), Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.), and Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) joined the All Pueblo Council of Governors (APCG) at a press conference to call for permanent protection of Chaco Canyon.

Located in northwestern New Mexico, the Greater Chaco landscape is a region of great cultural, spiritual, and historical significance to many Pueblos and Tribes and contains living sacred sites. Chaco was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987 and is one of only 24 such sites in the United States.

Last week, the Trump administration announced a proposal to fully revoke a 20-year mineral withdrawal that has protected public lands surrounding the Chaco Culture National Historic Park, and only allowed 14 days for public comment. The N.M. Delegation released a statement strongly condemning the Trump administration’s actions.

This week, Heinrich, Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, led a N.M. Delegation letter urging U.S. Department of the Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to extend the public comment period to 90-days and conduct genuine Tribal consultation and extensive public engagement before revoking protections for the Chaco region. Most importantly, the Delegation urged Secretary Burgum to withdraw this proposal and leave Public Land Order No. 7923 in place. The Delegation also, once again, invited Secretary Burgum to visit Chaco before taking any action that would put this irreplaceable cultural landmark at risk.

VIDEO: The N.M. Delegation joins the All Pueblo Council of Governors to call for permanent protection of the Chaco Canyon Cultural Protection Zone, July 22, 2026.

“Chaco Canyon is not for sale.New Mexico has an important role to play producing energy for the nation. We’re the second largest producer of oil in the country, we produce far more electrons than we consume, and we have never had to sacrifice our most sacred places to do that — and we should not do that going forward,” said Heinrich, Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. “Chaco Canyon is not just a place on a map. It is not a museum. It is not about what happened 1,000 years ago. It is about the future. It is about these governors and their communities, their identity, and their relationship to this sacred place that they use now. This is about our state’s ability to stand up for what is right and moral. Our New Mexico Delegation stands arm in arm and shoulder to shoulder with these Tribal governors and their communities in standing up to protect this place. And we will fight that fight until we win.”

“Chaco Canyon is more than a place on a map — it is thousands of years of culture, history, and the enduring spirit of the Pueblo peoples. Protecting Chaco is our sacred responsibility. Once Chaco is damaged, it cannot be undone. That’s why we are standing together to make our voices heard,” said Luján. “I am deeply grateful for the Pueblo leaders whose leadership and tireless advocacy are at the heart of the fight to protect Chaco Canyon. Now is your turn to make your voice heard. Submit your comment today to tell the Trump administration to keep its hands off Chaco.”

“There is not a single molecule of gas worth sacrificing a landscape that holds more than 4,700 archaeological sites, the prayers and history of generations, and the living culture of Chaco Canyon,” said Leger Fernández, Ranking Member of the House Indian and Insular Affairs Subcommittee. “Secretary Burgum lied when he promised meaningful, in-person tribal consultation before any decision was made. Our Chaco Cultural Heritage Area Protection Act will permanently protect Chaco. In the meantime, we will use every tool at our disposal to stop the bulldozers from tearing up living history.”

“Chaco Canyon is not for sale! As one the most sacred places on the planet — the Greater Chaco Landscape has been a sacred landscape for Pueblo and Diné people since time immemorial,” said Stansbury, Democratic Vice Chair of the Congressional Native American Caucus. “The Trump Administration’s plan to open these sacred places to oil and gas drilling is a direct attack to Tribal Sovereignty and New Mexico’s history, cultures, and living traditions. I am proud to stand today and every day with the entire New Mexico delegation, the All Pueblo Council of Governors, Tribal leaders, advocates, and communities across our state to protect this irreplaceable landscape for generations to come. We ask the American people to stand with us — and please submit a public comment and help save Chaco Canyon.”

“Chaco is central to New Mexico’s identity — a living cultural landscape, a sacred place and an irreplaceable unit of our national public lands. The Administration’s attempt to revoke the protections of this landscape, built through years of consultation and community engagement, with just 14 days of public comment is disingenuous and disrespectful,” said Vasquez. “Secretary Burgum must withdraw this proposal and come to New Mexico to hear directly from Pueblo leaders. He has an open invitation to come to Chaco and meet with Pueblo leaders. We can support responsible energy development without sacrificing places like Chaco that, once damaged, will be lost forever.”

The New Mexico Congressional Delegation has worked tirelessly to permanently protect Chaco Canyon.

Last week, the N.M. Delegation released a statement in response to the news that the Trump administration is proposing to fully revoke a 20-year mineral withdrawal that has protected public lands surrounding the Chaco Culture National Historic Park, and only allowing 14 days for public comment.

In April, the N.M. Delegation submitted a comment letter to the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) urging the Trump administration to reverse course on its decision to initiate the process to undo a 20-year mineral withdrawal that has kept public lands in the Chaco Canyon Cultural Protection Zone off-limits to new oil and gas leasing. Earlier that month, the N.M. Delegation sent statements in opposition to the Trump administration only granting seven days to submit scoping comments.

Last November, Heinrich, Luján, and Stansbury hosted a press conference with Pueblo leaders on the actions needed to permanently protect the landscape.

Last September, the N.M. Delegation hosted a press conference in front of the U.S. Capitol with 20 Governors and leaders from the Santa Ana, Picuris, Cochiti, Zia, Tesuque, Acoma, Santo Domingo, and Laguna Pueblos to demand the Trump administration permanently protect Chaco Canyon, and to invite U.S. Department of the Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to visit the Greater Chaco landscape before deciding its fate. Watch the video of the full press conference here.

In June 2025, the N.M. Delegation sent a letter initially inviting Secretary Burgum to visit Chaco Canyon and engage directly with Tribal leaders and local communities to hear about the profound cultural and spiritual significance of this sacred landscape. Secretary Burgum issued the directive to begin revoking the Chaco protections without experiencing it firsthand. Following Secretary Burgum’s directive, the N.M. Delegation sent a letter urging the Trump administration to reverse course on its decision to initiate the process to fully revoke Chaco Canyon’s protections.

In April 2025, the N.M. Delegation reintroduced legislation to protect Chaco Canyon and the greater sacred landscape surrounding the Chaco Culture National Historic Park. The legislation is led by Luján in the U.S. Senate and Leger Fernández in the U.S. House of Representatives.

title: N.M. Delegation Urges Trump Admin to Extend Comment Period for Chaco Canyon Protection, Calls for Genuine Tribal Consultation, Invites Burgum to Visit Chaco Canyon Before Taking Further Action
text:
WASHINGTON – This week, U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, U.S. Senator Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), and U.S. Representatives Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.), member of the U.S. House Natural Resources Committee, Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.), member of the U.S. House Natural Resources Committee, and Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) sent a letter to U.S. Department of the Interior (DOI) Secretary Doug Burgum expressing deep concern and opposition to the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) only allowing 14 days for public comment in response to the Trump administration’s proposal to fully revoke a 20-year mineral withdrawal that has protected public lands surrounding Chaco Culture National Historical Park.

The lawmakers requested that the Department immediately extend the comment period to no fewer than 90 days and withdraw their proposal to gut protections for Chaco Canyon. The Delegation additionally invited Secretary Burgum to visit Chaco Canyon before taking any action that would put this irreplaceable landscape at risk.

“Since your confirmation, we have written numerous letters and spoken to you directly expressing why protections for the greater Chacoan landscape are important and popular in New Mexico. Yet the process to revoke the protections continues to move at a rapid pace… We would like to register immense concern and frustration with the fourteen-day public comment period. Fourteen days does not represent the scope of this action, is arbitrary, and not representative of the work that went into implementing PLO No. 7923,” the lawmakers began.

“The Chacoan region is a natural and cultural landscape and not represented by isolated individual sites. The withdrawal you are proposing to erase was built from over a decade of community and Tribal input… The previous public process was robust and ended in protection of the Chacoan landscape. In contrast, the current process to remove protections is based on an inadequate and incomplete review. It certainly does not constitute full and meaningful Tribal consultation,” the lawmakers continued.

“You committed before the House Natural Resources Committee to send an official with decision-making authority to conduct in-person consultation with every Tribe with an interest in Chaco. The draft assessment itself shows that commitment has not been met. Several Pueblos received nothing more than an invitation, others received only ‘informational meetings.’ No Secretarial-level official appears anywhere in its consultation record. An informational briefing or a group meeting in D.C. is not consultation. And despite repeated invitations from Pueblos and from every member of this delegation, you have not yet visited Chaco,” the lawmakers continued.

The lawmakers concluded by urging Secretary Burgum to extend the review process on his proposal to revoke protections for the Chaco Canyon Cultural protection zone, meaningfully engage with Tribes in good faith, extend the comment period to 90 days, visit Chaco Canyon, and, ultimately, reverse the proposal to fully revoke a 20-year mineral withdrawal protecting Chaco Canyon from drilling.

Read the full letter here and below:

Since your confirmation, we have written numerous letters and spoken to you directly expressing why protections for the greater Chacoan landscape are important and popular in New Mexico. Yet the process to revoke the protections continues to move at a rapid pace. Today, we write in response and in strong opposition to the Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM) draft environmental assessment proposing the full revocation of Public Land Order No. 7923, which protects approximately 336,404 acres surrounding Chaco Culture National Historical Park. We would like to register immense concern and frustration with the fourteen-day public comment period. Fourteen days does not represent the scope of this action, is arbitrary, and not representative of the work that went into implementing PLO No. 7923.

The Chacoan region is a natural and cultural landscape and not represented by isolated individual sites. The withdrawal you are proposing to erase was built from over a decade of community and Tribal input. Over the span of a year-and-a-half, the BLM conducted 150 days of public comment, eight public meetings, full and meaningful Tribal consultation, and a full environmental review to implement the existing withdrawal. BLM is now proposing to completely undo it after a seven-day scoping period and a fourteen-day comment window, while characterizing the revocation as a mere “continuation” of the original process. The previous public process was robust and ended in protection of the Chacoan landscape. In contrast, the current process to remove protections is based on an inadequate and incomplete review. It certainly does not constitute full and meaningful Tribal consultation.

Two months ago, the National Trust for Historic Preservation named the Greater Chaco Cultural Landscape as one of America’s Eleven Most Endangered Historic Places. There are 4,730 documented cultural sites within the 10-mile withdrawal radius and there could be countless more needing protection. This is a process that should not be rushed.

On June 12, 2025, you committed before the House Natural Resources Committee to send an official with decision-making authority to conduct in-person consultation with every Tribe with an interest in Chaco. The draft assessment itself shows that commitment has not been met. Several Pueblos received nothing more than an invitation, others received only “informational meetings.” No Secretarial-level official appears anywhere in its consultation record. An informational briefing or a group meeting in D.C. is not consultation. And despite repeated invitations from Pueblos and from every member of this delegation, you have not yet visited Chaco.

We, therefore, call for an actual review process regarding revoking protections for the Chaco region, with genuine Tribal consultation, as with the previous public process included. We request that the Department immediately extend the comment period to no fewer than 90 days. And, most importantly, we urge you to stand down, withdraw this proposal and leave Public Land Order No. 7923 in place. Further, we once again invite you to come to Chaco before taking any action that would put this irreplaceable landscape at risk.

Sincerely,

title: Lummis Releases Updated Clarity Act Text
text:
Washington, D.C.— Today, Senate Banking Digital Assets Subcommittee Chair Cynthia Lummis (R-WY) released updated text for the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act (H.R. 3633), which reflects the merged work products of the Banking and Agriculture Committees.

“This is another step in my years-long journey to ensure the U.S. leads the way on digital assets,” said Lummis. “The U.S. has always been at the forefront of financial innovation, and the coming weeks are likely the last real chance we will have for years to get this right. I want to thank Chairman Scott, Chairman Boozman, and Leader Thune for their support and leadership, and I look forward to partnering with them to ensure the U.S. leads the way in digital assets for generations to come. I also want to thank my Democratic colleagues for their important contributions to this draft, and express my commitment to reaching a deal in the coming days that will allow this legislation to become law.”

Chairman Boozman, who is leading the Agriculture Committee portion said:

“This legislation establishes a clear, regulatory framework for digital commodities,” said Boozman. “It delivers the certainty consumers, businesses and markets have been calling for by creating strong safeguards while supporting responsible innovation. This is the result of months of bipartisan collaboration and continued conversations with stakeholders to strengthen the final bill. It’s time for the Senate to pass this legislation and provide the regulatory clarity the marketplace needs to ensure the U.S. remains a global leader.”

Chairman Scott, who is leading the Banking Committee portion said:

“As a kid raised by a single mom in South Carolina, I saw firsthand how access to opportunity can change the course of a family’s life,” said Scott. “That’s what the Clarity Act is about: protecting everyday Americans and their hard-earned money, giving entrepreneurs a fair shot to build and create jobs here at home, and strengthening our national security by making it harder for criminals and foreign adversaries to exploit our financial system. I’m grateful to the Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman Boozman and Digital Assets Subcommittee Chair Lummis for their partnership, and I look forward to working together to get this bill across the finish line.”

In 2022, Senator Lummis and Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) introduced the Responsible Financial Innovation Act, a comprehensive bipartisan bill to establish the first regulatory framework for digital assets in the United States, dividing oversight jurisdiction between the SEC and CFTC.

In 2023, Senators Lummis and Gillibrand reintroduced the legislation.

In July of 2025, Senator Lummis, Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott (R-SC), and Senators Bill Hagerty (R-TN), and Bernie Moreno (R-OH) released a Senate discussion draft of the Responsible Financial Innovation Act of 2025.

In May 2026, the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act passed out of the Banking Committee by a 15 to 9 bipartisan vote.

Senator Lummis is the Senate’s leading voice on digital assets, having authored the foundational legislative framework that helped shape the path for comprehensive market structure. As Chair of the Senate Banking Subcommittee on Digital Assets, she continues to lead the effort to establish clear, commonsense rules that keep the U.S. at the forefront of financial innovation and give consumers the confidence they need to safely participate in the U.S. economy.

title: Markey, Blumenthal, Wyden Demand FTC Reject X’s Frivolous Petition to Evade Privacy Obligations
text:
Letter Text (PDF)

Washington (July 22, 2026) - Senator Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.), member of the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, along with Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) today wrote to Andrew Ferguson, Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), urging the agency to reject X’s petition to terminate the company’s privacy responsibilities under a 2022 FTC order. The FTC unanimously approved the 2022 order in response to Twitter’s repeated privacy violations, which were well publicized before Elon Musk purchased the company and rebranded it as “X.”

In its petition, X makes the extraordinary claim that rebranding Twitter as X somehow frees the company from the privacy obligations it inherited. Beyond this claim, X’s other arguments — that the order’s compliance is too costly, that the company should be trusted to self-regulate, and that ending the obligations under this order would serve the public interest in the American AI race — are similarly frivolous. The senators therefore call for the Commission to reject X’s self-serving attempt to evade its legal responsibilities.

In the letter, the lawmakers wrote, “Despite X’s arguments otherwise, the company is no stranger to the 2022 order; it is Twitter’s successor. Although Twitter rebranded as X in 2023, X kept Twitter’s assets, its users, and their data. Notably, the FTC order contemplated such a corporate rebranding. The 2022 order defines ‘Respondent’ to include Twitter’s ‘successors and assigns,’ and its carve-out for genuinely distinct businesses applies only to entities that do not ‘collect, maintain, use, disclose, access, or provide access to’ data that previously enabled Twitter’s services — a condition X plainly does not meet. A name change and new leadership do not undo that legal continuity. If they did, any company could escape an FTC order simply by merging with a new entity or changing its name. The Commission should require X to comply with the 2022 order it inherited.”

The lawmakers continued, “X’s claim that compliance with the 2022 order is too costly rings hollow given the company’s scale and the nature of the obligations it knowingly inherited. X puts the cost of compliance at roughly $17 million over the past four years — or around $4.25 million per year. When Musk bought Twitter in 2022, he valued the company at $44 billion, making those routine compliance costs a fraction of the value assigned to the company just a few years ago. Furthermore, Musk, the company’s owner, is the richest person in the world, with sufficient personal wealth to support the company. More importantly, independent privacy and security oversight is not an optional expense to be cut when it becomes inconvenient. A company cannot earn early release from a privacy order simply by saying that compliance costs money.”

title: Markey, Blunt Rochester Lead Senate Democrats in Seeking to Pass House Bill Designating Haiti for Temporary Protected Status
text:
Watch: Senators Markey, colleagues urge Senate to designate Haiti for TPS

Washington (July 22, 2026) – Senator Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.) and Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) today led Senate Democrats on the Senate Floor in seeking to pass the House bill that would designate Haiti for Temporary Protected Status (TPS). Senator Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) blocked its passage.

Senators Markey and Blunt Rochester, along with Representative Ayanna Pressley (MA-07), have been championing Representative Laura Gillen’s (NY-04) House bill H.R. 1689, which passed the House in April.

“For generations, Massachusetts has been shaped by our immigrant communities. We have a moral duty to protect Haitian TPS holders and provide them with a permanent pathway to citizenship. I am utterly disappointed that Republicans blocked passage of the bill I introduced with Senator Blunt Rochester to designate Haiti for TPS until after the next presidential election. Haitian TPS holders deserve the stability of preserving their status, the dignity to live without fear, and the security of not being returned to danger. I will not stop in my fight to protect the Haitian TPS community,” said Senator Markey.

“The Trump Administration’s attempt to uproot Haitian TPS holders and send them back to a country in complete chaos is as cruel as it is harmful to our communities. TPS was created to give people fleeing unrest in their home countries a safe place to call home - born out of the American spirit of welcoming immigrants seeking a better life,” said Senator Blunt Rochester. “It’s time for Congress to step in, stand up for the core values that built America, and extend TPS for Haitian immigrants.”

Senator Markey has worked consistently to protect TPS for Haiti and support the Haitian community in Massachusetts amid the Trump administration’s attacks on TPS and Haitians.

On June 25, after the U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration’s termination of TPS for Haiti and Syria in the consolidated case, Mullin v. Doe, Senator Markey, alongside Representatives Ayanna Pressley (MA-07), Katherine Clark (MA-05), Maxwell Frost (FL-10), and Debbie Wasserman Schultz (FL-25) held a press conference outside the Court denouncing the decision.

In April 2026, Senator Markey, Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), Congresswoman Wasserman Schultz, and Congresswoman Pressley led 26 Senators and 157 Representatives in filing an amicus brief in the U.S. Supreme Court in Miot v. Trump, a consolidated case challenging the Trump administration’s unlawful termination of Haiti and Syria TPS.

In September 2025, Senator Markey led an amicus brief in Miot v. Trump, the companion case to Mullin v. Doe, when the case was before the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. In February 2026, Senator Markey applauded the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia’s decision to pause the Trump administration’s termination of TPS for Haiti, which was set to expire on February 3.

In March, Senator Markey welcomed the D.C. Circuit’s ruling blocking the Trump administration from immediately terminating TPS for Haiti.

In January, Senator Markey and Rep. Pressley held a field hearing at Jubilee Christian Church in Mattapan to highlight the importance of extending TPS for Haiti. The lawmakers heard from panels of individuals, advocates, and community leaders impacted by the Trump administration’s decision to end Haiti TPS.

title: Markey Decries Trump-Saudi Nuclear Deal: “Irresponsible and Dangerous”
text:
Senator Rubio was against Saudi nuclear deal before Secretary Rubio was for it

Washington (July 22, 2026) - Senator Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.), co-chair of the bicameral Nuclear Weapons and Arms Control Working Group, today released the following statement on Trump’s deal with Saudi Arabia that would open the door to providing the Kingdom with the most sensitive nuclear technologies without requiring the most stringent safeguards against the development of nuclear weapons.

“As a Senator, Secretary Rubio was among the loudest voices warning about the dangers of giving Saudi Arabia, which has openly vowed to develop nuclear weapons, access to nuclear technology. Now, Secretary Rubio and President Trump risk the security of the United States and its allies in the Middle East by potentially enabling nuclear proliferation in Saudi Arabia and igniting an arms race in the region. Let us be clear: allowing Saudi Arabia to develop nuclear weapons would be irresponsible and dangerous.

“Since the start of his second term, President Trump has launched two illegal attacks against Iran, in part to prevent Tehran from enriching uranium. Ironically, the administration is now opening the door for Saudi Arabia to gain access to that same technology. The Trump administration has needlessly abandoned the ‘Gold Standard,’ which would ban enrichment and reprocessing and require International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) additional protocol safeguards.

“Trump’s and Secretary Rubio’s hypocrisy is matched only by their recklessness. They are allowing Saudi Arabia, a belligerent and authoritarian nation, to develop nuclear weapons technologies while starting a war with Iran under the guise of preventing an Iranian nuclear bomb. This deal would make us all less safe. We must stop the proliferation of nuclear weapons.”

As a founder of the national Nuclear Freeze movement, Senator Markey has long been the Congressional leader on ending the proliferation of nuclear weapons.

On March 25, Senators Markey and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) reintroduced the No Nuclear Weapons for Saudi Arabia Act, legislation that would mandate that any nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia can go into effect only if it receives the affirmative vote of Congress.

On March 18, Senator Markey led his colleagues in writing to Secretary Rubio demanding the Trump administration must meet the “gold standard” of nuclear non-proliferation protections by denying Saudi Arabia the means to produce weapons-grade uranium and plutonium, materials that could be used in a nuclear bomb.

In January, Senator Markey wrote to President Trump urging the strongest possible non-proliferation measures in any revised nuclear cooperation agreement with South Korea.

In November 2025, Senator Markey and Congressman Joaquin Castro (TX-20) wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, urging the Trump administration to include the strongest possible “gold standard” nonproliferation measures in any nuclear cooperation agreement with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to foreclose any pathway to a nuclear weapon.

In July 2025, Senator Markey introduced the Senate companion to H.Res.317, urging the United States to lead the world in halting the nuclear arms race.

In November 2024, Senator Markey wrote to the Biden administration seeking answers about any agreement that would normalize relations between the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and Israel in exchange for civil nuclear energy cooperation and a U.S. defense commitment to the Kingdom.

As far back as 2017, Senator Markey pressed the first Trump administration on the status of all current and ongoing discussions between the United States and other countries, including Saudi Arabia, on 123 agreements after it was reported that former National Security Advisor Michael Flynn was peddling a plan to build nuclear reactors throughout the Middle East.

title: Senator Marshall: AI Will Not Replace Us—It Will Assist Us
text:
Senator Marshall At Semafor’s World of Work Event with Burgess Everett

Washington – U.S. Senator Roger Marshall, M.D. (R-Kansas), joined Burgess Everett at Semafor’sWorld of Work event to discuss his Patients Deserve Price Tags Act and lowering the cost of health care for Americans, AI use in health care, how AI will affect the workforce, the federal government’s place in AI and data center legislation, and more.

Click HERE to download the full video.

On current Senate priorities and the Patients Deserve Price Tags Act:

“You know, I think number one, the election is starting to wear heavy on our shoulders. Like I feel like I should be back — I’m up this year so I feel like I should be back in Kansas. And at the same time, I’m already focused on: can we keep the government open? That would probably be the big long-term goal here — September 30th. But then today we have our price tags bill. Patients deserve price tags, not surprise billing; it forces transparency and competition into healthcare. This is why I came to D.C., was to do this bill. This is a concept I had 15 years ago, I’ve been in Congress now nine years, and this is one of the big three reasons I came. And we’re going to get it through committee today.”

“Oh, I think it’s going to pass the committee, or we wouldn’t be on it. We’ve got lots of co-sponsors on both sides of the aisle; it is a bipartisan issue. This will bring down the cost of healthcare by $1,000 a month, is what we’re expecting for an average family. There’s no other bill out there, there’s nothing out there that would bring down the cost of living more than this bill would. The President’s very motivated, I think that we’re all in Congress motivated, so I think it has a real chance of getting to the finish line.”

“That MRI, you know, it might be $600 here, and it might be $3,000 here for the same quality. You know, I ran a hospital along with my doctor’s practice, oversaw health departments — I’ve seen healthcare inside and out, and this is the great boogeyman. Why do you have to wait? You still won’t know what the price is till three months from now.”

On AI use in health care:

“Right. So, I think the big picture to me — my theme — would be ‘human in the loop.’ You want to be the human in the loop of AI. Even today, I use AI two or three hours a day and on Saturdays, I’ll spend four or six hours researching something. You know, preparing for this meeting. So, what does AI mean to other people besides me? So, the fact-finding part of this — usually we had leg staff working on the fact-finding. So, I’m constantly working ahead and trying to get that fact-finding part out of this, and once I find the facts, then I can jump to the future. So, for the doctor, I think it’s going to help us with the medical records; it’s going to help the data entry portion of this — interpreting the data, making sure we’re not missing something. Really, for the most part in medicine, AI is really machine learning. So, reading Pap smears, reading mammograms. If you show AI what we’re looking for in a mammogram — so pull out all the ones that look like this, this, and this. But you still need a human in the loop to say, ‘Okay, of these 10, this is the one that needs biopsied.’”

“So, speaking of legislation — our prior authorization bill, which we think will get across the finish line this year as well. Again, something I’ve worked eight years on to streamline prior authorization. So, AI will be used, but I think it can be used to an advantage. I think that if AI looks at…let’s say that I need to replace someone’s hip. If Medicare Advantage needs to say, ‘Here’s the boxes the doctor needs to check.’ The nurses do that for us of course; we send it to the company, AI looks at that, and then great. And if one of the boxes is missed, AI kicks it out and then automatically emails my nurse and says, ‘Why didn’t you do physical therapy for three months?’ or whatever it is. So, I think it can expedite it. Just like nuclear physics — it can be used for good, it can be used for bad.”

On AI’s effect on the workforce:

“Oh, absolutely, and I think we’re already seeing it. Thousands of jobs at Meta, Amazon — it’s already happening as well. But I’m not fearful of it. When my grandfather was born, 30% of Americans worked in agriculture: 30%. When my dad was born, 10% of Americans worked in ag, and today 1%. So those jobs — people went to the city. Now they’re building airplanes or electricians, all those other types of things that require a human to do them. Now we’re building airplanes in Boeing and Textron in Wichita, but they’re using AI for quality assurance. So, they’re able to scan all the rivets on this plane’s wing at one moment, and then AI identifies — and again, it’s machine learning, really — and says, ‘This is the abnormal rivets. Now go back and look at it.’ The human in the loop says, ‘Yeah, we circle this, this, and this one,’ and they go back and redo those as well. So, I’m fearful of it — not fearful, that’s the wrong word — I’m cognizant of it; we need to embrace it. And I think as a Senator, who’s going to solve the riddle here? I’m a big community college, technical college fan. I don’t know how to solve the riddle — the federal government will throw money at it, but I really have faith in people back home in solving this riddle. Community colleges, technical colleges can quickly flex to the needs of the day. My wife and I are both community college graduates, first-generation college students as well — huge fans of it. So, I think if you’re a data entry person right now, and even if you’re a legal aide, all those types of things like that, you better be figuring out what Plan B is. And I think our community colleges and technical colleges are the players. The interesting thought I had yesterday — we were discussing this amongst ourselves at lunch, and I said, ‘Certainly the early-entry accountants and lawyers, those jobs will be taken over by AI. But how do we get seasoned lawyers and seasoned accountants if they don’t start here?’ So, if you’re an accountant that’s graduating, you’ve got to figure out how you’re going to get in that loop. Interpreting that data, I guess, and then giving it to your senior partners — you better be able to understand, once the data is assimilated, and be able to contribute to what this data means.”

On AI data centers and whether Senator Marshall would support a statewide moratorium:

“Yeah, people in Kansas are on fire against them, and several dozen counties have placed moratoriums on them. Certainly, it is a state issue— it’s a county issue, really, a zoning issue. But I certainly support their moratoriums — I think they need to figure out the water issue and the electricity issue. I don’t know why we would give them any tax breaks because they really don’t bring a lot of jobs after they’re built. I mean, once they’re built, there’s some maintenance to them as well. But I certainly don’t want it to drive up other people’s electricity costs, and I see that over and over. Panasonic came to Kansas, built this huge plant, and they had huge electricity needs, and guess what? Everyone around in that area has got increased rates because of the increased demand as well. So, we need to solve the energy problem. The closed-loop systems are going to make up for a lot of it as well. But Kansans are really upset about it, and I’ve learned that we better listen and figure out. I wonder if, in the backdrop of this, they’re really worried about the job issue, but we’ll see how that plays out.”

“Oh, I think certainly that’s not a Senate decision to make. I don’t think if I were a governor I would push for that; I’d rather try to keep the decisions local.”

On federal AI legislation:

“Preemption is just impossible right now. I feel like Goldilocks — not too hot, not too cold, let’s get it just right. You know, the big part of AI I’m probably most concerned about is pornography, going after children, some of those types of things. I am ready to pass some type of legislation that would impact it from that standpoint, but that would probably be part of a bigger social media legislation. The quick thing I would say about AI is the national security side of this. And I really think that’s what’s going to drive Congress’s decisions up here more than the job issue— I think we’re going to quickly respond to this. When quantum computing becomes a real thing combined with AI, I think that foreign countries, terrorists, and our own government will be able to break down blockchain technology and encryption as well. So, I think that’s my big fear— what terrorists could do to assault all the cyber issues as well. So, quantum— keep your eye on quantum computing; I think it’s real. And again, the good part though is we’re going to be able to do precision medicine, precision agriculture, all those types of things by using this quantum computing. Looking at your DNA— let’s say you have hypertension— if I got a menu of medicines I can use for hypertension now, which one of those is the best one for your DNA? You have type 2 diabetes, which one of the GLP-1s will be best for you? Rather than traditionally, it’s kind of like, ‘Well, here’s the recipe we start with,’ and it might take us six months or a year to get it right.”

On a possible HELP Committee chairmanship:

“So, Lisa Murkowski would be in front of me as well— so they would have to give up their committee assignments. It would be a great honor, but certainly respect what Lisa and what Rand are going to do. But I think I have my experiences in the real world.”

“So, it’s not just health— it’s health, education, labor, and pensions. And more than being a doctor— I mentioned I ran a hospital; I’ve overseen health departments. But the labor part of this— I was raised in a union town, I’ve worked at refineries, so I think I understand a little bit more about the labor part of this. Education— I think being a first-generation college student, I have a special appreciation for education as well, and want to make sure that our public schools and our public universities and colleges survive through all these transitions as well. They need to become more efficient, but I think that those experiences in life have prepared me for this moment. And if I have the opportunity, again, why did I come here? I think you can impact the priorities on that committee, of all the priorities out there. My leadership skills, what I’ve done, running a hospital, military experience, I think leadership is just so important right now. Picking up on all these things we’re talking about today: where can government make a difference without overreaching?”

On Senator Marshall’s reelection and whether Republicans have done enough on the economy:

“I think just to be frank here, the Democrats have money to burn. They’re able to raise money at the candidate level way beyond what we’re able to for a whole lot of reasons, so I think they’ve got the money to burn. They’ll have a solid candidate as well. I’m confident, but not cocky. But we’ll run this to the finish line. We’re assuming it’ll be a tight race, and we’re taking it for real.”

“So, I think we have, but the real issue is the price of gas. I’ve never seen anything like this— that my numbers just go up or down with the price of gas. We could talk about the Working Family Tax Cuts— manufacturing is booming back home because of it, best cattle prices in my entire lifetime, really good jobs back home as well. It’s one of the best economies I’ve lived through. At the same time, there’s a group of folks out there that’s struggling. It’s people my children’s age, folks under the age of 40, the folks that graduated with large college debt; they didn’t buy a house yet. And gas and groceries and living credit card to credit card is where they are right now. So, we need to continue to focus on the cost of living— which we did with our housing bill, and we’re going to do today with our price tags bill as well. And then we got to get the price of gas down. And it’s totally: can we get Iran wrapped up sooner than later, and get that price of gas down? Because we’re energy independent, the price will come tumbling down if we just get this situation in Iran wrapped up.”

On ending the war in Iran:

“Yeah, you know, I think every day’s a new day. I stay true to my goals from the beginning: Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon; next, no boots on the ground. I hate war. My dad served, my brother served, I served, my son is serving now. We’ve lost 18 soldiers now, and that’s why President Eisenhower said, ‘I hate war, as only a soldier who lived it can, with all its brutality, futility, and stupidity.’ I’m supporting our Commander-in-Chief; I’m supporting our troops. If we’re going to be there, we need to rip the band-aid off and get this done sooner than later. When will Iran finally capitulate? You’re dealing with religious, irrational theocrats, so I just don’t think Americans have an appreciation for how hard it is to deal with people that have no value for human life— especially women’s lives, children’s lives; they’re murdering tens of thousands of Christians, and on and on. So, it’s really day to day, and I just hope and pray. I just left a bipartisan prayer breakfast; there are about 24 of us that get together once a week like this, and of course one of our prayers is that these wars would end. But we cannot let Iran have nuclear weapons. And right now, the doctor in me says the benefits outweigh the risk. But I sure mourn the loss of those 18 soldiers who made the ultimate sacrifice.”

###

title: Senator Marshall: Patients Deserve Price Tags, Not Surprise Bills
text:
Senator Marshall Hosts Press Conference on Patients Deserve Price Tags Act

Washington – Today, U.S. Senator Roger Marshall, M.D. (R-Kansas), hosted a press conference following the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) Committee’s overwhelming bipartisan approval of his Patients Deserve Price Tags Act, bringing the legislation one step closer to becoming law.

Senator Marshall was joined by the bill’s original cosponsor, Senator John Hickenlooper (D-Colorado), and Senate HELP Committee Chairman Bill Cassidy, M.D. (R-Louisiana) to celebrate the bill’s advancement and highlight its potential to lower healthcare costs for American families through greater price transparency.

Click HERE or on the image to download Senator Marshall’s full remarks.

Remarks as delivered:

“I’m honored to be up here with Senator John Hickenlooper from the great state of Colorado, and, of course, Dr. Bill Cassidy, chairman of our committee.

This was a big win today – 21 to 1. Our Price Tags bill comes out of committee, and our message is simple: patients deserve price tags, not surprise bills.

We believe this bill can save the average American family about $1,000 a year. If you take an average Kansas family making around $70,000 a year and give them an extra $1,000 in savings, that’s real money.

The number one issue back home in Kansas – and I know it’s true in Colorado and Louisiana as well – as the cost of living. I believe this is the bill that will actually make a difference, sooner rather than later, in bringing down the cost of living for families.

Patients deserve price tags instead of surprise bills. Our bill forces transparency. It forces competition. And, like Senator Hickenlooper said, there will be penalties if hospitals don’t comply.

Could you imagine driving down the street needing gas? There are four convenience stores on the corner, and you’re trying to guess how much the gas costs. That’s essentially how our healthcare system works today. Not only would they refuse to show you the price, but you wouldn’t even know what it cost after you filled up. You’d simply hand them your credit card, wait three months, and then find out how much they charged you.

The same thing applies at the grocery store. Could you imagine standing at the meat counter trying to decide between hamburger and steak, or chicken and pork, without knowing what any of them cost?

Just like every other industry, when you force transparency, when you require prices to be posted, and when you create real competition, prices come down. In our case, we believe this bill can save families about $1,000 a year. We also think those savings will spill over into Medicare, Medicaid, and other payers. As those prices come down, it will help those folks as well.

So, I couldn’t be prouder. I couldn’t be prouder of our staffs. Again, John, thank you to you and your staff for all your work, and thank you to the committee staff on both sides of the aisle as well.

Bill Cassidy, thank you for your leadership. With that, I’ll turn the microphone over to you.”

###

title: Senator Marshall’s Patients Deserve Price Tags Act Passes Senate HELP Committee
text:
Washington – Today, U.S. Senator Roger Marshall, M.D. (R-Kansas) released the following statement after his and Senator John Hickenlooper’s (D-Colorado) bipartisan Patients Deserve Price Tags Actpassed the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) with overwhelming bipartisan support, marking a major milestone toward lowering healthcare costs for American families.

The legislation requires hospitals and insurers to publicly disclose healthcare prices, giving patients the ability to compare costs before receiving care. By increasing transparency and competition, the bill will help lower healthcare costs, empower patients, and put consumers back in control of their healthcare decisions.

“Patients deserve price tags, not surprise bills. This is the only bipartisan healthcare reform before Congress today that can begin lowering the cost of living immediately by bringing real competition to our healthcare system,” said Senator Marshall. “Americans have waited far too long to know what their care will cost before they receive it, and I’m proud this commonsense legislation passed out of the HELP Committee today with overwhelming bipartisan support. It’s time to put patients back in charge – not the big hospital systems and insurance companies.”

Senator Marshall thanked his bipartisan partner, Senator John Hickenlooper (D-Colorado), for his leadership in introducing the legislation and expressed his appreciation to HELP Committee Chairman Bill Cassidy, M.D. (R-Louisiana), Ranking Member Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), and members of the committee for advancing the bill. Senator Marshall looks forward to working with his colleagues to build on this momentum and bring the Patients Deserve Price Tags Act to the Senate floor.

“Right now, Americans walk into a hospital blind and walk out with a bill nobody could have predicted. That’s not a health care system — it’s a gamble,” said Senator Hickenlooper. “Our bill makes hospitals and insurers publish their prices and backs it up with real fines, not empty threats. If we’re serious about getting universal coverage and lowering costs, we start by following the money.”

title: Merkley Applauds Committee Passage of His Bipartisan Bill to Boost America’s Nursing Workforce
text:
Washington, D.C. – Oregon’s U.S. Senator Jeff Merkley today announced his bipartisan Title VIII Nursing Workforce Reauthorization Act cleared a key hurdle by passing out of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP). Merkley’s bill reauthorizes, updates, and improves critical Nursing Workforce Development Programs under Title VIII of the Public Health Service Act, a law passed in 1944 to support public health and health care professionals.

“As the proud husband of a nurse, I know that nurses make the world so much better, one bedside at a time,” said Merkley, Co-Chair of the Senate Nursing Caucus. “Our bipartisan bill ensures America’s nurses have the resources and support necessary to meet care needs now and in the future, including in rural and medically underserved communities that too often face unique challenges in accessing quality and timely care. As this bill takes one step closer to becoming law, we must keep fighting to strengthen all aspects of the American nursing workforce and the programs that are critical to these health care heroes, including education, practice, recruitment, and retention.”

Merkley led the introduction of the Title VIII Nursing Workforce Reauthorization Act with U.S. Senators Susan Collins (R-ME), Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), and Marsha Blackburn (R-TN). Their bipartisan bill would:

Reauthorize funding for the Title VIII Nursing Workforce Development Programs from FY2027 through FY2031;

Make technical changes to the Advanced Nursing Education Program and make clear that grants for traineeships can cover the costs for clinical education and preceptors;

Allow existing funding for Nurse Education, Practice, Quality, and Retention grants to be used to cover the cost of audiovisual or other equipment, simulation and augmented reality resources, telehealth technologies, and virtual and physical laboratories, as well as to be used to increase the number of faculty and students at schools of nursing to address nursing workforce shortages; and

Clarify that Nurse Education, Practice, Quality, and Retention grants can be used to provide care for survivors of sexual assault and to partner with a health care facility that provides educational opportunities for the purpose of establishing or expanding clinical education.

U.S. Representatives Dave Joyce (R-OH-14), Suzanne Bonamici (D-OR-01), Lauren Underwood (D-IL-14), and Jen Kiggans (R-VA-02) lead the House version of the bill.

As amended by the Senate HELP Committee during the markup, the bill also includes language based on Senators Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE) and Merkley’s National Nursing Workforce Center Act, which would support state-based nursing workforce centers, as well as language based on Senators Dick Durbin (D-IL) and Lisa Murkowski (R-AK)’s Nurse Faculty Shortage Reduction Act, which would address the pay gap between clinical and faculty nursing positions.

To learn more about the Title VIII Nursing Workforce Reauthorization Act as originally introduced in the Senate, click here.

title: Merkley, Hyde-Smith, Bentz, Thompson Launch New Bipartisan Effort to Promote Renewable Fuels, Boost Wildfire Resiliency
text:
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Jeff Merkley (D-OR) and Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-MS) partnered with U.S. Representatives Cliff Bentz (R-OR-02) and Bennie Thompson (D-MS-02) to introduce the Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act. This new bipartisan, bicameral legislation proposes to modernize the definition for renewable biomass under the Renewable Fuel Standard, establishing a strong market for woody biomass generated through forest management activities and boosting wildfire resiliency efforts at the same time.

“Reducing wildfire risk demands innovative solutions and using all the tools at our disposal to invest in wildfire prevention efforts,” said Merkley. “Woody biomass that comes from responsible forest management activities—like hazardous fuels reduction—presents a huge opportunity for communities in Oregon and across the nation. By updating the definition for these materials to qualify as renewable fuels, we can harness their power to create new markets for these materials, reducing wildfire risk and supporting healthier public, private, and Tribal lands.”

“This bipartisan bill creates avenues to help reduce the wildfire threats in the West but also clears the way for biomass produced from non-federal lands in heavily forested states like Mississippi to contribute to the nation’s renewable fuels resources,” said Hyde-Smith. “With this bill, we will make it easier to develop a new revenue stream for the thinnings, logging residuals, and mill byproducts that Mississippi landowners and forest products manufacturers already generate, without requiring them to change how they manage their timberland.”

“Hundreds of thousands of tons of new wood grow in Oregon’s forests each and every day, increasing the chance and the danger of cataclysmic wildfire. This danger can be reduced by removing brush and excess trees from the forests. Technology has found a way to convert wood into biofuel, so this wood does have value. The challenge, resolved by this bill, is to properly focus existing financial support systems on the removal, transport, and processing of qualified wood from our forests to processing facilities. This bill would provide financial support for such removal by expanding the Renewable Fuel Standard to include woody biomass removed from federal forest land. Removal of this biomass will reduce costs of fire suppression, protect forest health, and improve and preserve watersheds,” said Bentz.

“This bipartisan legislation recognizes that healthy forests and strong rural economies go hand in hand. By creating new markets for woody biomass generated through responsible forest management, we can help reduce wildfire risk, support jobs in rural communities, and expand America’s renewable fuel supply. This commonsense approach creates economic opportunity while helping protect our forests and natural resources for future generations,” said Thompson.

Merkley has been a longtime leader in Congress to advocate for wildfire resiliency efforts, leading a series of bipartisan bills to support mills processing hazardous fuels coming off public lands, train the new generation of wildland firefighters, aid toxic debris cleanup following wildfires, and promote collaborative forest management.

In addition to Merkley, Hyde-Smith, Bentz, and Thompson, the Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act is co-sponsored by U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-CA), John Kennedy (R-LA), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Susan Collins (R-ME), and Angus King (I-ME), and U.S. Representatives Bruce Westerman (R-AR-04), James Gallagher (R-CA-01), Mike Ezell (R-MS-04), Ami Bera (D-CA-06), Derrick Van Orden (R-WI-03), Max Miller (R-OH-07), Kim Schrier (D-WA-08), and Bob Latta (R-OH-05).

The bipartisan, bicameral bill is supported by 75+ organizations, including the National Alliance of Forest Owners (NAFO), Intertribal Timber Council (ITC), Alliance for Wildfire Resilience, American Forest Resource Council, and American Farm Bureau Federation. A full list of supporting organizations can be found by clicking here.

“NAFO thanks Senator Merkley and Senator Hyde-Smith for their leadership in introducing the Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act of 2026. Supporting this legislation is an easy call. The bill creates a powerful new tool for addressing the wildfire crisis and the ongoing closures of wood-consuming paper mills by unlocking practical markets for low-value wood and mill residuals. It supports forest health and resilience through active forest management, strengthens the sawmills that supply our housing sector, bolsters rural economies, and helps America meet growing demand for renewable fuels. At a time when forest owners, mills, and rural communities are facing real economic peril, this targeted fix to the definition of wood in the Renewable Fuel Standard is exactly the kind of commonsense solution Congress should advance,” said Dave Tenny, President and CEO, National Alliance of Forest Owners.

“The Intertribal Timber Council supports reforming clean energy frameworks, including the Renewable Fuel Standard. Classification of forest residuals from all forestlands as eligible for market-based incentives will increase the use of these forest materials, which will accelerate hazardous fuel reduction, thus providing a critical defense against catastrophic wildfires that endanger tribal communities, water supplies, and cultural sites,” said Cal Mukumoto, ITC Executive Director.

“One of the biggest challenges impeding the nation’s wildfire risk reduction goals is the cost of treatments. As the Wildland Fire Mitigation and Management Commission recognized, expanding commercial markets can help to offset these costs and increase the amount of work accomplished for the same federal investment,” said Taylor Reed, Senior Government Relations Specialist at the Alliance for Wildfire Resilience. “The Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act of 2026 is an important step towards the expansion of a wood-based renewable fuel industry, helping to increase risk reduction, decrease fire intensity, and improve air quality. AWR applauds Senators Merkley and Hyde-Smith, as well as Reps. Benz and Thompson for their leadership on this issue.”

“The American Forest Resource Council strongly supports the bipartisan Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act. This legislation is a smart approach to help prevent catastrophic wildfires by creating new markets for low-value biomass fuels removed from at-risk national forests, protecting communities, increasing renewable energy supplies, and ultimately reducing wildfire suppression costs. Active forest management works. A recent large-scale study completed by UC Davis found that every dollar spent on forest fuel treatments saves about $3.75 in wildfire damages. We thank Senator Jeff Merkley and Congressman Cliff Bentz for being proactive and focusing on prevention to better protect our forests, communities, public health and safety, and the American taxpayer,” said Travis Joseph, President/CEO American Forest Resource Council.

“Farm Bureau appreciates the introduction of bipartisan legislation that supports farmers, foresters and both public and private forest lands across the United States. Updating the definition of renewable biomass for the Renewable Fuel Standard will support active land stewardship and reduce wildfire risk through improved management of public lands. Farm Bureau encourages the Senate to swiftly consider the Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act of 2026,” said Dr. John Newton, Vice President of Public Policy and Economic Analysis, American Farm Bureau Federation.

Full text of the Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act can be found by clicking here.

title: Merkley, Kamlager-Dove: Congress Must Ensure Safety, Well-Being of Children Seeking Asylum
text:
Lawmakers lead bicameral bill to protect migrant children in United States’ care

Washington, D.C. – Today, Oregon’s U.S. Senator Jeff Merkley and U.S. Congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove (CA-37) led a bicameral effort to establish strong federal safeguards for unaccompanied and accompanied children throughout every stage of our immigration system.

The Children’s Safe Welcome Act responds to the Trump Administration’s escalating attacks on vulnerable migrant children, including ramping up cruel family separations and deportations of unaccompanied minors. The bill strengthens comprehensive child welfare protections and establishes guidelines and best practices for better care for these vulnerable children.

“Trump’s total disregard for the legal process directly threatens the safety of vulnerable migrant children, which is just plain wrong under any moral code,” said Merkley. “Like during his first administration, Trump’s inhumane detention policies are traumatizing kids and families fleeing persecution—inflicting lasting harm and trauma. We must shine a light on these dangerous, cruel policies, and Congress must pass our Children’s Safe Welcome Act to keep these kids safe.”

“The immigration system for children is a moral disgrace. From ICE raids at schools to children being ripped away from their families, the inhumanity of the Trump Administration’s immigration policies is appalling. Clearly, the system is ill-equipped to protect children and the absence of safeguards for children is a significant policy failure,” said Kamlager-Dove. “That’s why I am proud to partner with Senator Merkley to introduce the Children’s Safe Welcome Act, comprehensive legislation designed to ensure that every step of the immigration process prioritizes the welfare of children. Immigrant children should not bear the consequences of our broken immigration system.”

In addition to Merkley and Kamlager-Dove, the Children’s Safe Welcome Act is cosponsored by U.S. Senators Dick Durbin (D-IL), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), Peter Welch (D-VT), Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Ron Wyden (D-OR), Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Mazie Hirono (D-HI), Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Brian Schatz (D-HI), Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), Tina Smith (D-MN), Jacky Rosen (D-NV), Edward J. Markey (D-MA), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), and Michael Bennet (D-CO), and U.S. Representatives Mike Quigley (IL-05) and Henry C. “Hank” Johnson, Jr. (GA-04).

The Children’s Safe Welcome Act would:

Codify minimum child welfare protections such as health and safety standards, state licensing requirements, and the best interests of the child standard.

Mandate child protection professionals at children’s first point of contact with the federal immigration system.

Increase minimum health and safety standards for children and families in Customs and Border Protection facilities.

Prohibit family separations, with extremely narrow exceptions only in cases where it is critical to protect the safety of the child.

Prohibit the use of family detention facilities, without exception.

Ensure all children are placed in a non-adversarial setting for their asylum case processing.

Create a process for keeping families together by allowing unaccompanied children who arrive at the border in the care of grandparents, adult siblings, or aunts or uncles (non-parent/non-legal guardian family members) to stay together.

Phase out large congregate care facilities and prioritize family-based placements for unaccompanied children.

Require children to be placed in the least restrictive environment and limit the placement of children in harmful restrictive facilities.

Prioritize the swift release of unaccompanied children with disabilities and access to services in the community.

Limit the use of influx facilities and prohibit the placement of unaccompanied children in influx facilities for more than 20 days.

Guarantee legal representation for unaccompanied children at every stage of removal proceedings.

Prohibit information sharing about unaccompanied children, with narrow exceptions.

Replace the outdated and offensive word “alien” with “noncitizen” in federal statute.

Establish an Ombudsperson to monitor and oversee compliance with this Act.

Mandate access for members of Congress, accompanying staff, and credentialed press (without cameras) to visit federal immigration facilities.

The Children’s Safe Welcome Act is supported by 100+ experts, advocates, and organizations representing migrant children in all stages of our immigration system, including the Young Center for Immigrant Children’s Rights and National Center for Youth Law.

“Every child deserves safety, dignity, and care—not detention,” said Mina Dixon Davis, Senior Policy Analyst at the Young Center for Immigrant Children’s Rights. We hear children’s stories—the fear, the loneliness, the lasting harm—and we know it doesn’t have to be this way. The Children’s Safe Welcome Act gives Congress the chance to end these cruel practices and put children’s safety and dignity first. Lawmakers must act now to ensure that every child is treated as a child—with care, compassion, and hope for the future.”

“We have interviewed children in federal immigration custody for decades, and their harrowing accounts make one thing clear: federal law was never designed with children in mind, and children pay the painful price for that gap every day. Basic questions about how a child should be housed, cared for, and released have been left to court orders and agency discretion for far too long. The Children’s Safe Welcome Act finally answers those questions in statute,” said Melissa Adamson, Senior Attorney at the National Center for Youth Law. “Today, as the Administration pursues an unprecedented campaign to decimate basic legal protections for children, leaving them indefinitely detained and without the protection of legal counsel, this legislation has never been more critical.”

Full text of the Children’s Safe Welcome Act can be found by clicking here.

title: Senator Moody Introduces Staged Accident Fraud Prevention Act to Protect All Drivers on our Roads and Prevent Con Artists from Driving up the Cost of Insurance
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C.—Today, Senator Ashley Moody introduced the Staged Accident Fraud Prevention Act, legislation that would extend criminal penalties to make intentionally staging an accident with a commercial motor vehicle a federal crime.

“With over 450,000 trucking jobs in Florida, it is safe to say that truck drivers keep the economy moving. Unfortunately, there are crazed and dangerous fraudsters out there who would rather put people’s lives in danger for a quick payday instead of making an honest living putting in a hard day’s work. Anyone who stages or helps stage an accident with a commercial motor vehicle endangers people’s lives and livelihoods. On top of that, these stunts run up insurance premiums for everyone. Unacceptable. This legislation sends a clear message: if you do this, you will be prosecuted,” said Senator Ashley Moody.

American Trucking Associations: “When con artists seeking a big payday intentionally collide with commercial motor vehicles, their reckless disregard for safety puts innocent truck drivers and the motoring public at risk. The Staged Accident Fraud Prevention Act is also supported by:

Associated Industries of Florida

Truckload Carriers Association

Georgia Motor Trucking Association

Texas Trucking Association

American Property Casualty Insurance Association

American Tort Reform Association

BACKGROUND:

Despite an increase in staged truck accidents, few states have taken action to combat staged accident fraud schemes.

A notable example of this staged fraud occurred multiple times in Louisiana, where scammers over the course of 5 years caused dozens of intentional crashes with 18 wheelers.

Following an FBI investigation into these kinds of accidents, Danny Patrick Keating, a personal injury attorney, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Keating admitted to paying another cooperating government witness, Damien Labeaud, to stage 31 accidents.

Keating told investigators he represented 77 plaintiffs in subsequent lawsuits. Federal authorities say such fake crashes predominantly took place in New Orleans East and Gentilly, often close to one truck stop.

Florida is one of the nation’s largest freight hubs, supporting more than 460,000 trucking industry jobs and over 130,000 trucking companies.

The Staged Accident Fraud Prevention Act would:

Make intentionally staging a collision with a commercial motor vehicle a federal criminal offense.

Establish criminal penalties for individuals who organize or participate in staged crashes

Hold attorneys, physicians, and other co-conspirators accountable if they knowingly participate in this fraud.

This legislation was introduced in the House by Representatives Mike Collins (GA-10) and Brandon Gill (TX-26).

title: VIDEO: Sen. Moran Speaks on Senate Floor to Honor 150th Anniversary of Burdett’s Founding
text:
Sen. Moran’s full remarks as delivered:

“This summer, from July 17th to the 19th, not too far away, residents of Burdett, Kansas, will come together to celebrate the 150th anniversary of the town’s founding. Burdett is a small community of fewer than 250 residents, and it’s particularly meaningful to me as a place that I have represented since I was first elected to public office as a state senator.

“The community is special to me because on election night of that state senate race, Browns Grove Township was the very first township to report its voting totals and the tally showed that I just might win my uphill race for the Kansas State Senate.

“Some of my best remembrances are the Monday community potluck lunches and the annual Tri-County picnic in the city park. I’ve knocked on every door in Burdett and talked with members of the community about their hopes, their concerns and how we can preserve our special way of life for another generation of Kansans.

“This summer, as local residents commemorate Burdett’s history, they will also pay tribute to one of their own, Clyde Tombaugh, whose significant contributions advanced the fields of scientific discovery and space exploration. It’s impossible to visit Burdett without seeing the pride the community has in his accomplishments.

“Born February 4th, 1906, Clyde was raised on a farm just outside Burdett, and he quickly developed a love of astronomy and learning. As a teenager, he taught himself how to build his own telescopes out of spare parts he found around the family farm. Later, his commitment to research and exploration would lead him to make a remarkable discovery that made history and helped unlock a new understanding of our solar system.

“On February 18th, 1930, at the age of just 24, Clyde discovered the existence of Pluto, the only major planet discovered here in the United States.

“Following this achievement, Clyde earned his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in astronomy from the University of Kansas, and he went on to make many more contributions to advancing the fields of scientific research and space exploration.

“In 2015, NASA honored him by carrying a portion of his ashes aboard the New Horizons spacecraft on its mission to Pluto. The heart-shaped region on Pluto’s surface was officially named Tombaugh Regio in his honor, paying tribute to his accomplishments and cementing the legacy of a Kansas farm kid in one of the most remote parts of our solar system.

“As Burdett celebrates its 150th anniversary, and I say congratulations to them, it’s a history that is embodied by the story of Clyde Tombaugh, someone who with determination, hard work, curiosity, whose discoveries helped to shape how future generations understand our universe.

“For decades, this tight-knit community of Burdett has reserved his legacy and made certain the world remembers his contributions to science, research and discovery.

“I hope everyone passing through southwestern Kansas will take the time to visit Burdett to learn the history and the legacy of this little town on the plains of Kansas.

“On behalf of the United States Senate, to the citizens of Burdett, past, present and future, I congratulate the community of Burdett on its 150th anniversary and express my gratitude for the way in which its residents have honored and preserved the memory of one of our most notable Kansans and how kind they have always been to me.”

title: Murkowski and Colleagues Lead Efforts to Bolster Made-In-America Hydropower
text:
Washington, D.C.–Yesterday, U.S. Senators Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Steve Daines (R-Mont.), and Jim Risch (R-Idaho) introduced the “Hydropower Licensing Affordability Act.” This bill will reform the Federal Power Act to reduce delays and costs of hydropower licensing. Specifically, the bill would limit Section 4 (e) and Section 18 mandatory conditioning of hydropower licenses under the Federal Power Act to those conditions that are related to “direct adverse effects” of the project.

“Throughout my time in the Senate, I have heard the same message from Alaska’s utilities and local leaders: the hydropower relicensing process is broken,” said Murkowski. “With 40 percent of our nation’s non-federal hydropower licenses set to expire by 2035, including 12 projects in Alaska, we need to address the unwarranted delays and costly federal requirements that often bear little connection to a project’s direct impacts. Those burdens make it much harder to maintain and expand one of Alaska’s most reliable sources of renewable, baseload power. By ensuring mandatory licensing conditions are tied to a project’s direct adverse effects, this legislation will provide greater regulatory certainty, reduce unnecessary costs, and help keep electricity affordable and reliable for Alaskans.”

“Hydropower is a growing source of power in both Montana and across the nation. The demand for U.S. energy is increasing every year, and we need to do everything we can to ensure we’re prepared to meet this rise in demand. These reforms will ensure the hydropower licensing process is more efficient, so we can get critical projects done in a timely manner,” said Daines.

“More than half of Idaho’s in-state electricity generation comes from hydropower, underscoring the importance of continued investment in the operation of both public and private dams. The Hydropower Licensing Affordability Act improves the relicensing process to ensure our dams continue to meet growing demand for affordable, reliable baseload power while efficiently serving our communities,” said Risch.

Read the bill text HERE.

The senators also wrote a letter to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the Department of the Interior, the Department of Agriculture, and the Department of Commerce urging support and action on these reforms. The letter urges the agencies to:

Limit mandatory conditions to those that address direct effects of a project,

Limit the scope of the project area to its immediate vicinity,

Reasonably define ‘fishway’ to clarify that prescribed structures are intended only to address direct impacts to fish passage;

Require conditions to be backed by the best available science,

Require agencies to provide a statement with any conditions that demonstrates equal consideration to the effects of the condition “on energy supply, distribution, cost, and use; flood control; navigation; water supply; and air quality (in addition to the preservation of other aspects of environmental quality),” as required in Section 33, and

Ensure that conditions are not overly burdensome or costly.

“Taking steps now to address these issues will usher in a generational shift in hydropower production, keep costs lower for consumers, build jobs, maintain reliability for the grid, and protect blackstart assets, all while continuing to protect our natural resources. We urge you to immediately initiative rulemakings at each of your agencies and look forward to working closely with you to support new and existing hydroelectric generation,” they wrote in the letter.

Senators Mike Crapo (R-Idaho), Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.), Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) and Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.) joined Murkowski, Daines, and Risch in sending the letter.

Read the full letter HERE.

Statements of Support:

“Hydropower is a critical resource in meeting Alaska’s growing energy needs while providing long-term electricity cost stabilization for families and businesses throughout the state. Alaska Power Association strongly supports the Hydropower Licensing Affordability Act, which will ensure permitting agencies properly scope their mandatory conditions to address the direct effects of hydropower projects. Too often projects, and ultimately ratepayers, are asked to bear higher costs due to issues unrelated to project operations or impacts. We commend Senator Murkowski and Senator Daines for their leadership on this issue and urge Congress to quickly pass this much needed legislation,” said Crystal Enkvist, Executive Director, Alaska Power Association.

“Common sense hydropower reforms mean we need to pair the permit with the project. That’s why the Hydropower Licensing Affordability Act is so important. For too long, hydropower producers have been forced to pay for wish-list items that have nothing to do with the reliable power they provide. With rising energy demand and 16,000 MW of hydropower up for license renewal over the next decade, we can’t afford to keep the status quo. I thank Senators Daines, Risch and Murkowski for taking action on this top priority, along with Rep. Cliff Bentz, who is leading this effort in the House. NHA looks forward to working closely with these water power champions to move this bill through Congress as quickly as possible,” said Matthew Allen, Senior Director of Legislative Affairs, National Hydropower Association.

“Thank you Senators Daines, Risch and Murkowski for introducing the Hydropower Licensing Affordability Act. This legislation will help create greater certainty in the permitting process for our hydropower assets, while ensuring our projects maintain their environmental integrity to protect fish and wildlife. Hydropower makes up nearly 23% of our generation portfolio at NorthWestern Energy, allowing our company to meet customer demand with affordable, reliable, and carbon-free power,” said Brian Bird, President and Chief Executive Officer, NorthWestern Energy.
