title: Senator Murkowski Applauds DOJ Settlement Resolution Supporting Alaska Native Healthcare System
text:
Washington, DC—U.S. Senator Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Chairman of the U.S. Senate Committee on Indian Affairs, welcomed the resolution of a longstanding legal dispute between the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium (ANTHC) and the federal government, which will provide $400 million, plus approximately $63 million in interest, to address improperly withheld contract support cost reimbursements under the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (ISDEAA).

The settlement resolves the case, Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium v. Kennedy, following years of litigation over the federal government’s obligation to reimburse tribal health organizations for the costs associated with carrying out health care services on behalf of the federal government. The agreement follows the Supreme Court’s decision in Becerra v. San Carlos Apache Tribe, which affirmed tribal rights to contract support cost reimbursement under ISDEAA.

"Contract support costs are essential to ensuring tribal health organizations have the resources they need to provide the care the federal government has entrusted them to deliver. I have long fought to ensure the federal government honors its commitments to Alaska's tribal health organizations and fully meets its trust responsibility,” said Senator Murkowski. “In Alaska, our tribal health system is a lifeline. For many people in rural and remote communities, it is their primary access to essential health care. Resolving this lawsuit is a significant victory because it provides long-overdue certainty and resources that will allow ANTHC to strengthen health care delivery, invest in critical infrastructure and workforce needs, and focus on serving patients rather than continuing costly litigation. This settlement represents an important step forward for Alaska's tribal health system and the communities it serves. I thank the Department of Justice for helping bring this longstanding matter to a successful resolution."

title: At Hearing, Senator Murray Presses VA on Menopause Research, Slams Trump Admin for Pushing Cuts to VA Research Funding, Politicizing VA Grants
text:
***WATCH and READ: Senator Murray’s opening remarks***

***WATCH: Senator Murray’s full questioning***

Washington, D.C. — Today, at a Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee (SVAC) hearing on the future of Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) research—U.S. Senator Patty Murray (D-WA), a former chair and senior member of SVAC, questioned Dr. Mark Zhang, DO, Acting Assistant Under Secretary for Health for Discovery, Education and Affiliate Networks, Veterans Health Administration (VHA), on the Servicewomen and Veterans Menopause Research Act, proposed budget cuts to VA research, the proposed OMB rule politicizing how federal agencies award and research grants.

[MENOPAUSE RESEARCH]

Senator Murray began by asking Dr. Zhang about the gaps in menopause research and why continued investment in research among women veterans is critical. She noted how her Servicewomen and Veterans Menopause Research Act would invest in menopause research at VA and DOD.

MURRAY: Women, as we know, are the fastest-growing veteran population, but I am still very frustrated by the lack of progress and investment in understanding their really unique health care needs. Women veterans actually—especially those with PTSD or military sexual trauma—are more likely to experience early menopause, with one VA study finding that they are three more times likely than any civilian women to reach menopause before the age of 40.

It’s really important to make sure that our women veterans receive the evidence-based, high-quality health care that they deserve. But to get there, we need a really strong investment in menopause research at both VA and DOD. Which is why I was very proud to introduce the bipartisan Servicewomen and Veterans Menopause Research Act, which will work to do that.

Dr. Zhang, I wanted to ask you today, what are the biggest gaps in our understanding of menopause among women veterans?

ZHANG: Thank you, Senator Murray, for that question, you know, just to kind of set the stage—the Office of Discovery Education and Affiliate Networks is really the office that oversees both research, academics, innovation, and partnerships. And I tell you this because I think that women’s health, and I agree with you, that women’s health and the women population of veterans is clearly growing and going to be incredibly important, not just for research but for academics, for innovation, and frankly for partnerships.

So, to that end, I think that we are going to try and continue to support that from a research standpoint. Our budget for women’s health research remains steady at approximately $40 million a year. When it comes to your specific question about where the biggest gaps are, I’d like to take that for the record and get you the actual accurate information as best we can.

MURRAY: If you could get that back to me and just tell me why you think continued investment in menopause research is critical?

ZHANG: I think all investment in areas of increase for veteran care is going to be important. And although I don’t know specifically about that particular component of women’s health, clearly, given that the increase in women veterans utilizing VA resources is growing, we have to partner and do this work and find the places where we can make an impact and difference.

MURRAY: Well, I think that is why my bill is so important is because we clearly have a lack of understanding, but it is really critical and I hope I can work with the Chairman to get that passed.

[VA RESEARCH BUDGET CUTS]

Senator Murray continued by pressing Dr. Zhang on Trump proposing funding cuts to VA’s research program, which would be detrimental to future treatment options for not just veterans, but all Americans who may benefit from VA research.

MURRAY: The President’s budget proposes a substantial reduction to VA’s research program—not only through cuts to the dedicated research appropriations but also through reduced support from Medical Care accounts and lower projected reimbursements that many of our research programs rely on. Those reductions raise very serious concerns about VA’s ability to sustain its ongoing research and continue developing new innovations that improve our veterans’ care.

So, Dr. Zhang, if Congress were to cut $43 million from the budget, that’s what President Trump is proposing, which high-priority research areas are most at risk? Can you tell us? Is it cutting toxic exposure research? Or prosthetic research? Or cancer research? Where would we see the cuts?

ZHANG: Thank you, Senator Murray, for that question. To be very direct, I think our goal would be to try to preserve the gem that is VA research as much as we could. Now, certainly, I do not have direct control of the budget, so we will do whatever we will take whatever we can get.

MURRAY: In your capacity you know where the money is, where do you see those kinds of cuts hitting research the most?

ZHANG: Yeah, thank you for that question. I don’t know right now. I would say that I would look for things that are not our actively managed portfolios which are our key acceleration priorities and to focus on things that we were exploring at an early stage as the places to make cuts if we had to.

MURRAY: So the budget has been proposed but you haven’t thought about what the consequences are?

ZHANG: Excuse me? Sorry?

MURRAY: The President sent that budget proposal, you see the cuts in it, $43 million, you haven’t thought as an agency about where you’re going to have to put those cuts in?

ZHANG: Oh, I see. Thank you, Senator Murray, from our perspective, the budget cut is really reflecting the attrition of contracts and also staff that have left during that time. Our actual plans and the support for research have not been affected by those budget cuts.

MURRAY: Ok, well we do know last year nine researchers were terminated with no warning and their research stopped, so you can’t say that cutting personnel doesn’t impact research. But I only have 5 seconds left, I just want to emphasize a comment I made in the opening remarks about the pending OMB rule that would really undermine our current system and take away decision-making power from our experienced scientists and just allow political appointees whether this administration or a future decide where research is going to go. That is really concerning to VA researchers. We need decisions based on science not based on if somebody’s mad at somebody or a political decision in any administration.

###

title: Murray, Schumer, Wyden, Jeffries, Clark, Pallone, DeGette, Raskin, and Pressley Lead 250+ Congressional Democrats in Fifth Circuit Fight to Protect Mifepristone Access, Women’s Health Care, and FDA Authority
text:
More than 250 House and Senate Democrats filed an amicus brief to the Fifth Circuit arguing that mifepristone has undergone a rigorous FDA approval process and has repeatedly been found to be safe and effective.

ICYMI: Following Emergency Stay, Murray, Schumer, Jeffries Lead 250+ Democrats in Supreme Court Brief

ICYMI: Senator Murray Statement on Fifth Circuit Ruling to Harshly Limit Access to Medication Abortion Nationwide

Washington, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Patty Murray (D-WA)—alongside Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY); Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR); House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY); and Representatives Katherine Clark (D-MA), Frank Pallone Jr. (D-NJ), Diana DeGette (D-CO), Jamie Raskin (D-MD), and Ayanna Pressley (D-MA)—led more than 250 Senate and House Democrats in filing an amicus brief to the Fifth Circuit in Louisiana v. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) focused on pushing back against Louisiana’s attempt to reinstate the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone. Following the Supreme Court’s stay of the Fifth Circuit’s nationwide ban on telehealth access to mifepristone, the case went back to the Fifth Circuit. Louisiana is seeking a ruling that would force the FDA to reinstate the in-person dispensing requirement nationwide for mifepristone—a safe and effective abortion medication that has been FDA-approved since 2000. This medically unnecessary move would end patient access to mifepristone through telemedicine, the method by which more than 1 in 4 abortion patients receive their care in America today. It would remove patients’ ability to get mifepristone from their pharmacy, forcing them to find a provider that dispenses the medication.

The lawmakers argued that mifepristone already undergoes a rigorous FDA approval process, and the medication has repeatedly been found to be safe and effective. The court overturning this decision not only limits who is able to receive this vital and life-saving medication, putting lives at risk, but it also undermines the longstanding, congressionally mandated, and evidence-based decision-making process at the FDA.

“For more than a quarter century, FDA has repeatedly and consistently affirmed that mifepristone is safe. Over seven million patients in the U.S. have safely used mifepristone. And as with other drugs, FDA continues to monitor the post-marketing safety data on mifepristone—data confirming that mifepristone is safe without regard to how it is dispensed,” the members wrote.

The lawmakers emphasized that the in-person dispensing requirement was eliminated in 2021, prior to the Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization decision of 2022, and not in response to the Supreme Court’s decision.

“The in-person dispensing requirement was first suspended by a court in 2020 and later eliminated altogether by the FDA in 2021, before Dobbs came down. Louisiana knows these facts but continues to make this spurious claim in its attempt to reimpose an unnecessary burden on all Americans, even residents of states that protect abortion. Decades after FDA’s initial approval of mifepristone and years after the in-person dispensing requirement was eliminated, Louisiana now seeks to re-impose this onerous nationwide restriction on all Americans. Granting such relief would undermine the science-based statutory framework Congress requires and threatens patient access to reproductive health care. As has been well documented, many Americans in states where abortion is legal live far from any reproductive health care provider. Reinstating an in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone exacerbates an already significant reproductive health crisis by limiting access to the most common method of early abortion,” the lawmakers continued.

Louisiana’s request for a stay of FDA’s 2023 rule would result in the reinstatement of the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone nationwide—and if granted, would have no basis in law, and would threaten the congressionally-mandated evidence-based process for drug regulation. The lawmakers argue that the Fifth Circuit should deny the stay, protecting telehealth and pharmacy access to mifepristone.

In the Senate, the amicus brief was signed by all 47 Democratic U.S. Senators.

In the House, the brief was signed by 212 Democratic U.S. Representatives.

The amicus brief can be read in full HERE.

title: On Senate Floor, Murray Slam Republicans for Gimmick Resolution on Canadian Wildfires, Demands Trump Apologize to Canada
text:
Murray: “Maybe my colleagues across the aisle don’t realize this, but Canadian firefighters cross that border to help us fight our wildfires right here—all the time. And guess what? Our firefighters do the exact same when they are able… In fact, for the information of all Senators, a firefighter actually just passed away, who was helping us fight a wildfire in Colorado—he was from British Columbia.”

ICYMI: Murray Sounds Alarm on Trump’s Reorganization of USFS & USDA Amidst Wildfire Season

***WATCH: Senator Murray’s full speech***

Washington, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Patty Murray (D-WA), Vice Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, spoke on the Senate floor objecting to Republicans’ ridiculous decision to ask for unanimous consent to pass a resolution which reads, “Expressing the sense of the Senate regarding the adverse impacts on the United States of the recent Canadian wildfires and the importance of the Government of Canada to take responsibility for such impacts by increasing efforts to extinguish these fires and prevent their recurrence.”

The effort to pass the resolution came after Trump blamed Canada for wildfire smoke in the United States, stating he would add the “incalculable cost” of dealing with the smoke on existing tariffs on Canadian goods. On the Senate floor, Murray went on to call on her Republican colleagues to work with her to undo much of the damage the Trump administration has inflicted on our federal capacity to prevent and respond to wildfires.

Senator Murray’s remarks, as delivered, are below:

“M. President, reserving the right to object, I’m going to ask pretty bluntly—what on earth are my colleagues doing here? I don’t know why Republicans are focused on making a really petty and offensive statement to Canada—saying they need to do a better job of containing wildfire smoke?

“As if the Canadian government is letting their forests burn—and its own citizens inhale wildfire smoke—just to spite us. This is a joke.

“Maybe my colleagues across the aisle don’t realize this, but Canadian firefighters cross that border to help us fight our wildfires right here—all the time. And guess what? Our firefighters do the exact same when they are able.

“In fact, for the information of all Senators, a firefighter actually just passed away, who was helping us fight a wildfire in Colorado—he was from British Columbia.

“Now, what we don’t do is pass resolutions here telling our friends and our neighbors to do a better job of handling wildfire smoke!

“And also, maybe somebody should alert the President and my colleagues, but wildfire smoke from the United States often make its way into Canada—it’s happening right now, where wildfires are burning in Oregon and in Washington.

“I think what this might be really about—is telling Trump: ‘Mr. President, look how much we agree with you.’ This is a waste of everybody’s time.

“So, respectfully, to my colleagues, understanding that time on the Senate floor is precious, here are my suggestions.

“Maybe we should pass legislation to rehire all of the red-card holders that Trump fired? Those are the forest service employees who are trained here to help fight wildfires.

“Or how about we pass legislation to stop the Trump administration’s so-called ‘reorganization’ of the forest service? Which would actually shutter offices across the country—including the research labs that help us study the wildfires—and push out even more forest service employees.

“Or maybe instead of entertaining Trump’s outrageous request for a $1.5 Trillion war budget, Republicans could work with us to adequately fund our needs here at home?

“Our Forest Service, right here in the United States, is desperately understaffed and under resourced. Maybe my colleagues don’t realize it, but Trump’s chaotic funding cuts and freezes, along with the chaotic mass layoffs, have actually hurt our public lands and leave us, here, less prepared to prevent and respond to wildfires here at home.

“I remember speaking with a Forest Service Ranger last year, he’s a longtime, dedicated employee. He was a former marine, he served our country in more ways than one. And he did an incredible job. He literally saved people’s lives on forest trails. And he fought wildfires here and even saved a small rural town in my state from being burnt to the ground. And what happened to him? Trump and DOGE fired him. No cause. Just fired him. That was a huge loss for our state and for our country.

“So I do want my colleagues to get serious about wildfires.

“And I’ll just say this: the President should actually apologize to our Canadian neighbors—for the many threats and insults, and, of course, drop those absurd tariffs he is imposing on these wildfires. I’m not holding my breath. So, enough with gimmicks M. President.

“You want to work together to prevent wildfires? My door is wide open and I hope we can all work together do that.

“But I’ll tell you what I’m not going to do: insult our Canadian friends to suck up to a President who does nothing but threaten our neighbors.

“Thank you, M. President, I object.”

[In response to Sen. Hoeven]

“Mr. President, let me just say to my friend, and he is a friend. I do hear his quiet, calm tone, and I appreciate it. It’s not something we all often hear here.

“But I will say this. It’s in the words that you hear from this resolution, if you are a Canadian, is that we are insulting them by saying, ‘you are not trying to fight your forest fires.’ I will tell you this, I am working my tail off to help us fight our wildfires, our Canadian friends are as well.

“And I think in this very heightened time, when I know I don’t live far from the border either, we have a lot of trade with our Canadian friends, we go back and forth. They feel insulted by a lot that is going on. So, I think that adds fuel to that fire.

“And so what I say to my friend, let’s work on our country, making sure that we are fighting our forest fires. Which I outlined in my response to you, of some of the things we can do. And I believe that our Canadian friends are doing the same.

“But that is why I object at this time. Thank you.”

title: Senator Murray Outlines How Trump Administration Has Undercut VA Research, Vows to Reject Budget Cuts
text:
***WATCH: Senator Murray’s full opening remarks***

Washington, D.C. — Today, at a Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee (SVAC) hearing on the future of Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) research—U.S. Senator Patty Murray (D-WA), a former chair and senior member of SVAC, delivered the following opening remarks.

Senator Murray’s remarks, as delivered, are below:

“Look, I think Senators on both sides of this aisle have a real appreciation of VA’s research enterprise, which has been at the forefront of cutting-edge science for more than 100 years, it’s led to breakthroughs like the pacemaker, the first successful liver transplant, the nicotine patch, and CT scanning.

“But I am not sure that the Trump administration has that same appreciation. And I am very concerned the actions by this administration have demoralized VA research staff, and have created instability in research funding, and put up barriers that has slowed the research process.

“On the very first day of the Trump Administration, all VA research staff became subject to a hiring freeze and probationary firings. As a result – research at the Pittsburgh VA to predict stroke risk was put on hold, enrollment into clinical trials for advanced cancer was delayed, and a clinical trial in Florida on preventing dementia and heart disease was cancelled.

“And look, Mr. Chairman, I could go on. I have heard a lot of stories like that.

“The Department also enforced vacancy cuts and staffing caps on its facilities. Though these cuts technically exclude research staff, a study at a VA site in the Pacific Northwest was delayed because staffing caps prevented them from hiring nurses who were needed to administer that study.

“These workforce actions have also taken a toll on employees at VA’s Central Office responsible for getting new research studies up and running.

“VA researchers now report startup times for their studies often stretch to more than a year. Those delays are partially due to a wildly inefficient hiring process for VA research staff. Researchers are reporting to us that the time to hire a new member of their staff now often takes up to six months. As a result, a planned study on RSV missed its enrollment window and could not even enroll participants. Another clinical trial closed after it took six months to hire a researcher. The study’s principal investigator and its lead clinician both resigned from the VA after this debacle.

“VA researchers are not only being undermined by delays and cuts at the Department, but also by instability and cuts at other federal agencies like the National Institutes of Health, which frequently provides funding for our VA researchers. For example, a VA researcher’s NIH grant for studying opioid use disorder among minority veterans was cancelled—why? Because it was deemed ‘DEI-related.’

“Large VA research sites are also reporting their non-VA federal funding is down one-third or more compared to the previous year.

“And in one final blow to research, the Office of Management and Budget published a proposed rule that would require all federal grants, including those for VA research, to be approved by political appointees. That doesn’t make sense—let the political appointees overrule the scientist on what research is worth pursuing and funding.

“Given the current state of VA research under this administration – there is a demoralized workforce with limited access to non-VA federal funding – so it is really inexplicable to request a decrease in funding for VA research for fiscal year 2027.

“I am speaking here in place of Senator Blumenthal, but I can tell you right now as Vice Chair of Appropriations it is my intention to rip up Trump’s budget up and write a new one.

“I really hope our VA witnesses will take the concerns raised in this hearing seriously and commit to taking action to address them. If VA wants to ensure it can recruit and retain the brightest minds to conduct research and provide clinical care for our nation’s heroes, it has to work to restore the trust it has lost with many of its research staff.

“This committee and this congress should stand up for research. And it should stand up for science. And it should stand up for veterans—that’s where I am, Mr. Chairman.”

title: Padilla, EPW Committee Members Introduce Bipartisan Legislation to Prevent Wildfires, Increase Use of Prescribed Fire
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), John Curtis (R-Utah), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), John Boozman (R-Ark.), and Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), members of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, introduced the bipartisan Wildfire Emissions Prevention Act (WEPA) of 2026.

WEPA would make it easier for states and communities to use prescribed fires to prevent wildfire emissions, protect ecosystems and wildlife habitats, and make American forests and communities safer, healthier, and cleaner. The bill also promotes the efficient use of state air quality resources and provides certainty that states will not be penalized for taking action to prevent wildfires.

“We know prescribed burns help prevent catastrophic wildfires and save lives,” said Senator Padilla. “This bipartisan bill cuts red tape so California and the whole country can make greater use of this proven, cost-effective tool to protect communities before the next major wildfire. It’s a commonsense step that prioritizes prevention instead of waiting to respond after disaster strikes.”

“If we’re serious about reducing the size and severity of wildfires, we need to stop punishing local authorities for doing the right thing to improve forest health and remove hazardous fuels,” said Senator Curtis. “By removing unnecessary regulatory burdens on prescribed burns, our legislation helps ensure states and localities can take proactive measures to help keep our forests and communities safe from the threat of wildfires.”

“When the 2020 Labor Day fires swept across Oregon, I drove over 600 miles and never once escaped the thick, dark smoke that blanketed our state. As Oregonians face yet another record-breaking fire season this year, we need to tackle this crisis at every stage,” said Senator Merkley. “Our bipartisan bill supports more prescribed fire on the landscape—an essential forest management activity—while giving our communities the resources to plan and prepare for smoke events. Climate chaos is fueling more severe wildfires, and I’ll keep fighting to ensure Oregon and communities nationwide have the tools they need to protect public health and save lives.”

“I am very proud to cosponsor this legislation, which will help reduce the impact of wildfires on our land, our air, and our people,” said Senator Capito. “Wildfires have ravaged many parts of our country over the past several years, and change is necessary to ensure that states can successfully prevent the most dangerous and damaging fires. States should have the right to use known prevention practices, including prescribed fires, to mitigate potential catastrophes and care for their land. This bill gives states another tool in their toolbox, and will reduce barriers to successfully managing wildfires and protecting communities nationwide.”

“In light of the devastating wildfires we now see far too often, Congress should do everything it can to encourage better forest management practices,” said Senator Boozman. “Prescribed burns are an important way to prevent large-scale fires that threaten homes and property while damaging natural resources. I am proud to join colleagues on both sides of the aisle on this legislation to ensure controlled burns do not generate an adverse Clean Air Act impact or penalize states taking proactive mitigation steps.”

“Arizona knows the damage catastrophic wildfires can do to our communities and forests,” said Senator Kelly. “Prescribed burns are one of the best ways to reduce that risk before a fire gets out of control, and states shouldn’t be penalized for taking action. This bipartisan effort will help prevent larger, more destructive wildfires, keep our forests healthier, and better protect families from the smoke and pollution they leave behind.”

Specifically, WEPA would:

Make it easier for states and communities to use prescribed fire to prevent wildfire emissions;

Provide certainty that states won’t be penalized for taking action to prevent wildfires;

Promote the efficient use of state air quality resources; and

Make our forests and communities safer, healthier, and cleaner.

title: Padilla, Kim Introduce “MediKids” to Guarantee Healthcare for Every Child in America
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — As millions of children remain uninsured or underinsured and Congressional Republicans advance deep cuts to Medicaid, U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) and Andy Kim (D-N.J.) introduced the MediKids Act, legislation that would guarantee every child in America access to comprehensive healthcare regardless of their family’s income, immigration status, or health condition from birth through age 26.

“At a time when families are watching healthcare become more expensive and MAGA Republicans and Trump are ripping coverage away from millions of Americans, we should be expanding care, not taking it away,” said Senator Padilla. “No parent should have to worry whether their child can see a doctor because of cost, health condition, or where they were born. The MediKids Act would guarantee every child the care they need to grow up healthy and give every family the peace of mind they deserve.”

“As parents – we promise to do all we can to look after the health and safety of our children. Nothing is more essential than caring for our kids – but as a country, we are failing to uphold that same promise,” said Senator Kim. “Millions of children are falling through the cracks of our healthcare system, and we are the only ones who can stand up and help. I built MediKids to be a step we can take right now to guarantee every single child in the United States the care they need, when they need it. No kid should go without care in our country.”

Today, more than 4.4 million children in America do not have health insurance, while another 23 million kids are underinsured — meaning their healthcare coverage still leaves families unable to meet their needs. To provide free, high-quality insurance coverage to every kid, MediKids would automatically enroll every child and young adult in America in Medicaid’s robust Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) benefit, which provides comprehensive and preventive health care services for children who are enrolled in Medicaid.

The legislation comes as recent federal actions threaten children’s access to healthcare by reducing Medicaid coverage and making it harder for families to enroll and stay covered. Specifically, this legislation would:

Automatically enroll every child in MediKids at birth;

Provide continuous coverage through age 26;

Cover every child regardless of income, immigration status, or health condition; and

Fully fund coverage through a 100 percent federal match.

In addition to Padilla and Kim, MediKids is co-sponsored by Senators Cory Booker (D-N.J.) and Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), and endorsed by: First Focus Campaign for Children, What To Expect Project, American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists, (ACOG), ZERO TO THREE, Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine, American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (AACAP), Association of Women’s Health, Obstetric, and Neonatal Nurses (AWHONN), Association of Maternal and Child Health Programs (AMCHP), National Association of School Nurses, National Education Association (NEA), Families USA, MomsRising, Save Our Schools, New Jersey Citizen Action, SPAN Parent Advocacy Network, and American Academy of Pediatrics.

“At a time when the uninsured rates for children is rising and children face unacceptably high rates of infant and child mortality, a growing mental health crisis, and declining immunization rates, Senator Andy Kim’s MediKids bill puts children back on the path toward ensuring all children have health coverage and improved access to care,” said Bruce Lesley, President of First Focus Campaign for Children. “No child in this country should go without health care simply because of what their parents earn, their zip code, or whether they can navigate a complex and fragmented health care system. In an effort to improve the health, development, and well-being of children, MediKids represents the kind of ambitious, child-centered thinking that the moment demands for our children and grandchildren.”

“Medicaid is first and foremost a children’s program that was created with their health needs in mind, helping families receive everything from milestone checkups, to sick care, to immunizations,” said Andrew D. Racine, MD, PhD, FAAP, President of the American Academy of Pediatrics. “Pediatricians see first-hand how Medicaid works for the children and families who rely on it – support that should be available to all children, regardless of where they live or where their parents work, and MediKids would do just that. The American Academy of Pediatrics applauds Senator Kim for his leadership on this bill and urges Congress to advance it.”

The MediKids Act builds on Padilla’s broader effort to expand access to affordable healthcare, including recent legislation to strengthen maternal health coverage through Medicaid, establish healthcare as a protected civil right, and guarantee healthcare for every American through Medicare for All.

Last week, Padilla joined Senators Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Cory Booker (D-N.J.) in reintroducing the Mamas First Act, legislation that would help address the maternal mortality crisis by expanding Medicaid coverage to include prenatal, delivery, and postpartum care provided by doulas, midwives, tribal midwives, and lactation support providers.

Last year, Padilla joined Senator Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and over 100 lawmakers in reintroducing the Medicare for All Act, legislation that would guarantee healthcare as a fundamental human right to all people in the United States regardless of income or background.

Padilla and Booker introduced the Equal Health Care for All Act, bicameral legislation that would make equal access to medical care a protected civil right to help address the racial inequities and structural failures in America’s healthcare system.

title: Padilla Leads Tri-Caucus in Introducing Sweeping Health Equity Bill
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), along with Senators Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) and Cory Booker (D-N.J.) and Representatives Raul Ruiz (D-Calif.-25), Robin Kelly (D-Ill.-02), and Grace Meng (D-N.Y.-06) announced the reintroduction of the Health Equity and Accountability Act (HEAA) of 2026, bicameral legislation that would address health disparities among racial and ethnic minorities as well as women, the LGBTQ+ community, rural populations, and socioeconomically disadvantaged communities across the United States. HEAA was introduced in coordination with the Congressional Hispanic Caucus (CHC), Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus (CAPAC), and the Congressional Black Caucus (CBC), collectively known as the Congressional Tri-Caucus.

“Affordable, culturally competent healthcare is a right all Americans deserve,” said Senator Padilla. “Systemic inequities coupled with the Trump Administration’s attacks on Medicaid and cuts to hospitals have led to historically marginalized groups without access to essential care. Our bill will help dismantle barriers to care by expanding access to mental health and reproductive care, addressing diseases that disproportionately impact underserved communities, and improving the data we need to better identify and reduce health disparities.”

“As The Trump regime and Congressional Republicans continue to attack healthcare and diversity initiatives from all fronts, working to ensure healthcare is affordable and accessible to all has never been more relevant. We know that people of color and other marginalized groups face unique challenges that require targeted solutions, and restoring the coverage the Trump regime stripped away is just the baseline,” said Senator Hirono. “From investing in stronger data protection to ensuring health resources are accessible to all, this legislation is a critical step to ensuring our healthcare is truly equitable.”

“For too long, too many people in underserved communities have been forced to fight harder for the care they need—facing higher barriers, fewer resources, and a health care system that too often fails them,” said Senator Booker. “These disparities are not just statistics; they represent lives lost, families impacted, and communities left behind. This legislation takes a critical step toward breaking down the systemic barriers that stand between people and the timely, effective, and equitable care they deserve.”

HEAA builds upon policies enacted under landmark healthcare legislation, including the Affordable Care Act and the Inflation Reduction Act, and lays out additional investments and policy changes to improve the health and well-being of underserved communities, address systemic health inequities, and ensure access to high-quality and affordable healthcare for all. The bill aims to increase access to healthcare for vulnerable communities across the entire spectrum of care by taking a comprehensive approach to health equity.

Specifically, HEAA would eliminate racial and ethnic health inequities by:

Expanding access to culturally and linguistically appropriate care

Strengthening and diversifying the healthcare workforce

Removing cost, citizenship, and administrative barriers to coverage and care

Increasing federal support for Medicare, Medicaid, and public health systems

Establishing innovative models for maternal, child, mental, and behavioral health

Funding prevention programs for high-impact diseases that disproportionately affect marginalized populations

Modernizing data collection efforts and expanding telehealth access

Addressing the social determinants of health through investments in nutrition, environmental justice, and community-based supports so that health outcomes improve and disparities are systematically reduced

Reinstating all offices and agencies which have worked tirelessly to ensure people have access to the healthcare every American deserves and rescinds recent Executive Orders attacking American communities

In addition to Padilla, Booker, and Hirono, in the Senate the bill is cosponsored by Senator Reverend Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.). In addition to Ruiz, Kelly, and Meng, in the House the bill is cosponsored by Representatives Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.-33), Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-D.C.-AL), Suzanne Bonamici (D-Ore.-01), Judy Chu (D-Calif.-28), Frederica Wilson (D-Fla.-24), Nydia M. Velazquez (D-N.Y.-07), Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.-03), Pablo Hernández (D-PR-AL), Jesús “Chuy” García (D-Ill.-04), Ted Lieu (D-Calif.-36), Jonathan Jackson (D-Ill.-01), Doris Matsui (D-Calif.-07), Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.-10), Andrea Salinas (D-Ore.-06), Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.-07), Adriano Espaillat (D-N.Y.-13), Analilia Mejia (D-N.J.-11), Christian Menefee (D-Texas-18), Shri Thanedar (D-Mich.-13), Gwen Moore (D-Wis.-04), Troy Carter (D-La.-02), Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.-07), Jill Tokuda (D-Hawaii-02), Jahana Hayes (D-Conn.-05), and Emily Randall (D-Wash.-06).

“I grew up the son of farmworkers, and I became an emergency physician because I saw what happens when our communities don’t have access to care in time,” said Representative Ruiz. “No family should have to choose between a day’s wages and a doctor’s visit or go without care because of their zip code or income. The Health Equity and Accountability Act takes real, comprehensive steps to close these gaps, strengthening our health care workforce, investing in maternal and mental health, and holding our health care system accountable for results. I’m proud to lead this fight alongside my Tri-Caucus colleagues and partners.”

“The Health Equity and Accountability Act (HEAA) is a comprehensive, bold commitment to closing health equity gaps, expanding language and mental health access, and improving research diversity on health disparities across our entire healthcare system,” said CBC Health Braintrust Chair, Congresswoman Robin Kelly. “With the inclusion of my legislation, the Access to Birth Control Act and the WELLS Act, HEAA directly strengthens reproductive healthcare and ensures every mother receives safe, dignified care during childbirth. On behalf of the Congressional Black Caucus, I am proud to co-lead the introduction of this bill to deliver the equitable, high-quality care that every American deserves.”

“Every American—no matter their race or socioeconomic background—deserves access to affordable, high-quality health care,” said Representative Grace Meng, Chair of the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus. “Yet too often, Asian Americans, Native Hawaiians, and Pacific Islanders face obstacles to care, from language barriers to a shortage of culturally competent providers. That’s why I am proud to join my Tri-Caucus colleagues in introducing the Health Equity and Accountability Act, a bold piece of legislation that will improve health outcomes and address everything from health disparities to language access for minority and underserved communities across the country. At a time when the president and congressional Republicans are stripping health care coverage from millions of people, we will keep fighting for a future where health care is accessible for all.”

“Health disparities for some are a drag on health care for all. This legislation is designed to make our health care system more robust by targeting structural inequalities. Latino communities continue to face some of the starkest barriers to care in our nation—from language access to insurance coverage to chronic underinvestment—and those inequities have only deepened under the relentless attacks on health care from the Trump administration and MAGA Republicans,” said Representative Adriano Espaillat, Chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus. “That is why CHC Members are proud to take up the mantle of Tri-Caucus leadership in introducing this bill, because at a moment when so much is under threat, our communities cannot afford anything less than a bold, comprehensive vision for health equity.”

“Every American deserves access to quality health care, no matter where they come from, what language they speak, or how much they earn,” said Congresswoman Matsui. “The Health Equity and Accountability Act recognizes that our communities are not monolithic and strengthens language access, improves health data, and expands culturally responsive care so every patient is treated with dignity. That means building a healthcare system that reflects the people it serves and meets their distinct needs.”

Padilla also joined his Democratic colleagues in introducing HEAA in 2024. Over 300 racial and health equity organizations, researchers, provider groups, and community-based organizations have contributed to the development of HEAA since its inception.

HEAA is endorsed by over 40 organizations, including UnidosUS; National Minority Quality Forum; Asian & Pacific Islander American Health Forum (APIAHF); Prevention Institute; AIDS Alliance for Women, Infants, Children, Youth & Families; National Black Women’s HIV/AIDS Network, Inc.; First Focus Campaign for Children; American Kidney Fund; National Hispanic Health Foundation; National Urban League; Housing Works; Hepatitis B Foundation; Association of Asian Pacific Community Health Organizations (AAPCHO); Montefiore Starfish Program; Health Betterment Initiative; National Health Law Program; The Praxis Project; National Kidney Foundation; Healthy Kinder International, LLC; The LGBTQIA+ Cancer Network; Autistic Self Advocacy Network; Families USA; Justice in Aging; National Black Justice Coalition (NBJC); CenterLink; African American Health Alliance; Equality California; Silver State Equality; Coalition for Asian American Children and Families; National Partnership for Women and Families; In Our Own Voice: National Black Women’s Reproductive Justice Agenda; American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network; National Latina Institute for Reproductive Justice; Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids; Center for Law and Social Policy (CLASP); Hyperemesis Education & Research (HER) Foundation; Power to Decide; AFT: Education, Healthcare, Public Services; Korean Community Services of Metropolitan, Inc.; Southeast Asia Resource Action Center (SEARAC); Disability Rights Education and Defense Fund (DREDF).

“At a moment when historic cuts to Medicaid and Affordable Care Act coverage threaten the health and financial security of millions, the Health Equity and Accountability Act (HEAA) offers a vital path forward,” said UnidosUS President and CEO Janet Murguía. “For Latino families, HEAA would help ensure that language, cost, immigration status or ZIP code never stand between a person and the care they need, while strengthening a diverse healthcare workforce for the future. We commend the Congressional Tri-Caucus for its decades of persistence and solidarity in advancing the principle that every person deserves the opportunity to live a healthy life.”

“The National Minority Quality Forum (NMQF) is honored to support the reintroduction of the Health Equity and Accountability Act (HEAA), which includes thoughtful and impactful measures to close gaps in health and in health care that have long plagued the nation,” said Gary Puckrein, President and CEO, National Minority Quality Forum. “As a national patient advocacy and research organization focused on the reduction of patient risk across all populations, NMQF believes that if we are serious about ending health inequities, we have to be serious about evaluation, oversight and accountability. We must ensure that programs designed to eliminate all health inequities are not only well-intentioned, but rigorously evaluated, transparently reported, and relentlessly improved in service of a healthier and fairer nation. Health equity cannot be achieved by good intentions alone; it requires a system that tracks outcomes, exposes gaps, and demands progress until every community has a fair chance at optimal health.”

“At a time when many of the hard-won gains in health equity are under threat, the Health Equity and Accountability Act reaffirms our nation’s commitment to ensuring that every community has the opportunity to achieve optimal health,” said Juliet K. Choi, President and CEO of the Asian & Pacific Islander American Health Forum. “This landmark legislation reflects the enduring partnership between the Congressional Tri-Caucus and community leaders to advance evidence-based policies, from improving representative data collection and language access to expanding clinical trial participation and addressing persistent disparities affecting Asian Americans, Native Hawaiians, and Pacific Islanders and historically and medically underserved communities.”

“NHeLP is proud to support the reintroduction of the Health Equity and Accountability Act (HEAA),” said Jennifer Cannistra, Executive Director, National Health Law Program. “Now more than ever, HEAA lays the groundwork we need to ensure people of color, women, immigrants, people with disabilities, LGBTQ+ individuals, and people with limited English proficiency can get equal access to the high-quality, culturally and linguistically appropriate care they need.”

“Individuals with limited English proficiency (LEP) need effective communication with their health care providers and the health care system to enroll in coverage, prevent medical errors, understand diagnosis, and actively participate in their care,” said Mara Youdelman, Managing Director of Federal Advocacy, National Health Law Program. “HEAA provides critical steps to ensure that language access services are both widely accessible and paid for. An LEP individual should never have to face the question of whether language services are provided but instead only has to answer what is the best way to communicate with them.”

“Families USA proudly supports the Health Equity and Accountability Act of 2026, which offers vital policy solutions to eliminate the long-standing health disparities worsened by recent historic federal health care cuts,” said Anthony Wright, Executive Director, Families USA. “As a longtime health consumer advocates, we support these bold policies to improve our health system for everyone, and especially to meet the specific and immediate needs of vulnerable communities under attack right now, including immigrants, LGBTQ+ people, and communities of color. HEAA recognizes that our health system is stronger when everyone is included, with broad improvements for all coupled with specific efforts to address the health gaps and issues in specific communities.”

Senator Padilla has been a leader in the fight to make healthcare more equitable, affordable, and accessible in the United States. Yesterday, he and Senator Andy Kim (D-N.J.) introduced MediKids, monumental legislation guaranteeing healthcare to all children in America from birth to age 26. Earlier this year, Padilla and Representative Josh Harder (D-Calif.-09) introduced the Health Investment Zones Act, bicameral legislation to help address healthcare disparities by designating Health Investment Zones (HIZs) for areas facing measurable gaps in income, life expectancy, or the number of providers. Last year, Padilla, Booker, and Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) announced the Equal Health Care for All Act, legislation that would make equal access to medical care a protected civil right to help address the racial inequities and structural failures in America’s healthcare system that have led to higher mortality rates in communities of color. Padilla also is a co-sponsor of the Medicare for All Act, historic legislation that would guarantee healthcare as a fundamental human right to all people in the United States regardless of income or background.

title: Padilla, Whitehouse, Booker, Blumenthal Push Supreme Court Term Limits Bill to Restore Americans’ Trust in the Court
text:
The Supreme Court Biennial Appointments and Term Limits Act would ensure a new justice takes the bench every two years and would establish 18-year terms for participating in the Supreme Court’s full docket of cases

WASHINGTON, D.C. — As Americans’ approval of the Supreme Court nears a historic low, U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Cory Booker (D-N.J.), and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), members of the Senate Judiciary Committee, introduced the Supreme Court Biennial Appointments and Term Limits (BATL) Act to establish 18-year term limits and regularized appointments for Supreme Court justices. Under this legislation, a new justice would take the bench every two years and spend 18 years participating in all Supreme Court cases, after which the justice would be limited to hearing a small number of constitutionally required cases.

“The Supreme Court has reached unprecedented and unacceptable levels of politicization,” said Senator Padilla. “Term limits are a commonsense solution to lower the temperature on the Judiciary and start restoring trust in the highest court in our land.”

“The Supreme Court’s disastrous Citizens United decision supercharged an organized, dark-money funded scheme by right-wing special interests to capture and control the Court. The result is a distorted judicial process that sides with the wealthiest interests at the expense of ordinary Americans, and President Trump is only eager to keep up the scheme to consolidate his own power,” said Senator Whitehouse, the Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Courts Subcommittee. “Term limits and regular appointments would make the Court more representative of everyday Americans and help restore the Supreme Court to the proper independent body it was created to be. More than ever, it’s important we get this right.”

“It is unacceptable that our highest court has the lowest standards of accountability, and no one should hold immense, unchecked power for decades in the manner our Court currently operates. The Supreme Court is not the possession of any president or political party; it is a sacred institution meant to reflect our nation across generations, not a single political moment. This legislation strengthens trust in our highest Court, protects its impartiality, and ensures it can fulfill its constitutional purpose: delivering equal justice for every American,” said Senator Booker.

“As the Supreme Court faces a legitimacy crisis, fundamental reforms are needed to restore trust and credibility. Implementing term limits would make the Court more representative of America, and preserve an institution that is increasingly influenced by toxic politics and partisan obstruction. This legislation is critical to the Supreme Court’s survival as an independent branch of government, and its accountability to the American people,” said Senator Blumenthal.

The Court primarily hears cases that are brought under the Court’s “appellate jurisdiction”—cases decided by lower courts that are appealed to the Supreme Court. These include major cases like Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, Shelby County v. Holder,and Citizens United v. FEC. This legislation would allow only the nine most recently appointed justices to sit for appellate jurisdiction cases. The justices who no longer hear appellate jurisdiction cases would retain the authority to hear “original jurisdiction” cases and to exercise all other powers of the office. If one of the justices who regularly hears appellate jurisdiction cases has a conflict of interest or is otherwise unavailable to hear a case, another justice who hears only original jurisdiction cases may fill in.

The legislation also creates regular appointments of Supreme Court justices every two years by requiring the president, within the first 120 days of the first and third years of the president’s term, to appoint one Supreme Court justice, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate. The bill would not take effect until the start of the first new presidential term after the bill is enacted.

The Supreme Court Biennial Appointments and Term Limits Act is endorsed by the Brennan Center for Justice, National Women’s Law Center Action Fund, Public Citizen, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), Project on Government Oversight (POGO), Alliance for Justice, People for the American Way, Newtown Action Alliance, National Association of Consumer Advocates, Stand Up America, True North Research, End Citizens United, Voto Latino, and Reproductive Freedom for All.

“The Supreme Court needs term limits. It has vast power and minimal accountability. A single justice can now shape the law for generations. This is at odds with the democratic principle that no one should hold too much power for too long. At a time when trust in the Court is hovering at record lows, term limits should be at the top of the list of reforms. It would bring new perspectives and voices on to the Court while strengthening the link between the Court and the American people. Congress should work to pass Supreme Court term limits into law,” said Michael Waldman, President and CEO of the Brennan Center for Justice.

“We applaud the re-introduction of the term limits proposal spearheaded by Senate champions of a fair Supreme Court. We are all witnessing the disastrous consequences of the appointment of ideologues hand-picked to use judicial power to limit our freedoms. The regressive billionaires who have backed Leonard Leo’s court capture agenda are counting on ringers, like Clarence Thomas, who are biased in their favor spending thirty or forty years dismantling our rights. This proposal–which limits the gaming of retirement for partisan purposes and disincentives the selection of young operatives for the bench–is one of several worthy reform initiatives that must be considered in order to restore and expand the rights of We the People in our democracy,” said Lisa Graves, Executive Director of True North Research.

“Congress cannot remain passive while a corrupt Supreme Court continues to favor the powerful and harm the rest of us. The BATL Act recognizes that we can and we must structurally reform the Court,” said Marge Baker, Executive Vice President at the People for the American Way.

“At one point, the U.S. Supreme Court was the most respected institution in American government — and it can be again. Today’s Court has found itself being used as a tool in the middle of partisan politics. It has been packed with staunchly conservative justices out of touch with most Americans. The Supreme Court Biennial Appointments and Term Limits Act, introduced by Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) and others, would restore balance to the Court by ensuring that every president, regardless of party, gets to nominate a justice to the Court in their first and third year of the term. The most recently appointed nine justices will hear appellate jurisdiction cases. The remaining justices will be rotated to hear only original jurisdiction cases. Public Citizen heartily supports this effort to bring balance back to the Supreme Court,” said Craig Holman, Ph.D., of Public Citizen.

“Right-wing dark money groups orchestrated a capture of the Supreme Court over many decades. It’s how we got Citizens United and a corrupt government that only works for its donors while failing the American people,” said End Citizens United President Tiffany Muller. “The fix is simple: judicial term limits and biennial appointments would make the Court fairer, more accountable, and less susceptible to dangerous partisan schemes. This is a first step toward restoring public trust in an institution meant to be a last line of defense for justice and protecting Americans’ rights. We’re grateful to Senators Whitehouse, Blumenthal, Booker, and Padilla for their commitment to making government work for all Americans.”

“Supreme Court justices hold too much power for too long. We applaud this common-sense solution to bring the Supreme Court in line with courts throughout the country and the world by ensuring regular turnover,” said David Janovsky, Acting Director of the Project on Government Oversight.

“It’s long past time for Congress enact serious reforms to ensure that the Supreme Court is made up of fair-minded, independent justices guided by the Constitution and the rule of law—not wealthy interests, political loyalty, or ideological agendas,” said Alison Gill, senior director of democracy and nominations at the National Women’s Law Center Action Fund. “This commonsense Supreme Court term limits bill would help restore public confidence in the Court’s independence and integrity. At a time when public trust in the Court is at an all-time low, this legislation would take a meaningful step toward ensuring that the nation’s highest court remains accountable to the Constitution—not politics.”

“The Supreme Court’s decision to take up the challenge to Connecticut’s assault weapons ban—enacted after the Sandy Hook massacre to protect future generations from the same horror—underscores why Supreme Court reform can no longer wait,” said Po Murray, Chairwoman of Newtown Action Alliance. “When a handful of lifetime-appointed justices can put lifesaving laws and millions of lives at risk decades after they were enacted, our democracy is out of balance. Biennial appointments and eighteen-year terms would restore accountability, reduce the political warfare surrounding every vacancy, and help ensure the Court remains connected to the American people it serves. Survivors should not have to relive their trauma every time the Court reconsiders whether their states have the constitutional right to protect themselves from weapons of war.”

“Serious and repeated allegations of ethical misconduct at the Supreme Court have undermined public faith in the judiciary. This self-inflicted crisis raises serious concerns about whether the Supreme Court’s credibility can survive without meaningful reform,” said Debra Perlin, Vice President for Policy at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW). “The Supreme Court Biennial Appointments and Term Limits Act of 2026 is a strong response to this crisis. It uses the Court’s jurisdiction to create term limits for Supreme Court justices and permits those justices whose terms have ended to retain their seats in a senior status position. This legislation could help both end partisan manipulation of the Court’s composition and reduce ethics problems among justices. CREW commends Senators Whitehouse, Booker, Blumenthal, and Padilla for continuing to lead the charge on the need to address Supreme Court ethics and introducing this crucial piece of legislation.”

“No one should hold power for life. Lifetime appointments to the Supreme Court give nine individuals the power to shape federal law for decades, if not generations. Eighteen years is long enough. Every major democracy in the world except the United States, and 49 of 50 states, limit their top judges with term limits, elections, or mandatory retirement ages. That’s why three-fourths of Americans support term limits for Supreme Court justices. We applaud Senator Whitehouse’s leadership and urge his Democratic colleagues to rally behind this commonsense legislation,” said Brett Edkins, Managing Director of Policy and Political Affairs at Stand Up America.

In addition to Padilla, Whitehouse, Booker, and Blumenthal, the legislation is cosponsored by U.S. Senators Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Peter Welch (D-Vt.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), and Patty Murray (D-Wash.).

title: Reed’s EMPOWER for Health Act Approved by Key Committee
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – As the U.S faces an aging population and growing demand for health care, it needs a well-trained health care workforce that can meet these future demands.

In an effort to respond to the critical need for health care professionals in Rhode Island and throughout the country, U.S. Senators Jack Reed (D-RI) and Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) introduced the Educating Medical Professionals and Optimizing Workforce Efficiency and Readiness (EMPOWER) for Health Act (S.4110).

Today, the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) Committee voted to advance this bipartisan bill to reauthorize the Health Resources and Services Administration’s (HRSA) Title VII health professions to increase access to health care in underserved areas and diversify the health care workforce to meet the needs of different populations. It would also enhance federal support of programs that help grow and strengthen the pipeline of health care professionals in primary care, mental and behavioral health, dental services, pediatrics and more.

The good news is, Americans are living longer. Much of the increased demand is driven by the high prevalence of disease among older adults, with 93 percent of older Americans living with at least one chronic condition, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

“I am pleased the HELP Committee voted unanimously to advance the EMPOWER for Health Act. In Rhode Island, we know we urgently need more doctors, nurses, and other health care professionals. The EMPOWER for Health Act responds to that need. Through investment, innovation, incentives, and interventions, the EMPOWER for Health Act would help boost America’s health care workforce to keep up with demand, deliver care and ensure people have access to the services they need,” said Senator Reed. “Our bipartisan bill would support health care worker education, effectiveness, and retention. It would help grow the talent pipeline and ensure people can make a good-living providing high-quality care for patients. And that enhances everyone’s well-being.”

Specifically, the EMPOWER for Health Act would reauthorize the Title VII health professions education and training programs through Fiscal Year 203 and provide loan repayment for health professionals that agree to work at least two years in specific types of medicine, such as pediatrics. It would also help reauthorize successful, state-based training programs.

The bill has been endorsed by numerous health organizations, including: AIDS Action Baltimore, AIDS Foundation Chicago, the AIDS Institute, the AIDS Vaccine Advocacy Coalition, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Association of Medical Colleges, the American Public Health Association, the American Society for Microbiology, the Association of Schools and Programs of Public Health, Big Cities Health Coalition, the Children’s Hospital Association, Fast-Track Health, the Gerontological Society of America, the HIV Dental Alliance, the HIV Medicine Association, the Infectious Diseases Society of America, the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care, the National Alliance of State and Territorial AIDS Directors, the National Association of County & City Health Officials, the National Association for Geriatric Education, the National Hispanic Medical Association, NMAC, the San Francisco AIDS Foundation, and the Society of Infectious Diseases Pharmacists.

“The Children’s Hospital Association is proud to endorse the EMPOWER for Health Act, which provides vital support for the pediatric health care workforce so children’s hospitals can mitigate staffing shortages and increase access to care,” said Children’s Hospital Association CEO Matthew Cook. “We applaud Senators Reed and Murkowski for championing children’s health through this legislation to reauthorize critical health care workforce programs like the Pediatric Specialty Loan Repayment Program, ensuring it incentivizes people to go into pediatric subspecialties where we see the greatest need. We look forward to continuing our mission to protect children's access to care and grow the pediatric workforce alongside our champions in Congress.”

Now that the bill has been approved by the HELP Committee, it must be considered by the full U.S. Senate.

title: Sens. Rick Scott, Dan Sullivan, Tommy Tuberville Introduce Bill to Create Secretary of the Coast Guard Position
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C.- Today, U.S. Senators Rick Scott, Dan Sullivan, and Tommy Tuberville introduced the Coast Guard Leadership Modernization Act. This bill would create a Secretary of the U.S. Coast Guard, mirroring a position across all other branches of the U.S Armed Forces. Currently, the Coast Guard lacks a dedicated civilian leadership position, and it defaults to the U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security.

Senator Rick Scott said, “The Coast Guard has a unique and highly specialized mission to protect our country from threats posed by smugglers, drug traffickers, terrorists, and other lawbreakers, and it deserves a service secretary to oversee and coordinate its operations, just like every other branch of the military. This bill creates a Secretary of the Coast Guard in federal law to ensure the Service has the leadership it needs to take on the challenges of the 21st century and beyond. This is a matter of readiness and national security; Congress should pass this immediately so President Trump can make his nomination, and the Senate can get to work on confirmation.”

Senator Tommy Tuberville said, “The men and women of the U.S. Coast Guard are critical to our national defense and security, which is why they deserve the same strategic organization as other branches of our military. Having a permanent Coast Guard Secretary will make the organization even more effective and enhance our national security. I’m proud to join this legislation with Sen. Rick Scott to give President Trump full authority to nominate a Secretary of the Coast Guard and further his mission of Peace Through Strength.”

Senator Dan Sullivan said, “I’m glad to join my colleagues in introducing legislation to provide even greater support and advocacy to our Coast Guard with a dedicated civilian Secretary who can represent the needs and perspective of the Coast Guard at the highest levels of our federal government. We rely on our brave Coast Guardsmen to monitor and defend vast maritime borders, execute life-saving search-and-rescue operations, respond to international crises, and support Department of War missions. No state is more aware of the important service of the Coast Guard than Alaska—home to more coastline than the Lower 48 states combined—which is why I spearheaded the largest investment in the Coast Guard in history in last year’s Working Families Tax Cuts Act.”

SCOOP:

Republican Senators Introduce Bill to Create Service Secretary for the Coast Guard

BACKGROUND:

Currently, all branches of the U.S. Armed Forces have a dedicated Secretary overseeing operations and representing the branch. However, the Coast Guard lacks an executive leader, creating confusion or delays in an organization responsible for protecting 95,000 miles of coastline and 3.4 million square nautical miles of the U.S. exclusive economic zone.

This legislation creates, in statute, a Secretary of the Coast Guard to run as the leader of the branch. Upon this bill becoming law, the President would have the authority to nominate a Secretary of the Coast Guard subject to Senate confirmation.

Full text of the bill can be found HERE.

title: Sens. Rick Scott, Marsha Blackburn Introduce Bill to Memorialize Victims of Communist Chinese Tyranny
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senators Rick Scott and Marsha Blackburn introduced the Honoring the Victims of Communist China’s Tyranny Act, a bill to create a permanent memorial in Washington, D.C. to honor those killed by authoritarian Communist ideology and the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) dating back to Mao Zedong. The memorial would be placed in a public park directly across from the CCP embassy in Washington, D.C.

Senator Rick Scott said, “Xi Jinping and Communist China are responsible for some of the worst human rights violations in human history. Those who are brave enough to fight back and speak up against them pay the price, like my friend, Jimmy Lai. Countless others have been forced into slave labor; some face torture, forced sterilization, organ harvesting, and other horrors. As Xi’s henchmen at the embassy walk into work every day, they should have to face the litany of crimes in which they’ve been complicit. The people of China deserve nothing less than the God-given liberty and unalienable rights America’s founders fought for 250 years ago. America should have zero tolerance for Communist China and its crimes.”

Senator Marsha Blackburn said, “The Chinese Communist Party is guilty of the worst human rights abuses imaginable, including genocide, brutal religious persecution, forced labor, and forced sterilization. Our legislation would honor victims of Communist China’s tyranny by allocating existing funds and donations to build a memorial that will ensure America never forgets the human cost of the CCP’s oppression."

SCOOP: GOP senators unveil move to memorialize communism victims on CCP's doorstep amid Dem civil war: 'No tolerance'

BACKGROUND:

The CCP is responsible for committing human rights atrocities, including genocide and persecution against ethnic and religious minorities, including the Uyghurs in Xinjiang. Many outsiders have expressed concerns about restrictions on political dissent, religious freedom, freedom of expression, and press freedom in Communist China.

A public memorial in Washington, D.C. would honor victims of persecution, educate visitors about these abuses, and reaffirm the United States’ commitment to human rights and individual liberty. Examples of events, campaigns, and episodes that could be referenced or reflected in the memorial’s educational elements include:

Mao Zedong killed at least 40 million people during his time in power.

Forced labor, forced sterilization, family separation, and other abuses against Uyghurs that led the United States Government to determine that genocide and crimes against humanity were occurring in Xinjiang.

The suppression of Tibetan religious and cultural practices, including restrictions on monasteries, language instruction, and expressions of loyalty to the Dalai Lama.

The 1989 Tiananmen Square protests and subsequent crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Beijing.

The imprisonment of democracy advocates, lawyers, journalists, and dissidents, including figures such as Liu Xiaobo, Xu Zhiyong, Ilham Tohti, and Jimmy Lai.

The crackdown on Hong Kong’s pro-democracy movement in 2020.

The persecution of religious groups, including underground Christian churches, Falun Gong practitioners, Tibetan Buddhists, and other faith communities.

Restrictions on freedom of expression, censorship of the press and internet, and the use of advanced surveillance technologies to monitor citizens.

The history of political campaigns under Communist Party rule resulting in widespread suffering (i.e. the Anti-Rightist Campaign, the Great Leap Forward)

title: Rosen Co-leads Bipartisan Bill to Better Support Families of Fallen Servicemembers
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – U.S. Senator Jacky Rosen (D-NV) joined Senator Tim Sheehy (R-MT) in leading a bipartisan bill to better support the families of fallen servicemembers. The bipartisan Honor Gold Star Families Act would double the death gratuity payment given to families of fallen servicemembers from $100,000 to $200,000, establish an annual adjustment to match the cost of living and inflation, and require the Department of Defense to publish the adjusted benefit amount annually in the Federal Register. The legislation will apply retroactively to servicemembers who lost their lives on or after January 1, 2026 – prior to the beginning of Operation Epic Fury. Congress created the military death gratuity in 1908 to provide immediate financial assistance to surviving family members following the death of a servicemember. However, the gratuity amount has gone unchanged for two decades, without accounting for inflation or rising costs.

“Our servicemembers and their families sacrifice so much to protect our freedom. The least we can do is support their families after they make the ultimate sacrifice, when they need us most,” said Senator Jacky Rosen. “This bipartisan bill will correct a failure to properly support Gold Star families by increasing the death gratuity payment and ensuring that it remains tied to inflation. No family of a fallen servicemember should ever have to go through the stress of not being able to make ends meet, which is why I will continue fighting across the aisle to support our servicemembers and their families.”

Senator Rosen has continuously fought to ensure that servicemembers, veterans, and their families have access to all the benefits and federal resources that they have earned. Recently, she introduced the bipartisan Sergeant Dave Crete FORGOTTEN Veterans Act, which would require the Department of Defense to join the Department of Energy in identifying all servicemembers and veterans who worked at locations where radiation and toxic exposure occurred and provide them with the same presumption of exposure, allowing such veterans to better access the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) healthcare and benefits they have earned. Last year, she also introduced a bipartisan bill that would allow medical providers to more easily practice for both the Dept. of Defense and the VA – addressing the medical shortage and ensuring care for veterans and servicemembers. Last Congress, Senator Rosen helped pass the Love Lives On Act in the Senate, which would have allowed surviving Gold Star spouses to retain their benefits upon remarrying before the age of 55.
